div.p: 0 THE ELECTORS OV RUNCORN.

LADIES AND GENTLEMEN.—I have to thank you for the honour conferred on me through your votes in returning me as a membenof the Eoard of Commissioners. It is highly gratifying to me to know that the support which I had solicited on Thursday last has been so co dially responded to.
I can only repeat the assurance I gave you in my address, that your interests shall always receive my careful atten- tion.
Again thanking you for the honour conferred on me, I remain, Ladies and gentlemen, Yours sincerely, BARTHOLOMEW MANGAN, ALE. 103, Church-place, Runcorn, 2nd September, 1892.

div.head: PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS.
div.p: PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS.

A SUITABLE dower for a widow is a widower. LAW is no barrier to a politician who smells government pap. THE irony of the law is shown when a blacksmith is condemned for forgery. MARRIED life often begins with rosewood and mahogony and ends with pine. THE kind of food which a hungry beggar most dislikes is the "cold shoulder." A COCKNEY conundrum: Why may bees be pre- ventative of smallpox? Because they are a kind of Waxy-nation. AN amorous swain declares he is so fond of his in that that he has rubbed his skin from his nose by kissing her shadow on the wall. THE MORTAL COlL.—Fashionable young lady detaching her hair before retiring: "What dreams may come when we have shuffled off this mortal coil I" "WHAT is the final end of manr asked a lecturer, and a small boy in the gallery answered, "The Ltter N." Wilar this country needs is a scientist who will invent a placid smile to be worn by women when they enter a street car and can't find a seat. PROFESSOR—"James, where is Fayal?" "Dunno." "George, can you tell?" " Yessir." "Where is it?" n the play of 'Richelieu,' where the Car- dinal says it ain't in a respectable young man's curriculum." NONE LEFT.—Take two letters from money, and there will be but one left. But when a dishonest carrier took money from two letters there wasn't anything left. A BOASTER claimed that he once senta challenge written in his blood to a man who had insulted him: "Oh, yes," sneered a by-stander, "of course you wrote it in your best vein." An old gentleman who had been intolerably annoyed by the hideous noises made by a drove of donkies, mildly asked: "Do not those creatures ever die of softeniug of the brayin ' ?" A MAN with a very large bald head was compli- mented on the fact that his caput was analogous to Greenland. "Why so ?" he asked. "Because it is a great white bare place," was the reply. "I WONDER why it is." said old Deacon Wimble, "that a man who's very much intoxicated is so apt to be melancholy-like." "I'll tell yon," said his nephew: "it's because he's more'n full." CLASSIC RELlC.—Another relic of the classio age has been found in Kent, England, being a dog's collar, supposed to have belonged to Julius Ctesar, from the tact of having his name engraved on it!

A FRENCH wit says that the gibbet is a species of flattery to the human race. Three or four persons are hung from time to time for the purpose of making the rest believe that they are virtuous. "AN UNLOVED WIFE," who ought to know of that of which she speaks, because see has so much experience, says that the reason that ladies look so much to money„ in the matter of marriage, is, that now-a-days they so seldom find anything else in a man worth having. "How many young ladies in Boston could run a mile at any pace that could. be called a run ?" asked William Blaike in his lecture the other night. Not many, perhaps. It would depend on the staying qualities of the horrid cow. Mn. YouNo, of Wabash, Minnesota, locked his wife in the house; Mr. Potts, of Pekin, Wisconsin, locked his wife out of the house,, and now both women are suing for divorce. t certainly is a difficult thing to please a woman. Miss DE Sii,vw (of Boston)—" Were you at the flower show, Mr. Largepurse?" Mr. Largepnrse— "No, Mies Mary. To tell the truth, I haven't taken any interest in geology since I left college. Awful bore, don't you think so ?" A KENTUCKY father and his little daughter had bad colds. The family physician said that " rock candy and whisky equally divided" would be good for the colds. The father got a supply of those articles and divided them equally, giving his little daughter all the candy and taking all the whisky himself. . _ _

"COME home, my son," said a parent to one who had been absent from home for some time; " come home, and your mother will kill the fatted calf for you." "Tell her not to do it, father," replied the offspring; "for I have lived on veal ever since I've been here. Tell her to kill a quarter of a pig instead." ENRAPTULUED young lady, gazing upwards, and addressing young newspaper man—" What a wen- ded ul thing is space I Do you ever feel over- whelmed by its immensity ?" Young Newspaper Man—" I should rather think I do; I have a column of it to fill every day." &Eats (Table d'hoto at fashionable hotel on Dee- side ; big market day).—Farmer of the old school has dined. Waiter—" Finished, sir ?" Farmer— " Fat's the charge ?" Waiter—" Five shillings, please." Farmer (startled) "Five shillings I Well, Bm 'me deen yet." (Resumes operations). A WOMAN cured her husband of staying out late at night by going to the door when he came home, and whispering through the keyhole, "Is that you, Willie ?" Her husband's name is John, and he stays at home every night now, and sleeps with one eye open, and a revolver under his pillow. A HARTFORD boy had always declined to eat oatmeal, although his mother had urged it upon him as a strengthening diet. Suddenly he sur- prised her by one morning eating a liberal plateful and calling for "more." When she asked for an explanation he replied: "I am bound to eat oatmeal till I get strong enough to whip Gregory Scott." MONEYED MAN—" Consent to you two being engaged to be married? But how can you, Richard, afford matrimony? A struggling M.D. does not always get R.M.D., and with regard to that, I have a theory--" Richard—" But I intend to have a practice, sir; and when that comes your daughter will be R.M.D.—‘ Ready to marry Dick' —won't you, Marian ?" She simply blushed and said "Yes," and so papa consented. IT is said that Bronson Alcott was one day hold- ing forth on the advantages of a vegetable diet, and urged the argument that if a man eats pork he will grow to look like a pig; the beef-eater like a bull, and so on. Whereupon somebody rather confounded him by drily adding—" Yes, Mr. All- eott, and he who confines himself to vegetable diet will be in great danger of finally resembling a very small potatoe." X. is dangerously sick in bed, and his wife and an intimate friend, who are watching at his side, try to divert his mind by a little conversation. "It is a delightful thing," said his friend, "to have so devoted a wife; it almost makes one want to be sick 1" "Go, and get married, then." " I have been thinking of it, and already have my eye on a certain widow." A widow !" exclaimed H. bitterly. "Am I so low as that, then ? " DR. PALEY was so enamoured of angling that he hobbled to the river's side in spite of his bodily infirmities to ply the line, and had his portrait painted with a fishing rod in his hand. Being asked by the Bishop of Durham when one of his great works would be finished, he answered naively, as if fly-fishing, and not philosophy, were the main business of his life : "My Lord, I shall work steadily at it when the fly-fishing season is over." " YOUNG man," said a stern old professor to a student who had been charf;ed with kissing one of his daughters—"young don't get into that habit. si;ou'll End that ug is liking eating soup with a fork." "LI So, sir?" asked the student. "Because, ans Ot cd the stern old pro- fessor, "you can't get enough of it." Two newly-fiedged physicians met the other day, and the following highly interesting conversation ensued :—" Ah I good morning, doctor." "G')d morning, doctor.' "And how are you to-day, doctor ?" "First-rate ; and how are you. doctor "I'm all right. Got a good case of meningitis a your hospital, doctor ? " Yes, come down alai take a look at it, doctor. Anything special op your way, doctor?' " Man fell from a scaffolding two days ago ; still alive ; may get over it. Pleased to have you call, doctor." " rhank you ; I will, doctor. Good day doctor." "Good day, doctor." WHEN a young gentleman kisses a young lady, she very naturally says, "Oh, Dick, tae idea I " And he, also naturally replies, " laN ; not the eye, dear; but the cheek, dear." \Ville,. Li perfectly true.

EVERY day of my life makes me feel more and more how seldom a I act is accurately stated; how, al- most invariably, when a story has passed through the mind of a third person it becomes, so far as regards the impression that it makes in further repetitions, little better than a falsehood; and this, too, though the narrator be the most truth-seeking vez4ain existence.—Hazothorne.

The best bag that I have heard of this year is that obtained by Mr. W. 11. Deacon and his party of 110 guns on hid Gang moor, in the Swaledale district of Yorkshire. They killed 341 brace of grouse, by driving, in one day.

Professor:Huxley is at present staying in North Wales,to.which he has paid two visits this summer. He is greatly impressed with Barmouth and the Merioneth seacoast. As often happens, it is said the poor Professor has been once again set upon by the tract distributor and asked about his soul.

It is at Manchester that Mrs. Kendal will produce the new play "The Wife;' which is the work of two American dramatists unknown in this country, but in great repute in the United States—Messrs. Mille and David Belasco. Mr. Belasco is a member of the same family as our Mr. David James, whose proper name is also Belasco.

The impending production of " The Lord's Prayer" at the Gloucester Festival recalls the fact that the passage in Dante's " Puriatorio," which has furnished Professor Bridge with his text, was done into English verse more than 50 years age by Mr. Gladstone. But it is not Mr. Gladstone's ver- sion in 4ferza rime that has been used by Professor Bridge, who has availed himself oci)r.Plumptre's well known transtation. e

The Countess of Clancarty (" Belle Bilton ") has established herself as a prime favourite in society in Ireland. At the Horse Show in Dublin last week—the great social event of the year—she was 'much admired and courted as she moved about among the thousands in the showyard at Balls- bridge with her husband, and was voted not only the best dressed but the prettiest woman present, which is saying a great deal in Ireland.

When our English Princesses are in the country, they show a good example to their subjeets in the simplicity and good sense sense of their dress., For instance, the Princess of Wales when at Osborne was often to be seen in the simplest of black serge gowns, with a grey silk blouse and black straw sailor bat with grey ribbon. The Princess Louise adopted the same simple style of attire while at Trensham, and indeed seemed to have succeeded admirably in freeing herself for a, time from the shackles of Court etiquette and formality.

The Lord Mayor has quickly responded to the public desire and opened a Mansion House fund on behalf of the widows and orphans of the men Who met their death in the Bridgend colliery disaster. Mr. Evans is a native of South Wales, born within a short distance of the scene of the calamity, which he visited only three weeks ago. The appeal which lie makes is of painful interest to himself. Appeals from the Mansion House for fund's to relieve the misery which great colliery accidents cause have been always liberally responded to. In the present accident over a hundred miners have perished, leav- ing three times that number of women and children without the means of support.

Mr. Arthur Aciand is the first ex-clergyman of the Church of England who has become aCabinet Minis- ter, though Sir William Marriott, who was also at one time a clerk in holy orders, filled the post of Judge Advocate-General in Lord Salisbury's first and second Administrations. Several other gentle- men who have taken advantage of the Ecclesiastical Orders Relief Act have been elected members of the House of Commons. Among them are the late Professor Thorold Rogers, who sat for South wark from 1880 till 1885; and Mr. A. Macdonald, the member for one of the diviaions of the Queen's County in the last Parliament; and Mr. Bowen Rowlands; Q.C., who has represented Cardiganshire since 1886.

• .1. -- In all the great wheat-producing countries of Europe there is an increase in this year's harvest, but England, as usual, produces less than in the previous year. The blight of landlordism always shows itself in the agricultural returns. It is not our crop that fails us; it is that the acreage under cultivation shrinks every year. The land under wheat and barley shows a decrease of one hundred and sixty-two thousand acres this year as compared with 1861. Cultivated land is constantly lapsing into its natural condition, and is used for pasturage only. The tillers of t' soil are deprived of em- ployment and seek refugp in the over-crowded cities. Farmers find that they cannot make a living for themselves and support the landlord in- cubus.

Mr. Charming's Parliamentary papers respecting the acquisition of land by rural sanitary authorities and County Councils Under the Acts of 1887 and 1890, does not tell us the expense, to w.hich the country has been put on account of these 'wretched abortions. But it is otherwise excellent in its clearness and exclusiveness. Rather less than one in ten of the rural sanitary authorities of the coun- try have put the Act a 1887 into. operation. The 1,126 adres of land have been acquited, and 2,733 tenants have been benefited. There has not been in in' these'a single case of 'compulsory purchase itself ! Four county councils have acquired eighty one acres of land,. svhich, has been let to seventy- six tenants I There is one case of compulsory pur- chase—at St. Faith's in Norfolk! So much for the boasts of the United Coercionists.

The Hon. Mary Hughes, Maid of Honour to the Queen, was the young lady whose luggage was treated with such scant ceremony by certain mem- bers of the criminal classes when she was atcually leaving Court at the cl.:se of her turn of attendance on this queen. She is the daughter Of Lady Florentia Hughes, daughter of the late Earl Of Ravensworth, and of Mr. Robert Hughes of Xinmel- park, in North Wales. The duties of a 'Maid of Honour are not very onerous. She is at Court only for some three months of the year,and,berprincipal tasks are to read to the Queen and accompany her Majesty for walks and drives ifs required. She 'big a companion, however, who divides-the work, arid the greater part of the day is her own. Life at Court is not exciting, but £3OO a year is a very good salary for three months' work. Miss Hughes's sister recently married General Wynne.

Lord llrassey has stated in an interview that be was never-askedlo be Lord Lieutenant of Ireland— notwithstanding the many rumours to that effect. lymay odd- to this information that there was never any question of appointing anyoae but Lord Houghton. He was Mr. Gladstone's and Mr. Mor- ley's first and only choice, and it is a mistake to suppose that he was selected merely because of his wealth. That Lord Houghton will make an admir- able Lord Li6titenant all vilio-biiiemet the brilliant young peer confidently believe. Young and hand- some, he has a grace of manner and an amiable frankness rare even among the cultured sons of the aristocracy. He possesses literary gifts of no mean order. He has produced a volume of poems worthy, Mr. Reid says, "in their grace, humour, and refine- ment of his father's son, and showing signs of a deeper insight into human nature than the world credited Monckton Milnes with possessing." Lord Houghton may be regarded as one of the coming men in the new Government.

At Vie Trades Congress meeting in Gle,.gow next week, opposition will be made to the re-election of Mr. Fenwick as secretary. Mr. Fenwick, as is well known, does not hold the same views on the eight hours question as the majority in the congress. but he has proved a capable secretary. Ilis position is that of an executive officer, and no objection has been urged to the way he has discharged his duties. The argument will be raised this year, however, that the secretary should devote himself exclusively to the work of the office (salary £l5O a year), and Mr. Fenwick is the representative of the Durham miners. Mr. Threlfall and Mr. Shipton, who was formerly candidate for the office against Mr. Fen- wick, will not, it is understood, come forward this year. Mr.Koir-Hardie and Mr. Fred Hammill will be the candidates in opposition to the present secre- tary. The former will be the more serious opponeht. He is the agent of the Ayrshire miners and the re- presentative pf the workers of South West Ham, but the rule urged against Mr. Fenwick that he holds two offices would not seem to apply to Mr. Heir-Hardie. The difference is that, while Mr. Fenwick only holds two offices, Mr. Hardie would in reality hold three.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 3, 1892.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 3, 1892.

opinion that the canal would be opened by the end of 1893. That was the date he (the chairman) fixed when he last addressed them, and he was glad to find that there was now a reasonable hope of that being carried out. (Applause.) They had to congratulate themselves that the Rivers Pollution Act had been amended, and they would not 'suffer to anything like the extent they had done from pollution during the past two winters. He believed the estimate of the executive committee, as far as could be seen at present, was an accurate forecast of what from their 'recent experience would be the cost of the undertaking. Personally he did not think it was safe to be without some additional margin. (Hear, hear.) He had heard a good deal about the additional estimates having arisen entirely from the miscalculation of the engineers. He thought, however, in justice to to the engineers, he should say they were not prophets, and for that reason they could not possibly foresee all the contingencies which had arisen. What an engineer had to do was to deal with those difficulties which must arise as they arose, and he believed their engineers had successfully done that. (Hear, hear.) The causes of the extra cost were floods, faults in the banks, and especially the rotten character of a 'great deal of the stone which they thought would have turned out well and good enough for building. That stone had not been at all satisfactory, and they had had to rent quarries and purchase stone to a viny considerable extent. The defective character of the working of the Ship Canal Act of 1885, for which the present directors were not responsible, had been the cause of endless litigation. It I was owing to that that the estuary works were only I finished in the fourth year of the work . instead of the second, and it was Always calculated ,that there would be two years' work after the opening of the length be- tween Easthim and the Weaver. ' That would bring them down to September, 1893. Therefore, he did not think they were so very far wrong, taking all the diffi- , cultiea into consideration. There was another cause of delay—the claims of the London and North-Western Railway Co. That company were approached as far back as November last year, but they declined to enter into consideration of any Bill until their claims were settled. They put off sending in their claims until the first I week in August, when, at a personal interview with re- sentstives of the Ship Canal Company,they made a claim for the first time for the doubling of their main line at Warrington, which was required by the clauses, of the Act. They had not yet sent in a complete formal claim in writing, and he did not think it advisable to mention the amount of the claim. He trusted the shareholders of the London and North-Western Railway Co. were not attempting to delay the opening of a great undertaking by any dilatory proceedings, but unless, the Canal Com- pany was met in a fairer spirit than hitherto the whole question must be submitted to arbitration, and the open- ing of the canal must° depend upon the decision in the case now pending betvken the London and North-wes- tern Railway Company and the Ship Canal Company. On the other hand., the Cheshire Lines Company had taken a more reasonable action. (Applause.) Be only trusted that the London and North-western Rail, way Company would follow their example. (Hear, hear.) The executive committee who had had charge of the work of the canal for the last nine months had done all they could. They had reduced a great number of the employes of the coin pally, in consequence of the approaching completion of the undertaking. Be might say that at the present time there were 9,222 men ployed, of whom 4,500 were on piecework, and the remainder under coritract, so that they were pretty equally divided. It was quite clear that a further con- siderable sum would be required to finish the canal, and I he presumed that the ratepayers of Manchester, who had 11 so nobly Come itaravard to support. the undertaking II originated by them, would carry it out and make it a I success. He felt confident that the Corporation, who had already done so t much for them, would not desert the shareholders at this critical time. (Applause.) The question for the ratepayers now to consider was whether' in 'contributing 1E5,000,000 to the canal they had ac: quired a share in that valuable property that was worth what had been spent upon it. He ventured to say that they had--(hear, hear)—and that the present works could not be does at it less cost than had been incurred. They appealed to the ratepayers 'of Manchester and the Corporation. It was for them to decide—and he thought they would—whether they would bear the whole of the burden, or whether they would associate those towns which were equally interested in the future of the canal, namely, Warrington and Salford. Additional works after the opening of the canal to Manchester had to be carried out for the special benefit of those towns, and also for the general benefit of the undertaking as a pay- ing concern. Those towns might take power to com- plete the portions in their borough on certain terms and conditions. Lord Egerton concluded by moving the adoption of the report and statement of accounts. Mr. J.K. Bythell, in seconding the proposition said his last word was "Be hopeful," for he was convince.d that the time would come when people would wonder how it ever could have been doubted that the canal would be a successful enterprise. (Cheers.) Mr. A. Forrest, speaking on behalf of many share- holders,joi ned in the hopeful tone of the previous speaker, but regretted that the tone of the chairman had been so apologetic. The attitude of the London and North- , weston Railway Co. towards the Ship Canal was male- volent, spiteful, and unjustifiable opposition. (Cheers.) He was speaking within hearing of some of the largest traders, who were the feeders of that great monopoly, and he thought that some immediate and personal rind influential representatien should be made to the directors of the railway company. He did not like to adopt a policy either of reprisal or boycotting ; but the time might come when, in self-defence, they weuld have to do it towards this company. (Cheers.) The best answer they could give to those whose faith was droop- ing, and the best answer they could give to Liverpool —a croaker and a pessimist from the first—was that the canal was three-part a made, and that if it took as much money again as had been spent to complete it, it would be completed. The report of the directors was adopted without further comment, and the meeting terminated.

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL.
SHAREHOLDERS' MEETING. LORD EGERTON ON THE PROSPECTS OF THE UNDERTAKING.

- The 14th general meeting of the Manchester Ship Canal Company was held on Tuesday, in the Con- cert Hall, Peter-st., Manchester, Lord Egerton of Tatton, chairman of the company, presiding over a crowded attendance of shareholders.

div.head: REPORT OF THE DIRECTORS.
div.p: REPORT OF THE DIRECTORS.

The report of the Directors for the half year ended June 30th was submitted. Under the head of finance the report states as follows :—The available borrowing powers of the Company have been reduced by £65,420. In the accounts for the half-year ended 31st December last the sum of £65,420 was added to the £1,812,000 previously stated to be the amount of the Company's borrowing powers Feated under the Act of 1885. The amount authorised by that Act was £2,000,000 but the Act of 1886, which gave the Company power to pay in- terest out of capital during construction to the extent of £752,000, provided that the borrowing powers of 1885 should be reduced by one-fourth of the amount so paid. As it was believed that the wkole of the £752,900 would be thus expended, the first mortgage debentures already issued were stated to. be part of a loan,of £1,812,009. The Act of 1891 annulled the 33ower to pay interest out of capital after 318 t December, 1890, and the total amount paid was therefore only £490,318. One-fourth of that, amount being only £122,580, it was assumed that the borrowing powers of 1888 could be used, to the extent of £1,877,420. Counsel has advised, however, that as the amount of the first mortgage has been stated, both on the face of the deeds and officially, to be £1,812,000, nothing in excess of that amount should be issued, and the £65,420 added in December has therefore been deducted. The available borrowing powers on the 30th June were as follows :
irst mortgage debentures, balances unissued ...... £287,400 Second mortgage debentures, balance unissued 369,600 New debentures (Manchester Corporation) balance unissued

11.216.500 The Directors regret to have to report that the new esti- mate shows that it will be necessary to take steps at once to obtain further Parliamentary powers to raise at - least £1,500,000 in addition to the capital already autho- rized. As there seems to be no prospect of obtaining this additional capital in the open market, the Directors intend to apply to the Corporation of Manchester for the further financial assistance necessary to complete the undertaking, upon such terms as may be ar- ranged. In the statement of the resources of the company the accumulated revenue of the Bridgewater undertaking, estimated to reach £330,135 by 31st December, 1893, the 2.500 acres of surplus lands, the plant, the 23,159 ordinary shares taken nVer from the contractor, and some unpaid calls, which together may be valued at about £1,500,000, have been excluded from the calculation, because those assets will not be available before the opening of the canal for traffic to Manchester. The statement which accompanies this report contains a complete analysis and explanation of the increase of £1,291,284 over the estimate of Ist September, 1991, of which the following is a sum- mary :
Works and equipments (including £.85,000 adeled for possible further work £556,285 Plant

Interest and general charges caused by the prospec- . tive opening being postponed from let March to 31st December, 1893 (interest £242,900), charges £28,640 27%540 Land and charges connected therewith Depreciation in value of shares taken over from the contractor 40,486 Expenses of issue of Manchester Corporation stock 32,200 Stamp duty, rents. to 26,355 'Parliamentary and law charges 10,693 Added for general contingencies
The report continues as under : CONSTRUCTION OF WORKS.

Since the last meeting a large portion of the works between Runcorn and Manchester, with the exception of the dredging, has been let by tender in four main con- tracts based on schedules of prices, the quantities of which have been specially verified by an independent surveyor. The short lengths of wall required to com- plete the ,Palford docks are now being built, and the remainder of the excavation is being taken out. The old river course between Manchester and Barton has bet n closed, and the Irwell has been turned through the Ship Canal. The deviation railways are nearly finished. The signals and junctions are being put in by the Ches- hire Lines Committee, and when these are Completed the lines will be opened-first, for,goods and aftemards for passenger traffic. The embankments in the estuary to enclose the works of the Ship Canal between the river Weaver an-the Old Quay Docks above Runcorn Bridge have been completed, and the excavation of the canal is now actively proceeding. To enable this work to be done the port of Runcorn has been temporarily closed; and the traffic diverted to the docks at Weston Point and wharves at Saltport.

div.head: TRAFFIC.
div.p: TRAFFIC.

It will be remembered that the Act of 1885 made it compulsory to open the lower portion of the Ship Canal from Eastham to the-River We-aver foi the accommoda- tion of the Weaver traffic before beginning the works around Weston Point. Although the Parliamentary traffic estimates of the promoter's did not include any revenue from this portion of the Ship Canal, the traffic. obtaluible there has necessitated the provision of wharves and jetties, which are being constructed at a 'place that the directors have named Saltport, near to the junction of the Ship Canal with the 'River Weaver, the Weston Canal, and the Company's Runcorn and Weston Caeal. Some traffic is already. coming there although the wharfage accommodation is not yet completed. AP .an indication of the volume of tonnage which the Ship: Canal is capable of accommodating, it may be stated that during the six months ended 30th June last 10,245 vessels carried 1,057,962 tons on the opened portion. rhis quantity included upwards of 600,000 tons of dredged material, and the greater portion of the remain- der consisted of salt and other traffic passing to and from the Weaver and Shopshire Nevigations, the bulk of which, however, under the clausee of the Act of 1885, is exempt from toll. The Chairman, in proposing the adoption, dwelt at length on the present aspect of affairs of the company. It was, he said, again his lot to tell them some unplea- sant truths. He was there to say , that in spite of the gloomy prognostications which they had seen in some of the London papers, he confessed he had never leak deepaired of the future of the Ship Canal tkan he did at the present time. Six months ago he laid before them a statement of the affairs of the company as far as it was possible to give it, apd the accuracy of that statement had never been challenged. He could not claim the gift of prophecy, and the information it was in their power to give bad resulted in a considerable addition to the estimated cost. Since December last the spending de,. partment, and the conduct of the works, had been under the control of an executive committee which was composed of a majority of the •corporation directors: Up to now they had let four contracts for the four sec- tions, and those had not, considering the magnitude of the undertaking,very much exceeded the estimates made by the engineers. The estimates had been exceeded, it was true, by £91,000, but that was the gross difference. The net difference was about £63,ooo—that was to say, the difference between the £63,000 and £91,000 included items which were not in the previous estimates of the engineers. Although they had not been able to let the whole of the work he was not at all surprised at the fact, because it was, he believed, impossible for any engineer or any contractor to fix a sum for such works as those in the estuary at Runcorn, without leaving so much margin that it would not have been proper for the Ship Canal Company to accept any tender for that work. The fact that • six months lapsed before the contracts were entered into was not the fault of the Executive Committee. They had done every- thing they could to facilitate the letting of contracts. but in a work of this kind, mixed up as it was in vari- ous stages of progress, it was 'impossible tei do all the measuring and to meet all the necessary requirements without taking. up time, and therefore, he was not at- oll surprised that six months had elapsed before the four contracts were taken up. With regard to the pre- sent state of the undertaking, the works were now approaching completion, except on the site of the existing railways and the estuary portion in front of the Runcorn Decks, and the dredging. The Salford Docks were being completed iancl,tho fouiadattens of the rail- way which was to run round the docks were being laid. The railways by which they expected to tap thia.South Yorkshire and Wigan coalfields were virtually finished., Wooden jetties in the Weston Marsh dock had been coen-' pleted for the Weaver trustees. That was an additional expenditure which was absolutely necessary, to comply with the requirements of the Weaver Trust. It would also be an advantage to the company, be- cause they would have the joint use of these jetties. They had also practically completed the jetties at Saltport, and they had been at once made use of, not only for the traffic of the canal itself, but a timber and salt traffic had already arisen which they believed would largely develop ,itself there. The jetty was an example of what. could be done along the whole length of the canal. In a few months an inex- pensive jetty could be laid, along which ships could be moored, and he had no doubt it would be made use of by traders. He believed this would prove a source of future remuneration to the company, and therefore they thought that money ought to be found to do works of this kind. His lordship then referred in detail to the dredging which had been done and was in course of being done, and also read the riport of the responsible officer under whom the dredging had been placed. The approach to Eastham had been dredged to a depth of 12ft. below the old dock sill at Liverpool. and the entrance at Eastham was exactly the sameas the present entrance of the Liverpool docks. i(Aloplause.) It was proposed to excavate to a depth of 20ft. At Ellesmere Port more than half of the estimated quantity of dredging had been done. The Weaver Pool had been dredged to 24ft., which depth would be considerably increased. The officer concerned in the dredging operations, Lord Egerton said, was of

div.head: ~...,. – – • ...- , EVIL'S OF GAMBLING. ' '
div.p: ~...,. - - • ...- , EVIL'S OF GAMBLING. ' '

Mr. Chauncey M. Depew, in a reaent interview concerning the subject of gambling, said "A con- siderable proportion of failures in business, and 90 per cent.of the defalcations and thefts among people who are employed in places of trust are due dir- ectly to gambling., It is the one vice which seems to destroy immediately -the moral sense and to oblite- rate that absolutely essential quality in employer and employe fldelity•to the trust, the violation of which destroys the violater. and ruins those who confide in him. I have seen so many promising young men led astray in a small'. way, and finally becoming fugitives or landing in the criminal dock, that I have come to believe that the community which licenses and tolerates public gambling can- not have prosperity, in business, religion in its churches, or morality among its people." This is not the language of a minister, but of a man of affairs, whose experience enables him to speak with authority and whose language deserves to be care- fully , considered. The sin of gambling consists in taking money from another without rendering an equivalent. Its danger lies chiefly in the irresistible fascination which it exerts over those who begin to practice it.

A WARRINGTON SERVANT STEALS 420. At Stockport Borough Police Court, on Saturday, before the Mayor (Colonel Turner) and other magis- trates, Fanny Harding;aged 14, of Warrington, was charged with stealing a cloak, umbrella, and .£2,0 10s.,`on June 4; from the Temperance Rotel, Wel- lington Road South, Stockport.—William Henry Simpson, the proprietor of the hotel in question, said about the middle of-May last prisoner came to the hotel for lodgings, and as she said she was looking out for a servant's place NtS. Simpson &waged her, without a. character. on June 4 prisoner left suddenly, and he then missed the cloak and um- brella and the motley. ,The latter was in half- sovereigns and was kept in a drawer in the kitchen. In reply to the prisoner's solicitors, prosecutor said the money was locked in the drawer, and he could not imagine how prisoner got the key to get at it, as Mrs. Simpson kept the key. He was not in the habit of leaving money about in this way as a temptation to servants. This money was withdrawn from the bank for a special purpose, for which it would have been used in a fe* days.—Mr.'Wood, of George-street, Black- pdol, pawnbroker, spoke to taking in pledge the cloak and umbrella (produced) from the prisoner.—On behalf of the prisoner, who pleaded guilty to the charge, it was stated that she and her friend* were willing to make all restitution possible to the prosecutor. The prisoner,after taking the money, bad gone straight to Blackpool, where she was apprehended, and in that town had taken apartments, and spent the money in that way and in the purchase of " finery" of various deseriptions,—Prison- er's sister was called, and, in reply to the Mayor, said prisoner had left Warrington about three or four months since.—The Chief-Constable (Mr. WE H. Jones) said there was a previous conviction at Blackpool against Prisoner, for stealing an umbrella and £3. In that case a fine was inflicted and paid. The Bench, after considerable deliberation, sentenced the prisoner to a, month's hard labour, without the option of a fine.—The prosecutor asked that the pawnbroker should hand to him the articles pledged.—The Bench, holding that the pawn- broker had exercised reasonable caution, ordered the transference of the property on prosecutor agreeing to refund the amount advanced.

div.head: lONIE,
div.p: lONIE,
PRIDE OF THE MILL
A THRILLING LOVE STORY BY LAURA JEAN LIBBEY.
CHAPTER IX. THE HEIRESS OF BEECHVALE.

From the moment lonie entered her uncle's home she was, he told her, entirely mistress of It; there was no appeal against her authority. Most girls of her age would have been too yonig for such a posi- tion, but lonie was older than her years.

It- was a marvellous change for her. Some young heads would have been turned by it: hers was not. She fell into the position so naturally that no one would have dreamed that she had ever held any other. Joule never forgot the beautiful sunny day that she first saw Beechvale, as her uncle's place was called. It was the suburbs of the great smoky city, on the very summit of one of the sloping hills. "Is this )3eechvale, uncle?" asked lonie, in awe, as the horses dashed up the white, serpentine drive. "Yes, my dear," he 'answered. "It is mine now. It shall be yours when I die." He looked at her keenly, and he was glad to see no elation come into the lovely young face. . .
"Mine I" she exclaimed. And a solemn sense of heavy responsibility came over her. Her face grew pale with emotion. She turned quickly and threw her white arms lovingly about his neck.

"I pray Heaven that time may be removed for many a long year yet," she said. And these words touched the old soldier's heart deeply. Though grand and stately, there was something wonderfully home-like about Beechvale. The rooms were light and lofty, full of sunshine, and from most of them there was an uninterrupted view of the immense green lawn that surrounded the house. The corridors were long and spacious. In the whole mansion there was not one gloomy spot; the window 3 were large, and the perfumed breeze from the garden seemed to sweep through the place. The garden was the colonel's especial pride—it was so quaint and old-fashioned; where one least ex- pected it, was some.flowery nook, seemingly made for t6tes tetes.
As the caniage passed through the entrance gate, a tall, graceful lady came out on the porch to welcome them.
"Who is she, uncle ?" exclaimed lonie, in wonder. "Surely not a relative 9 You have said you had no one in the wide world but me."

"She is Miss Carriscourt, who is to be your com- panion—chaperon—di:mime. She is no longer young in years, but you will find her a lady of great amiability and rare qualities or character. She consented to take charge of Beechvale while I was abroad. I have but just returned, you know. I have written to her, askiugher if she will remain as companion to you, and she has consented. I hope you are pleased with this arrangement, lonic 7"
"Any arrangements you may make are sure to please me, uncle," returneclithe girl, .impetuously.

Miss Carriscourt had expeciee to ;ee quite a different sort of person from the timid, young girl that the colonel handed out of the carriage; any, fear she might have had was dissipated at once. " She is neither affected nor vulgar," she thought. "I am sincerely glad of that, for Colonel Whitney's sake."

• She was struck by lonie's face. There was more than mere beauty; poetry, affection, and eloquence were in it. Yet, beautiful as it was, there was something in its expression which Miss Carriscourt could not quite understand. "She is not like other girls," she th,ought. "There is a restlessness in those dark, velvety eyes which bespeak an unsatisfied soul. I hope she is grateful to the colonel for what he has done for her."

The coming of Miss Lawrence, the heiress, as lonie was called, was quite an event in social circles far and near, as the colonel was sure it would be, and he had given orders that a grand lawn fete, ending in a ball in the evening, should celebrate the event, and at the same time introduce her into society. The affair had been in charge of Miss Carriscourt, which was a sure guarantee of its success; for in earlier years the lady had been a politician's daughter of great wealth, and an acknowledged belle. Their fortune was lost by an unlucky specu- lation, yet, rare as the case is, the lady did not lose social caste, even when she went out into the world to earn her own living by teaching, painting, and music.
Colonel Whitney considered it qhite a gracious condescension when she had consented to take

charge of his magnificeat home during his absence, and a still greater one when she decided to remain as companion to his niece. He had frankly ex- plained the true situation of affairs, and for that reason Miss CarrLscourt had expected to see quite a different sort of person from the graceful young girl who stepped forward so timidly to meet her. As Miss Carrhibourt predicted, the garden party, and the ball which followed, was a great success. lonie became the rage at once. People went into raptures over her. Some young girls would have been both elated and flattered over the sensation she created. She as neither.'

Some of the noblest men in the land bowed before her with well-chosen compliments, but the beautiful face never flushed—the beautiful eyes never brightened with triumph. Men were quick to perceive that she was not of the ordinary type of girls—that flattery did not touch her—that she was above all coquetry and flirtation. " The world of society is at her feet, Colonel," Miss Carriscourt said that night. "No young girl ever made a more successful dant." The scene was like a dream to Joule—a dream that never quite faded. The golden flood of light that made everything so elear and distinct, the thousands of lovely, fragrant flowers, the magnifi- cent decorations, the grand crashing of the music, the fair faces, the rich dresses; the subdued silvery murmur of laughter and of gay voices, the rhythm a flying feet, the admiring eyes that had followed her al. out, the deep voices that had whispered com- pliments to her, lived in her memory for years. No other garden party in after years was quite like this—her first one.

When it was over, the colonel was surprised to find that his niece looked quite as fresh and dainty as in the earlier part of the day. The flowers had not withered in her hand; there were no signs of 11 fatigue in the beautiful face, or of weariness in the dark eyes. "It has been a grand success, lonie," said the colonel, as he bade her good night—" one of which we may both be proud." "A grand success, indeed," she replied; yet even as she said the words, a sense of desolation and loneliness filled her heart. A little later she stood in her own luxurious room. Everything that surrounded her was costly, from the delicate carpet of velvet pile beneath her dainty, slippered feet to the pink and gold hang- ings, the choice engravings, and the treasures of marquetry and carvings and the lovely statuettes, that made the room a gem. lout° stood in the midst of it all, her heart beat- ing with emotion she had not yet been able to still. A success, indeed! Yes, it had been that. Bat was she really happy ? What were the vague desires that filled her heart? Her maid had gone away, and she stood alone at the window, watching the moonlight that lay white and cold on the sleeping flowers and trees. No girl in this world had a brighter future. What constituted happiness? she asked herself. Money and position? All, no! Even these could not satisfy. What was it, then? Some exquisite lines were running vaguely through her brain of the desire of a moth for a star. Was she the moth and happiness the star There must be a bright, beautiful something in life which she had not reached yet; something higher, better than rank, fame, or gold; something that was the crown bf life and the treasure of womanhood. The knowledge came to her in that silent hour that nothing in this world would ever content her but recovering the love of the noble heart which she had cast aside.
"What made the ball so dreary? Robin was not there. What makes life so weary? 'Tis to live without the love of Robin Adair."

Tonle repeated the words to herself. She had twisted the lines in a vague fashion to suit her own thoughts, and they expressed them eloquently. Yes, the whole world would be lonely to her now without the love of the fair-haired, handsome lover who had caught her heart in the rebound, and whom she bad sent away. She could not write to him that she had repented sending him away. Ah, no, no, she could not do that; yet how was he ever to know? She thought of the story of "The Fair Lily Maid of Astelot " and of her bitter plaint:
"And must I die for want of one bold word? I have gone mad.; hove thee; let me die."
lonie would never die for a lover like poor Elaine, yet e realised that Ole eQvlsl never care for any

one but 'A Iteehester, yet in all probability they would never meet igain. lie would never dream Of looking for the little working-girl whom he had loved and lost, among luxurious • surroundings, wealth arid fashion. , •

The next day the society papers spoke in great praise of the beautiful lonia Lawrence, the new ddbutante, naming in connection with the para- graph that she was sole heir to her uncle's millions. lonic could not withstand the temptation of marking the parogrAph atcl mailing the paper to Arthur Roche-ter. "Now he will know where I am," she thought. • . .

Bat, alas I the paper was not destined to fall into his hands. He had quitted the eity, telling himself, as the cars steamed out of the depot, that he would put the whole world between himself and lonie if he could, for he never vrinted to look upon her face iigain. And as the train whirled on through the darkness, he could not help thinking of that beauti- ful pathetic strain "Perchance if we had never met, I had been spared this vain regret; Ard yet I could not bear the pain Of never seeing thee again,"
CHAPTER R. " ELS MY LOVER'S HEART GROWN COLD r

Frank Lyoris's surprise and chagrin knew no bounds when be heard, through his friend, that Colonel Whitney had found his niece, and that they had gone on at once to the iron merchant's home in Pittsburgh. "How in the world did he find her?" he asked himself, in amazement. It seemed a wonderful mystery to him. "That is why she refused me. She found out she was a great heiress," be muttered, frowning darkly ; adding, under his breath: "Who would have thought that eirl.mercenary 7 I imagined, from, the•first, that she was greatly in love with me. "She was in love with me," he declared, pacing hurriedly up and down the length of the room. "Something or someone turned her, I actually believe."

A sudden thaught came to him. Why not follow her to Pittsburgh and begin his wooing all over again—with desperate earnestness this time? He put his resolution into effect at once. The next day he started for Pittsburgh, and the next afternoon he ventured to call upon Thole. He looked about the elegantly furnished room, with its velvet carpets and lounging chairs, its costly statuettes and bric-a-brac, with an odd smile. How different this magnificent room was to the shabby little attic parlour in which she was wont to receive him. Of course she would be robed in sweeping silks and ablaze with diamonds. Young girls raised from poverty to affluence and luxury usually were 'apt to be. He heard the soft rustle of silks, and rose expec- tantly. It was lonic. He had never seen her more simply' yet more becomingly dressed. She wore a simple, clinging, pale-blue cashmere dress, relieved from severe plain- ness by the lace frills a her dainty throat and wrists. She wore no ornament, and looking at her, he thought of the : Beauty unadorned is adorned the most." " lonie l" he murmured, holding out his hands to her. _ .

She affected not to see him. He drew back in apparent pained surprise. 'We parted in anger, lonic," he said, "but I could not bear it any longer. I have followed you because I cannot live without you. You have had a wondrous change in surroundings and prospects, almost incredible to understand; but hearts don't change, lonic. You loved me once. You cannot have put the old love entirely from you so soon, my darling." She looked looked.at him, with her proud, dark eyes, with all the dignity of a woman of seven-and- twenty, instead, of a girl of seventeen. It was diffi- cult, he felt, to be sentimental with her. And yet, those same dark eyes had once brightened for him; he once had the power to bring the rose-bloom into those dimpled cheeks. Her beautiful face was raised quite calmly to his. Her dark eyes were serene, as though utterly-uncon- scious that he had said anything extraordinary. "Yon do not speak, lonie," he cried. "Say some- thing to give me hope." She did not answer him, and the calm scrutiny of those lovely dark eyes made him feel extremely un- comfortable. , He came nearer to her. The sweet, subtle per- fume of the rosebud she held in her hand reached him. She drew back with a haughty gesture. "lonic, do not be unkind to me," he murmured. "Let me come nearer, where I may kneel at your feet and pray my prayer." His face fluslied, his heart warmed with the words. All the passionate love that he really felt for her woke within him. There was no feigning, no pretence. It was all reality. It was not her prospective fortune he was thinking of just then, but of lonie—peerless lonie. And in that moment he felt that he could give his whole life to win her. "Let me pray my prayer," he repeated; "let me tell how dearly I love you, lonic—so dearly and so well that, if you send me from you, my life will be a burden, and I shall be the most wretched of men. Remember," he continued, "I loved you before you were Colonel Whitney's heiress; always remember that." There was no tenderness in the beautiful face turned toward bim. It was all aglow with scorn, lighted with pride, flushed with contempt. "Say no more, Mr. Lyons," she said, quickly. "We will not discuss the matter. The answer I gave you when I parted from you was final. I am amazed that you have followed me here to repeat that distasteful scene. The past is past. You must understand that. You force me to say, once and for all, I would rather die than marry you, because I have neither liking nor respect for you. You will allow me to wish you good afternoon, Mr. Lyons." Before he could recover from his dismay she had quitted the room. He quitted the mansion with love and hate fight- ing a fierce battle in his heart. Was ever so splendid a chance lost? It drove him mad to think of it. All was due to the willful caprice of a lovely girl. He vowed to himself that he should not give up so easily; that he would vanquish her pride; that he would make her care for him again; that the proud, dark eyes should soften and brighten for him. lie gave his whole mind to the conquest. _ . _

Now that lovely lonic Lawrence was out Of his reach, manlike, Frank Lyons had begun to love her with a passionate love that frightened even himself. He followed her about like a shadow, mid the hope of winning her by fair means or foul was dearer to him than his very life.

"All this would have been mine," he often thought, as he reviewed the colonel's cast poszes- sions, "hut for the obstinacy of one girl." Curses deep and burning rose to his lips, yet, for his punishment, he loved her with a love that mastered him in spite of his hate; that made him long to throw himself at her feet, while he could have slain her for the wrong he considered that she had done him.

"My turn will come sooner or later," he told him- self, grimly. "Everything comes to those who know how to wait." He was obliged to see her sought by others, to see her admired, her praises on every lip. He placed himself in her way on every possible occasion; she avoided him when she could, bowing to him so coldly when they were brought face to face, that any other suitor would have given up the pursuit in despair. The colonel had no end of proposals for lonie's hand. When he mentioned the aspirants one after another, lonic would turn to him with a look so full of pleading that he would actually laugh aloud. "You will have to make an election some time, my dear," he said. "Unless you intend to be an old maid, and you wouldn't like that."

"I sho'uldnia mind," she replied bravely. "Better that than marrying for aught save love." "It would be a better world if all women held to the same opinion," commented the colonel. "By the way, my dear," he exclaimed one day at luncheon, "do you recollect young Arthur Rochester 7"

He did not understand the great stillness that came over her. "Yes, uncle," she replied at length, in a stifled voice. Did she recollect him 7 Was there ever an hour in the day in which she had been able to forget him "He is in Pittsburgh," continued the colonel, "and here under rather bad circumstances, too. It appears that the old millionaire has disinherited him, and now the young fellow is obliged to make his own way in the world. I met him last night, and he told me about it, and straightway on the spot I ciTercel him a position in the iron works as overseer." "And he—did he accept ?" asked lonic, breath- lessly. "Yes," returned the colonel, "and takes his position to-day. The young fellow has the right mettle in him. Such a fellow is bound to succeed." lonie came nearer to him, knelt on the velvet hassock at his feet, and looked up eagerly into his lac*

"Did he speak of me—ask after me' uncle?" she whispered, in a low voice, her cheeks all aflame. " No " he answered, so promptly that a new hope that had sprung up in her heart died instantly. "He must know that you are my uncle," she queried, "and the wonderful story of how you took me from toil and poverty to make me your heiress." " I spoke of it later on," returned the colonel, "but he was teo well-bred, of course, to make comments." From that hour the listlessness left lonie. Both Miss Carriscourt and the colonel noticed the heightened colour in her face, and wondered much at it. They never once thought of associating It with the presume of young Arthur Rochester. _ Sooner or later she would see him now, lonia told herself; and the thought brought with it the keenest delight. She would let him know, in some sweet, delicate maiclenly*ay, that she did not know her own heart when she sent him away ; and then— , ah I who knows what might happen then? Frank Lyons had said love could not die in a day.. To love once was to love for ever. Would this be so of Arthur Rochester What mattered their change of fortunes? She • had refused him when he had been the millionas son and she only a working girl. But now—if he should ask her to marry him now, though she was an heiress, and he but her uncle's overseer, he would not have to plead in vain. He knew that she was here. Would he call on• her? she wondered. A week of expectancy passed: She bad heard from Arthur Rochester only through her uncle. He had sent her no word, not even a line, acquainting her with his near presence. Has he learned to forget me so soon? she asks. herself. Is it with him— " Enough that we are parted; that there rolls flood of headlong fate between our souls?" she murmurs, as she, the petted heiress, the beueP for whose smiles men sue in vain, turns her dark, curly head on her sleepless pillow and sobs herself to sleep. Another week passed. Once, whence she was riding by, she had seen him on the street. HOZ. her heart leaped and throbbed What would thell meeting be like? she wondered. A thousand things occurred to her to say to him. He gave her no opportunity. With a deferential bow, raising, his hat, he passed her by. She leaned back in her victoria xvith something very like a sob on her lips. "You may as well drive home," she said to the coachman. " I—l—do not care for riding anY more to-day."
(To be continued.)

div.head: MINISTERIAL SALARIES.
div.p: MINISTERIAL SALARIES.

Nasty allusions to "loaves and fishes" are among the minor ills of life that self-sacrificing Public men are obliged to endure in silence. Their state of mind was adequately summed up by Mr: W. S. Gilbert, in "The Mikado," when be made Pooh-Bah say, "I mortify my pride continually: A Pooh-Bah paid for his oervices! I a salaried minion! But 1 do it! It revolts me, but Idoit 1" A little patient digging into the ordinary and easily accessible books of reference gives the information. If ane were asked off-hand to make a guess at the total, the result would probably be a wild shot, tens of thousands of pounds away from the mark. AS a matter of fact, A ROUND SUM OF £150,000 A YEAR. goes from the ins to the outs every time the Queen, on the advice of her beaten Ministers, hands over the seals of office to a new Government. This is exclusive of the Household appointments, and of the pot-boilings,and off-scourings represented by private secretaryslaips and other minor posts which consti- tute part of " the spoils." In the matter of pounds, shillings, and pence the Viceroyality of Ireland heads the list. The Lord-Lieutenant receives yearly salary of £20,000, besides a residence and allowance; but the expenses incidental to his office soon reduce this big figure. The Lord Chancellor of Entland and the Lord Chancellor of lrelaud are in better case. The former draws £lO,OOO with a pension of £5,000 while he is out of office— the latter £B,OOO. It will be :noted, indeed, that THE LAWYERS EMERGE TRIUMPHANT from the scramble. Thus, the Attorney-General for, England has a salary of .£7,C/00 coupled with "lees and the right to carry on private practice ; the Soli- citor-General £6,000; the Lord Advocate £3,238, the Attorney-General for Ireland £5,000 ; and file, Solicitor-General for Ireland 12,000. By side el these salaries the £955 which falls to the lot of the Solicitor-General for Scotland sounds paltry sail inadequate ; and it is a puzzle, too, why odd figuree find place in the remuneration of Northern lawyerl; Possibly some calculation based on pounds Scots as distinct from the English guineas, may lurk at the root of the mystery. The Chief Secretary for Ireland is another Minister who draws a salary with odd figures at its tail—namely, £4,425. But there is a princely allowance for coals ;" and one of the problems that once exercised crities,was how se frequently" absentee" Chief Secretary could POSSIBLY GET THROUGH SO MUCH FUEL Except on the hypothesis that he was unduly 14: Touring the Viceroy, Lord Londonderry, who ws• "in the trade." There is plain sailing when we come to the great offices of State. Here the salary: is uniform--X5,000 a year—for the First Lord 01 the Treasury, the Chancellor of the Exchequer, the Foreign Secretary, the Home Sebretary, the War 4' Secretary, the Secretary for the Colonies. and the Secretary for India ; but it seems somewhat of an ' anomaly that the First Lord of the Admiralty -- who ranks in public estimation as higher, if Or. thing, than the Secretary for War—should receiy.„E; £sooa year less. Coming to other Slinisters,X27 a year is paid to the Lord President of the Cool& to the Lord Privy.Seal,to the Secretary for Scotland, to the President of the Board of Trade,and to , dents of the Local Government Board and of AFT'''. • culture,while the Postmaster-General receives a year more. The offices named above comprise AN ANNUAL CHARGE OF X 98,425. n. Along the best-paid members of the Gover merit telow Cabinet rank are the two Secretaries ri the ; to the Treasury (the Patronage Secretary all- ; Financial Secretary), each of whom draws .E 2,000 ' but according to the English standard of paYmels neither can be called excessive, for the forraeT , alio chief Whip, and the latter is the chancellor ot the Exchequer's right-hand man. The Secretor); to the Admiralty, the Vice-President of the Coue.c! and the First Commissioner of Works also recVS £2,000 each. Coming to the lower grades, we e that the five Under-Secretaries for tile newt: Secretaryively • are paid o Xt hle,s Foreign, Colonial, India, and War Offices resPqo Vl7OO a r apiece; U ffic e to the Board of Trade and the L°,,ca, Government Board each receive £1,200. And Tung lower on the Ministerial ladder are the Civ,is Lord of the Admiralty und the three Junior 1401, of Treasury—Xl,ooo each, In all, these subordinco, offices absorb £50,000 a year; the Ilougehold changing with successive Governments, senrur £17,000 or £lB,OOO, and private sccretarysh ips £lO,OOO more. By comparison these private s. trtito taries come off badly--only £3OO a year fcr the best paid, and as little as £5O per annum for le, ill-requited gentleman who is at the heck and c of the Civil Lord of the Admiralty.

div.head: DISASTER.
div.p: DISASTER.

FORTY-ONE MINERS SAVED. • VISIT OF THE HOME SECRETARY. Contrary to all expectations, of the 141 men and boys entombed in the Park Slip Colliery, near Tondu, by the explosion on Friday, 41 have been rescued alive. The I work of exploration went on unceasingly throughout Friday night. r, The exploring party which went down at midnight OR he was under the superintendence of Mr. Davidson, Al 'e manager of the colliery. By dint of great labour tb. ey succeeded in penetrating to the No. 7 range, situated about 950 yards down the slant. They passed eleven bodies, ono of which was identified as that of Mi. Williams,the pit engineer,but made no attempt tO bring them to the surface, considering it best to pro- losed with the work of restoring the ventilation. That This was the wisest course was abundantly proved by subsequent events. The party did not return to swe surface till half-past five on Saturday morning. About half-past eight: o'clock a number of colliers were sten to emerge from the upcast shaft or horseway, and tba spectators standing round at first thought they were "some of the rescuers. The next moment a loud shout of 103' and welcome was heard, as the men were recognised +8 some of the survivors. They were eighteen in num- ber, and appeared to very little the worse for their twenty-six hour's entombment. They were conveyed to the carpenter's shop, where hot beef tea and brandy were administered to them by Dr. Edmund Thomas, of Bridgend, and others. Meanwhile messengers were despatched to the homes of the men to tell the joyful news, and very soon women who had given up all hope of ever seeing the faces of their husbands or sons again were seen hastening to the pit to welcome their loved "es. The scenes that ensued were of the most pathetic Character. With touching expressions of endearment the women frantically embraced their restored husbands with eioV that was uncontrollable,while tears rolled down the cheeks of all who witnessed the scene. The men were afterwards conveyed to their homes in brakes. Their aPpearance was entirely unexpected, and, in fact, only ,a .Short time before, Mr. Robson had telegraphed to the uotne Secretary that the entombed men were probably all dead.

div.head: TERRIBLE EXPERIENCES.
div.p: TERRIBLE EXPERIENCES.

..... ,The escape of these eighteen men buoyed up the hopes Of those whose relatives were still in the mine, and, not- Withstanding that the rain fell in drenching showers, the numbers around the mine entrance were hourly aug- mented. Mr. Jonah Jones toiled without ceasing to restore the ventilation in the inner workings, and event- ually he had the satisfaction of leading a party to the rescue of thirteen other of the poor fellows who were entombed. These were found in the No. 7 range. They were all suffering from the effects of the after damp, but after the administration of restoratives were able to walk out with assistance. In the course of their explorations Mr. Jones's party Passed fourteen bodies. One was that of Griffiths the Overman. They also saw a haulier lad with his foot cut off a little 'above the ankle. The brave explorers re- doubled their exertions, and it was with difficulty they fic.uld be induced to come to the surface to take a little _ . .

refreshment. Search parties penetrated still further into the levels and in the afternoon they came upon twelve men in the No. 7 beading; tbey were completely pros- trated, and unable to walk without assistance. Mr. Jacobs, the ex-manager, penetrated to the end of the main shaft, but everything was as silent as the grave ; he does not believe it possible that any more of the un- fortunate men could be alive. The explorers passed between thirty and forty bodies. MR. ASQUITH ON THE SCENE. The Home pecretary visited the colliery on Sunday. He weTA from Cardiff by special train, in which. there 4180 rode three directors of the Colliery Company— Messrs, R. Harvey, R. R. Lockett, and J. Waite. Mr. Asquith had a long conversation witliMr. Foster Brown, another director, and also with Messrs. Robson,Sims,and Lewis, Government Inspectors of Mines. The right hon. gentleman also examinei the machinery and apparatus above ground, and next had a consultation with Police- superintendent Thomas, of Bridgend. The survivors having had time td compose thamselves several of them were interviewed on Sunday. David Jones while sitting in his mother's kitchen, told of the Jones, he and his companions had made to effect their escape. He said his first intimation of the explosion Was the hearing of a loud rumbling noise like thunder, only very much louder. After the noise of the explosion, followed -by that of the numerous falls from the shock, had died away, the men tried to make their way through the drift, but they were compelled to rush back, owing to the presence of the after-damp. Six times did they Make unsuccessful attempts to gain their liberty. On ttie seventh they were rewarded for their perseverance. 'eked how they were off for food, David Jones said they ,Were all right irk that respect, but they had no wish for "um'. " You can see," he added, " that my box is full *tow..

div.head: MANSION HOUSE FUND.
div.p: A MANSION HOUSE FUND.

• In response to a request from Mr Hughes, a member cif the Glamorganshire County Council, the Lord Mayor has opened a Mansion House Fund for the relief Of the Widows and orphans of those killed in the colliery acci- dent at Tondu,and he'earnestly commends the appeal to dle benevolence of the public at large. Of the number of miners who were in the pit at the time of the acci- dent, 60 were married men with families, eight were married and without families, 45 were widowers or un- /Harried men, and 21 were boys.

div.head: QUEEN'S MESSAGE.
div.p: THE QUEEN'S MESSAGE.

•The following telegrams were received on Saturday night at the Tondu Colliery, Glamorganshire, the scene of the disaster on Friday morning. They were addressed to Mr. Robson, her Majesty's Inspector of Mines:—" I am commanded by her Majesty to express her deepest sYmpathy and condolence with all the sufferers from this terrible catastrophe, and her earnest hope that the gal- lant efforts of the rescuers may he attended ' with suc- oess.--131SCRETARY OF STATE, Rome Office."

OPENING OF THE INQUEST. The Press Association's special correspondent, tele- graphing from Aberkenfigen Monday, says that the only dsad bodies recovered from the mine are those of two 03's, who, being small, were more easily got over the 1411- It is hoped, however, that some mere bodies will oe recovered. The Home Secretary, before leaving, saw MN. Thomas, of Cefn, who has lost two sons. He is understood to have told her that when he saw the Queen on Friday, her Majesty asked him to tell the sufferers that she herself knew what it was to lose both husband and children. Mr. Cuthbertson, coroner for West Glamorganshire, ?Pennd an inquire on Monday into the disaster, and formally adjourned it for a month, pending further Investigations in the pit. Evans Hopkins has succumbed, making the sixth death amongst the miners brought alive from the pit.

RECOVERING THE BODIES. The Press Association's correspondent, telegraphing ;in Aberkenfig on Tuesday, says a large crowd is col- -Itotedat the mouth of the Park Slip Colliery to witness the bringing out of such corpses as have been discovered uP to the present. By eight o'clock 14 bcdies had been brought out. The corpses presented a ghastly appear- ce, most ot the poor fellows being terribly burnt and 'Alsfigured. Having been identified, the remains were enclosed in plain elm coffins for interment. The mani- festations of grief were-general. The work of bringing the dead out of the Tondn pit was continued on Wednesday. In the afternoon some qf the bodies were interred in the presence of great crowds in the churchyards of the locality. Another miner, whose name is not on the Company's books, is reported to be in the workings and his death brings the list of killed to 111. At a meeting of the owners of the mine on Wednesday thanks were given to the es. Diorers, who had rendered such gallent service, and ZlBO to the Lord Mayor of London for his sympathetic OP. The Directors voted £5OO towards the relief

A SIGNIFICENT DISCOVERY. Bridgend correspondent, telearaphing on Thursday Illght, says no additional bodies were raised on Thursday 4.nfternoon. The total number brought to the surface is uo• Of these 16 were raised on Thursday morning. On th,e bodies of the overman, and the man employed in 'asting, lamp keys have been found,and on a third man !hatches werefound. One man had been so shattered 7 the explosion that he could only be identified by bis c'thing. A number of interments took place on Thurs- ay at the district churches and chapels.
