div.p: MR. LABOUCHERE AND Td

div.head: QUEEN.
div.p: QUEEN.

In " Truth "this week is published the correspondence between Mr. Gladstone and Mr. Labouchere on the sub- ject of the latter's exclusion from the Government. The correspondence is published by permission, and commences with a letter from Mr. Gladstone, stating that he alone was responsible for the recommendations submitted to her Majesty respecting the tenure of OW- cal office, and that, while aware of the high position Mr. Labourchere had created for himself in the House of Commons, he has arrived at .the conclusion that there were circumMances in his case which rendered it unfit that he should ask leave to submit Mr. Labouchere's name for political office. Mr. Labouchere' in reply, stated that, while thanking Mr. Gladstone for the kindly tone of his letter, he had never asked directly or indirectly for any post in the Administration. Be perceived the difficulty of Mr. Gladstone's position ;and while he could not admit that the Sovereign had the right to impose any veto on the I Prime Minister selected to form an Administration, he admired Mr. Gladstone's chivalry in covering the Royal action by assuming the constitutional responsibility of a proceeding in which lie retained the conviction that Mr. Gladstone was not a free agent. Mr. Gladstone, writing from Hawarden Castle on August 25th, states that at no time, and in no form, has he had from Mr. Labouchere a signification or a desire for office, and states that he is in agreement with Mr. Labouchere that men in political office are servants of the country as well as of the Crown. The correspondence closes by an acknewledgement of this letter from Mr. Labouchere. The latter states that last week he proved construc- tively the fact of the Queen's Interference, and adds— "I now say in the most unqualified manner I know she interfered. Mr.eladstone is perfectly correct in stating that he did not ask my leave to submit my name to the Queen. It is equally true that my not having been asked to become a servant of the Crown was due to the Queen, and to the Queen alone." Mr. Lahouchere at- tributes her Majesty's action to his attitude on Royal grants and the ' Truth " Christmas number. In con- cluding, Mr. Labouchere states he is going abroad, and shall not revert to the matter again in "Truth." But of those who hold the official belief that the Queen does not interfere in the formation of a Cabinet he asks—Did not the Queen write a letter to Lord Rosebery, urging him to accept the post of Foreign Secretart in Mr. Gladstone's Government? Was this done because she thought Lord Rosebery would be likely to carry out Mr. Gladstone's avowed opinions in regard to foreign policy, and dia Lord Salisbury advise her to write the letter?

div.head: DARESBURY BREWSTER SESSIONS.
div.p: DARESBURY BREWSTER SESSIONS.
TUESDAY.—Before Messrs. J. C. Parr (chairman), W. Long, and H. Nield. SUPERINTENDENT'S REPORT. _ .

.... The Superintendent (Mr. Atherton) of the No. 10 Run- 'corn division, presented his annual report, which was as follows :—" I have the honour to submit my annual report with reference to the conduct of the, licensed victuallers in this division during the past year. There are 23 licensed victuallers, 2 beersellers, and 4 authorised to sell beer to be consumed off the premises, total 29, which gives an average of 326 of the population to each license. Two licensed victuallers have been proceeded against during the year, both of whom were convicted, ' against two proceeded against and two convicted last year. No beersellers have been proceeded against, none being proceeded against the preceding year. 41 persons have been convicted of drunkenness during the year against 50 last year. There are no applications for new licences. The Chairman said the report was satisiactory, especially in the diminution of drunkenness compared with the previous year. All the existing licenses were renewed with the excep- tion of that of John Kirkham, Hatton Arms, Hatton, who had been convicted during the year,and whose case I stood adjourned till next sessions. -- • -----

div.head: APPLICATION,
div.p: APPLICATION,

Mr. Jenkins on begifOlTl;;-.6hosters Brewery Co., Limited, asked the sanction of the Bench for alterations and extensions to the Grimsditch Mill licensed premises at Whitley, plans for which he submitted. He asked the permission as a matter of courtesy rather than law. The premises would be erected on the base of the old licensed premises; and the old tap room would be used for carrying on the business in the meantime. It was proposed to convert the premises into a really res- pectable house. The present ones were very old, and it was thought better to reconstruct than attempt to repair. There would be a front room, a smoke room, kitchen, tap room, and all conveniences; and stabling for four horses would be provided.—The Chairman informed Mr. Jenkins that the Bench had no objection, but hoped that decent accomodation would be provided during the alterations, as in certain cases alterations had taken too long, and the public had been a good deal inconvenienced through baying to put up with very indifferent premises.—The magistrates were assured on this point.

TECHNICAL INSTRUCTION, WIN WICK ELECTORAL DIVISION. The first meeting of the Committee for promot- ing technical instruction in the Winwick Electoral Division in the ensuing session, was held on Wed- nesday at the Bewsey Chambers, Mr. J. C. Sutton, C.C., chairman, presiding. The CHAIRM&N said that he had nominated the Com- mittee for the ensuing session as follows :—The Rev. Canon Penryhn° Winwick, the Rev. G. F. Roberts, Hollinfare, the Rev. A. M. Mitchell, Burtonwood, the Rev. H. I. Wadeson, Croft, the Rev. J. J. Langham, Padgate, the Rev. T. Myerscough, Martinscroft ; Messrs Dignum (Penketb), also acting as hon. treasurer, Foster (Penketh), Parker, (Peoketh), Skelton, (Great Sankey), Wm. Houghton (Paddington), R. Owen (Croft), James Warburton (Burtonwood), and B.C.Cooper ( Winwick.) _ "

The SECRETARY, Mr. Samuel Sutton, read his report as follows : GENTLEMEN,—I have thought it well at this your first meeting for the present session to submit for your con- sideration a brief report of the work done during the last Session. I propose firstly to deal with the different sub- divisions seriatim. Those gentlemen who formed last year's Committee will remember that difficuties were experienced in making anything like a satisfactory start, principally owing to the fact that no definite informa- tion could then be obtained as to our mode of procedure. In some of the sub-districts the inhabitants were very apathetic, as to the formation of Technical classes, pro- bably from a want of information upon their purpose and character. However, a commencement was effected hy the opening of classes at Penketh and Sankey, followed in rapid succession by Fadgate, nixton, Orford, Win- wick and Croft. Earnest effort was made to form classes at Burtonwood, and it is to be regretted that the effort proved unsuccessful. It is to be hoped that this Session the inhabitants of •Burtonwoo,d will avail themselves of the privileges now again offered to them. Before completion of of the Class work in the last Session, Mr. J. A. Bennion the Director of Technical Instruction for the County of Lancaster accompanied me in a round of visits to the different centres to have an interview with the teachers. He was, I believe, satis- fied with the progress made in each centre in so short a time. I informed him that we looked forward to the sphere of the classes being extended in the next Session. Mr. Bennion, I am informed, is preparing a general report in book form, a copy of which report will be sent to me for your use. I believe it is contemplated to con- tinue the classes already inaugurated with the exception perhaps of the singing classes at Padgate; and with the addition of such other classes as your Committee may deem desirable, due regard being had to the amount allowed to us to expend in something like an equal dis- tribution in the various centres. Upon the question of Finance, I may explain that a considerable sum in excess of that expended was allocated to our use. It was then, as it will be now your desire to avoid any waste or frittering away of the fund. The general fund was thus benefitted by your economy, yet the sums again allocated to your use are limited to those fixed for the last Session. The maximum amount is £220 with an additional grant of £35 under the head of cookery. Mr. Dignum, of Penketb, kindly undertook the duties of Honorary Treasurer and he will no doubt consent to continue his services. The sums expended in the several centres were as contained upon the annexed statement. From an official circular I shall read to you, it will be seen that the County Com- mittee require a complete scheme of the work proposed and estimated cost thereof, on, or before, September 10th. I suggest that a sub-committee be appointed for each centre to draw up such a scheme with the assist- ance of the teachers and myself. Yours obediently, SAMUEL SUTTON.

The Secretary then submitted his financial statement from which it appeared that the sum of £145 had been paid by the County Council, and had been applied in the various centres for the maintenance of the following classes, viz :—Cookery, agriculture, arithmetic and mensuration, geometry and drawing, dressmaking, instrumental music and singing. These subjects will again be taken up with the exception,perhaps,of singing. It is probable that an Ambulance Class will be formed at Padgate, as such a class promises to be successful. The following gentlemen were appointed a pub-Committee for the purpose of drawing up a scheme for the coming session for stibmission to the County Council :—The Revs. Canon Penrhyn, G. F. Itoberts, H. J. Wadeson, A. Pd. Mitchell. MessrS. John Dignum, William Houghton, Charles E. Parker, Jonas Foster, and the Secretary.

div.head: EXAMINvp. S vriv-RDAY. SFPTEMBER 3, 1892.
div.p: THE EXAMINvp. S vriv-RDAY. SFPTEMBER 3, 1892.
nil NCO RN MUSICAL SOCIETY
ANNIJAL MEETING.

The annual meeting of the members of Runcorn Musical Society, was held in Bethesda Lecture Hall on Tuesday evening. There was a good attendance. lir. Joseph Littler was voted to the chair. The Secretary, Mr. R. W. Pierpoint, read a letter of apology for non-attendance from Mr. J. Brundrir, J.P., the president, who was away from home. The Secretary read the report as follows :-I have the honour to present to you the report of the fourth season of the Society's working. The vice-presidents for the season just closed numbered 106, which is an increase on last season of 14, which I hope will be considered very satisfactory, and is a proof of the good work done by our treasurer, Mr. Frith, who takes all the vice-presidents under his special care. When I come to the singing members I am sorry I cannot report so satisfactorily. Last season the chorus numbered 121 voices, this season only 96, a decrease of 25. This is a matter that will require full consideration by the Society. For the past season the Committee placed before you a costly and good programme,consisting of three concerts,all of which passed off successfully as regards arrangements, with the exception of the misunderstanding which arose with Mr. Bantock Pierpohat for the" Creation " concert, and for which full explanation and apology have been made. The first concert consisted of the Foil Concert Party and was the miscellaneous concert of the season. The " Staburt Mater " was the work given at the second concert with items by the band principals and chorus for the second part ; and the last concert consisted of the Creation with band and principals. All the concerts have taken place in the Public Hall, the acoustic proper- ties having proved to be not so deficient as was at the time considered. To meet the large demands for seats in the body of the hall the Society purchased 50 chairs, which has obviated the necessity and expense of hiring. I have only to notice that during the season the Committee had to be called together to specially consider the falling off in attendance at rehearsals, and they passed a rule limiting the number of rehearsals a member should attend before being eli- gible to sing at the concert, but which was revoked for the " Creation." This will be a matter to be fully con- sidered by the society. I can only hope and trust that a remedy will be found to bring about a better state of things with regard to the chorus. In closing this report, I have to express my thanks to all those who have given me assistance in the many arrangements that have to be attended to, and it is my earnest wish to see the society continue to grow and prosper, so that it may still more diffuse in the future than in the past, that in- estimable blessing of good music adequately rendered which is the great object for which the society exists. (Applause.) The Treasurer (Mr. W. B. Frith) read the statement of accounts, which showed the receipts to be as follows :- Balance brought forward, £1 is. ; subscnptions : presi- dent, £1 is. ; 104 vice-president, £lO9 4g.; 59 lady mem- bers, £8 17s. ; 37 gentlemen, £9 ss. ; total subscription £l2B 7s. ; further donations, 13s. ; receipts of first con- cert, £2B 4s. 6d. ; 2nd concert, £l6 18s. 6d. ; third con- cert, £2O 17s. ; total receipts from concerts, £66; half profit on sale of programmes at concerts, £1 Bs. 6d. ; bank interest, ls. 10 ; total receipts £197 11s. 4d. The following items make up the expenditure Adver- tising 7s. flIcl.; general printing £5 18s.; purchase of chairs £9 7s. 6d.; hire of piano £4 10s.; postages, &c., £2 Os. 3d.; carting, dr.c., 10s.; donation to Volunteer Corps £1 is.; Parr's Banking Co. cheque book 55.; ex- penses first concert £53 2s. 5d.; expenses second concert £57 18s.; expenses third concert £59 2s. 2d.; balance in Parr's Bank £3 10s. 6d.; total £197 lie. 4d. The out- standing accounts amounted to £7 55.-Mr. Frith said since last season he had removed from Runcorn, and it was not his intention to seek re-election.-Mr. W. Jones moved, and Mr. F. Scott seconded, the adoption of the , reports, and both gentlemen expressed regret at the announcement made by Mr. Frith.-The motion was carried.-On the proposition of Mr. Rogerson, seconded by Mr. R. Fryer, a vote of thanks to the officials and Committee was carried unanimously; the names of the conductor (Mr. E. Wynne Humphreys), the secre- tary and the treasurer being specially mentioned. The next business was the appointment of officers, and the Chairman said before proceeding to do this, perhaps it would be wise be take the feeling of the meeting as to continuing the Society. That meeting did not seem very encouraging.-Mr. Rogerson said it would be a crying shame if the society were allowed to drop now.-1 he Chairman : I like to hear you speak like that.-Mr. Rogerson said they bad beard of Runcorn disease, and it seemed to threaten that society.-Mr. W. B. Firth said It would be a great pity to let the society cease, and to test the feeling of the meeting he proposed that the society continue.-Mr. Humphreys said unless there was some motion that the society do not continue he thought It would be unwise to entertain a resolution of that kind. There was a capital meeting, and if such a resolution went to the public it would appear that there was a desire to break up the society.-Mr. Frith withdrew his motion, remarking that he had made it in order to get on with the business.

Mr. John Brundrit was then unanimously elected president, on the motion of Mr. W. B. Frith, seconded by Mr. J. E. Meredith. The vice-presidents were re-elected en bloc, and the Committee were given power to add to the number. - -

Mr. Davies(Widnes)Moved, and Miss Crosby seconded, the re-appointment of Mr. Humphreys to the position of conductor, and the motion was carried unanimously. Although pressed to again became secretary, Mr. Pierpoint definitely declined, and a number of other gentlemen were praposed for the office, but they refused the proffered honour. Eventually Mr. F. Scott and Mr. J. Booth agreed to take the office jointly. The same difficulty arose with the appointment of treasurer; not one Of the gentlemen proposed would accept the position, and at last Mr. Harry Wright, who was not present, was appointed. The appointment of librarian was the next business, and Mr. R. Moore declined to again accept the position. After a pause Mr. Hutnphrevs said after the apathy manifested in that meeting, he did not see much hope of continuing the society successfully, and he must ask them,amongst the other officers, to find a new conductor.—Mr. Scott said the lukewarmnesss displayed did not justify them in carrying on the society. He certainly did not understand from the position of the society,why there was thus want of interest. There was a good balance sheet. He did not feel disposed to give his services, seeing that there was an intention to shirk the society.—lt wits eventually decided to adjourn the meeting until Tuesday evening next, to fully consider the matter.

div.head: BOATING FATALITY. THREE MEN DROWNED.
div.p: BOATING FATALITY. THREE MEN DROWNED.

Three men were drowned on Wednesday- while going down the Tweed in a boat. The river is flooded by the heavy rains. The names af the drowned are Wm. Allan, and Jamos Allan (father and son), and a lad named Robinson. Another occupant of the boat, named Darling escaped.

div.head: DANGEROUS EXPLOITS OF LADS.
div.p: DANGEROUS EXPLOITS OF LADS.

At the Warrington borough ,police Court on Mon- day before the 'AI ityoil (Woman Greenell) and Alderman Francomh, George Gleare, 55, Bralker-st., and Philip WYteherley, No. 38 in the same street, very little boys, aged 8 and 9 respectively, were charged with removing, on the 19th inst., a sprag from the wheel of a truck belonging to the Cheshire Lines Committee, with intent to upset and injure the same. Mr. P. Davies prosecuted on behalf ot the Cheshire Lines Committee. Mr. Davies said the offence was a most serious one. The complainants had a num- ber of, waggons laden with iron in their siding which was on an incline that ran into Bewsey Forge. The waggons were spragged, and the prisoners tres- passed on the siding, climbing a wall to get there, and with extraordinary strength 'had loosed the the waggons, and sent one of them smashing into an- other waggon, and broken the axle box. They had done other damage which it would cost the Company £2 to repair. The waggons might have run into Bewsey Works and killed half-a-dozen men.—Thomas Davis, a shunter, said he placed sprags in the wheels of all the waggons, and the sprag of the first waggon broke, and he pinned the brake down.—John Cotterill, aged 10, said he saw the prisoners pull the peg out of the wheel of the first waggon, and release the waggons.—Gleave said he did it in play, and Wytcherley that he did it in mis- chief.—Alderman Francomb said he was afraid it was a case of imitation of what they had seen bigger boys do. —They were fined 53. 6d. costs, and ordered to be punished also with six strokes of the birch rod.—John Wm. Kelly 33 Guardian-St., and John Whittaker, 1, W ake- field-st-, both little boys, were then charged with a like offence in the case of waggons spragged on a siding of the Cheshire Lines Committee which runs into White- cross Works.—Mr. Davies prosecuted on behalf of the Cheshire Lines Committee in this case also, and said that in this case the defendants had not only unspra,eged the waggons but had had the audacity to ride on them, a most dangerous thing to do ;the siding being on an incline.—The tads pleaded guilty, and were fined 6s. costs each, and sentenced to six birch strokes,

THE RIXTON BURIAL GROUND QUESTION.—Tho Clerk stated that he had now obtained the signature of Mr. Davenport, of Widnes, who is an owner of property near the proposed new cemetery at Glazebrook, and who was said to object to signing any document to show that he did not object to the construction of the cemetery. The Clerk also read a communication from the Local Govern- ment Board stating that Mr. William Shaw, of Rollin- fare, had written mentioning the names of diree or four of the residents who had not given their sanction to the , making of the cemetery. The Clerk said he had gone ' over to Hollinfare, and they had now all given their con- sent. _ .
THE ESTIMATE OE EIPENDITUP.E.—The Clerk submitted an estimate of expenditure for the coming half year, and said a rate of a fd. in the £ would meet the expen- diture. .

A DILAPIDATED " Pun."—The Inspector reported that the Ram's Read hotel, at Grappenhall was in a very dilapidated condition and unfit for habitation. The thatch let the rain through, the floors were rotten, the walls damp, and the roof at the bar propped up in two places.—Mr. Long said it was a pity the magistrates had not that information before them at Daresbury, on Tuesday when licenses were granted.—The Clerk said the police should have known the condition of the public house.—ln answer to a question, the Inspector said the Ram's Head belonged to Messrs. Greenall, Whitley, and Company.—The Chairman thought it would be better that the Surveyor and the Medical , Officer should visit the place and report to the next meeting of the Authority.—The Clerk said he would also write to the owners.—Mr. Long thought the police were to blame in not bringing the condition of the house before the magistrates.—There were sufficient grounds for stopping the license.—The suggestion of the Chair- man was then agreed to.

div.head: ACCIDENT TO MR. GLA.DSTONE. ATTACKED BY A MAD COW.
div.p: ACCIDENT TO MR. GLA.DSTONE. ATTACKED BY A MAD COW.

Mr. Gladstone was the victim on Monday after- noon of an extraordinary accident. On Thursday week a farmer on the Hawarden estate bought a young cow at Chester fair,and the animal turned out to be almost wild. It gave great trouble to its owner from the first. Finally, growing more infuriated by restraint, it managed to break loose and to escape into Hawarden Park. Repeated efforts were made to recap- ture the animal, but it got into a wood, from which no device could coax or drive it. By some extraordinary oversight no notice seems to have been given at the Castle that such a dangerous intruder was at large wit in the park. On Monday afternoon (not Tuesday afternoon as originally reported) Mr. Gladstone and Mrs. Gladstone went for a drive in the park, and in accordance with a not unusual practice of his Mr. Glad- stone left his carriage with the intention of walking back, Mrs. Gladstone driving home alone. Quite unattended, he strolled along one of the cariage-drives, and had not proceeded far when he came across the escaped cow, which was lying quite near the roadway. Mr. Gladstone stopped to lock at the animal, which suddenly rose to its feet and furiously charged him. Mr. Gladstone, taken completely by surprise, was unable even to step aside, and he was knocked down by the animal. He retained his presence of mind, however, and seizing the first favourable opportunity, regained his feet and succeeded in getting behind a tree. In this position he would have been fairly safe in any event, but as it happened the animal made no further attack, and finally ran off at top speed. Luckily for Mr. Glad- stone, the beast's horns were turned in such a way that goring was next to impossible, and he escaped uninjured. He drove out later in the evening, apparently none the worse for his adventure, and on Wednesday attended church. The cow was shot by Mr. Torn Bailey._

In reply to inquiry at Ilawarden Castle on Wednes- day night it was stated that Mr. Gladstone was quite well and telt none the worse for his unfortunate experi- ence. A report circulated earlier in the evening to the effect that the cow had also attacked another member of Parliament turns out to be incorrect. The person attacked was a local resident named Peter Connah...

Mr. Henry Gladstone states that Mr. Gladstone on his return to the castle made no reference to his adven- fure, and it was not until about three hours later that a casual remark by a member of the family that there was a mad cow in the park induced his father to give details of the affair. Twenty-five men were subsequently engaged searching for the animal, which was eventually shot. Mr. Henry Gladstone said his father had suffered no ill effects whatever, and that he treated the whole affair very lightly.

FIGHTING IN AFGHANISTANT.

A Simla telegranh announces that the Afghan troops have recaptured Kamsan, out of which the Amer s troops were recently driven by the Hazsras. The vic- tory is descrbed,•however. as having been somewhat dearly bought, the loss of the Ameer's troops being estimated at 460 killed.
THE GAINSBOROUGH POISONING CASE.

.At the Gainsborough Police Court, on Monday, Alexander Morgan, fish hawker, was charged on remand with having wilfully murdered Tom Morley, a Hull grocer, by administering strychnine on August 18th. The prisoner, being duly charged with wilful murder, .made no reply, and Mr. Page, for the prosecution, de- tailed the charge; saying that Morley, Morgan. and a woman named Booth were drinking in the Newcastle Arms, Morley then being apparently in his ordinary state of health, but at 7.25 he was taken ill, and at eight o'clock he was a dead man. An hour afterwards they found Morgan making statements about what had taken place, in the course of which he said that he had given Morley some medicine, and he did not think that he would want another dose. Mr. Page went into details as to the conversation between the prisoner and people he met, all of which tended to the belief that he had given something to Morley which he knew to be poison. Prisoner was remanded again.

div.head: TERRIBLE COLLIERY EXPLOSION IN
div.p: TERRIBLE COLLIERY EXPLOSION IN
BELGIUM.
TWENTY-FIVE MINERS KILLED..

FRAMERIES, TRURSDAY.—A telegram received here states that an explosion of fire-damp occurred to-day in the Agrappe coalmine. 25'miners were killed and eight seriously injured. BRUSSELS, Tamansy EVENlNG.—Complete details are now to hand of ,the disaster lb the Aggrappe colliery, and fortunately the number of lives lost has been reduc- ed, but not by many. The actual number of men now ascertained to have been killed is twenty-five, but the search gangs found eight miners alive, and, without delay, sent them to the surface. They are so grievously injured, however, that the majority of them are not expected to recover, so that the total casualties are prac- tically only seven less than was originally telegraphed to here. The Aggrappe pit is owned by a company in which the Rothschilds are the principal shareholders. Whether it will be reopened for operations, or whether the company will be ahle to induce the men to once more brava the perils of this particular mine remains to be seen. As stated in my previous despatch, the colliery is of a very dangerous description, being always more or less permeated with firedamp. This, of course, is suffici- ent to account for the long series of disasters, the two most appalling, I now find from authentic records, occurring in 1875. when 121 lives were lost, and 1879, when the pit claimed 123 victims.

div.head: VIE WEAVER WATERILEN'S STRIKE.
div.p: VIE WEAVER WATERILEN'S STRIKE.
RIOTOUS SCENES NEAR WINSFORD.

On Thursday night intense excitement prevailed all along the Weaver upon it being known that a disturb- ance had taken place at Meadow Bank, near Winsford. In consequence of the decision of the salt workers not to load vessels manned by non-union men, the Salt Union was compelled to enegag other men to do the work A special train containing about 200 new hands who had been brought from Liverpool arrived at Newbridge Salt Works on Thursday afternoon, and were met by several Salt Union officials and a number of police. the men were then marched to Meadow Bank, and in crossing the river at Newbridge Locks encountered a large picket of the strikers. A severe struggle immediately occurred. The fight,it is stated, was commenced by one of the new comers, who drew a large knife and exclaimed, " Here's for the first man that steps up." All the new comers brought with them their beds, bedding, and other kit, and in the mhlie much of this property was thrown into the river. Stones were thrown and belts used, and some difficulty was experienced by the police in quel- ling the disturbance. About this time Mr. W. James, a Salt Union official, in returning from Hartford station, passed the locks, and drove through a shower of brickbats and clinkers. He was struck on the temple and stunned. He was then conveyed to the Salt Union offices at Meadow Bank, where he remained until he recovered. Shortly after the disturbance the steamers Lady Delamere and Australia, which were being worked by non-union men, entered the locks, and the men were asked by the strikers to leave the vessels without any disturbance. This they did, and they were marched off to Winsford station, where their fares to Liverpool were paid for them. On Thursday a deputation, consisting of the secretary and five members of the River Weaver Watermen's Association, had an interview with Mr. Thomas Ward, 1 one of the directors of the Salt Union, when the question of hours and other grievances were discussed. The men submitted a statement to Mr. Wara for the acceptance of the directors showing how the craft would be worked under the system proposed by them. One of the clauses in the statement was to the effect that no craft should be engaged shiftingslocks two nights in succession, and if the craft had already worked one night in going down to Liverpool, she was only to shift docks one night. Nothing was decided, and the matter now stands over. A large crowd assembled on the Town Bridge, North- wich, on Thursday afternoon, as the steamers Lady Delamere and Australia were seen coming up the river in charge of non-union men. The men on board were hooted, and in the excitement that prevailed they ap- peared to lose all control over their vessels,and the Lady Delamere stuck fast under the bridge. Some damage was done to the bow, and half an hour elapsed before the vessel was released. The Australia also caught the bridge, but sustained no damage. The crowd followed the steamers up the river to Barrow's Lock, where there was another hostile demonstration, which was suppres- sed by the police.

OBJECTIONS TO RENEWALS.-THE MAGIS- TRATES AND BACK DOORS._ _

div.head: OBJECTIONS TO LICENSES.
div.p: OBJECTIONS TO LICENSES.

The Chief Constable informed the magistrates that he objected to the renewal of licenses to all persons men- tioned in the black list, both beer-sellers and publicans. Mr. J. P. Mearns, who appeared for Mrs. Marsh, of the Sefton Arms, asked if the bench intended to deal with all such cases at the adjourned sessions. If so, there would be no necessity for him to address their worships that day.—The Chairman said that had been their prev- ious custom, and they should do so en the present occa- sion.—Mr. J. 0. Swift said that he appeared for several tenants in a similar position to that of Mrs. Marsh. The convicted persons did not now hold the licenses which had been regularly transferred by magistrates at special sessions with their eyes open. He submitted that the bench could have no legal ground for refusing renewals of the licenses under such conditions. Where new tenants were now in the houses under proper transfers, he maintained that the bench, as a matter of law, fairness, and right, could have no valid reason for adjourning the considera- tion of such renewals, and he ventured to protest against such adjournments unless some valid objection was made to the renewals.—The Chairman said the us- ual objections would be served upon those concerned.— Mr. Swift : But objections cannot now be served. The objections must be made to-day. They ought to have been made seven days ago if any objections were to be made, but the Act of Parliament gives your worships power in cases where no written objection has been served to hear any objection raised to-day and then ad- journ upon that objection.—The Chairman said the Bench were adopting the usual course.—The Clerk: I think the Chief Constable had better state his objections to the renewals.—The Chief Constable then read over the list of convictions during the year, and said he ob- jected to the renewal to Mrs. Marsh on the ground that there was no necessity for the house—Mr. Mearns : Is that the sole reason? The Clerk : That is quite suffi- cient.—Mr. Mearns: Quite sufficient for what ? The Clerk : To adjourn it, sir.—Mr. Mearns : But I object to that.—The Bench intimated that Mr. Mearns would have an opportunity of raising the question at the ad- journed sessions. The Chief Constable objected in the case of Andrew Moody, Plicenix Inn, Eccleston,on the ground that there was no necessity for the house, and made a similar ob- jection in regard to Thomas Whalley-, of the Bowling Green Inn.—Mr. Swift : But Whalley does not apply for the renewal.—Chlef Constable Wood said the license had been temporarily transferred to another person. He objected to the renewal of Mr. Griffith's license for the Bridge Hotel, Liverpool-road, as there was no necessity for the house. He also objected to the renewal of the licenses to William Davies, Oddfellows' Arms, Parr, and Thomas Banks, Ship lon, Blackbrook. Further, he objected to the renewal of the license of the Live and Let Live, Parr, on the ground that the man Mulligan,to whom it had been temporarily transferred, had failed to carry out his promise to the Bench to devote the whole of his time to the manage- ment of the house.—Mr. Swift submitted that the Bench had no power to refuse the renewals of licenses to the Live and Let Live and the Lion Inn, Windle, on the simple ground that the houses were not necessary.—The Chief Constable remarked that he opposed the granting of renewals to the Lion Inn, Bridge-street, and to the Canal Vaults (James Rigby). He also asked the magistrate to strike off the list the beerhouses known as the Pig and Whistle, Bridge-street; the Bowl and Skittle, Parr-street ; and an off license in Pocket Nook- street. The Pig and Whistle, he said, had not been used for a beerhouse for the last twenty years, though a license had been annually granted.—The Clerk: There is no application for its renewal to-day.—The Chief Con- stable said the Bowl and Skittle now belonged to the Society of Friends, who had given instructions that no more drink was to be sold on the premises, and the off. licensed house in Pocket Nook-street had not been used for three years. He also drew the attention of the bench to the fact that Mr. Charles Gallic held a full victualler's I license for premises in Market-street, but that the house was not used as a victualler's house.—Mr. Swift said when Mr. Gallie's license was first granted an expla- nation was given as to the use to which it would be put. The Chairman said the bench had decided to adjourn the consideration of all liceenses to which objection had been made until the adjourned sessions on the 26th 3f September. The renewal of the whole of the other licenses would be granted, and the applications for new licenses would be heard by the licensing justices on Wednesday. The magistrates had asked him to point out to the publicans of the town that it had lately be- come a practiee to place signs with names of public- houses over back entrances. Such back doors had been objected to by many benches throughout the country, and they had been talked about in St. Helens more than once. The bench desired him to say that they objected to these back doors. They would pot this year, at any rate, refuse any license on account oh the back doors, but they thought that the name of the public-house should not be put on back doors. There were several objections to the practice, one of ttiern being that it was prrctically creating another public-house. Very often back doors were in another street and could practically be made into another public-house. The bench were not prepared to deal with the matter this year, but they wanted publicans to consider in future whether they were or were not prepared to do witlisut the advertising of those back doors.

div.head: NEW LICENSES REFUSED.
div.p: NEW LICENSES REFUSED.

The annual licensing sessions for the borough of St. Helens were resumed on Wednesday, when the applica- tions for new licenses were heard. The magistrates on the bench were Colonel D. Gamble (in the chair), Alder- men Bishop, Harrison, and Coik. Dr. Gaskell, and Mr. A. Sinclair. There was again a good attendance of the Nonconformist ministers of the town. Before the applications were proceeded with, the Rev. R. W. Ayres (Baptist) asked if the bench would receive a memorial protesting against the granting of any new licenses. He had bee.; asked by the NLinconformist ministers to present such a memorial.—Mr. Mearns,who , appeared for one of the applicants, objected to any me- morial being received unless evidence was given on oath 11 in support. It had never been the custom in that court to receive any petition.—Mr. Ross Brown (barrister) : I would remark that it is usual for gentlemen who object to give their evidence on oath.—Mr. Mearns : Generally a memorial is not taken as an objection .—The Clerk said that if the memorial was formally handed in the bench would receive it.—The Chairman It will be read when we come to consider the applications.—Mr.Mearns I take it that the magistrates will only read it if evi- dence is offered on oath, and not otherwise.—The Rev. R. W. Ayres: I understand that the memorial would, be taken as evidence.—Mr. Mearns This Is very irre- gular, when an unprofessional gentleman argues with the bench.—The Clerk : If you come here to oppose on oath any specific application, the magistrates will hear you. Beyond that the magistrates cannot go. The first application was one by William Owen, 45. Rigby-st., provender dealer, for a full license forthe Peel Arms Hotel, at the corner of Westfield-at. and Water-St. Mr. R. Brown, barrister, instructed by Mr. R. W. 11. Thomas, appeared for the applicant. Mr. Brown ex- .

plained that both he applicant and his wife were o excellent cuaractet, and tad had a great deal of experr ence in zlei nseenn nt of licensed houses. The Peel Arms was for tnatly yearn a fol 3 -licensed house, and was situated in au important thoroLighfare of the town. Up to fiVt• years ar.,i) it was well ciniducted, but about that time it. ens in the hands of a tenant who miscon- ducted himself, and in consequence of that misconduct the bench had refused to renew the license. The offence —that of betting—was one affecting this a.ersonal char- acter of the teomit, arid not that of the owners, who got aid of hini at the first cpportunity. By the refusal of the license the owners of the house had lost about £3,000, and he hoped the mni•trates would think that sufficient punishment had already beeu inflicted upon them for an effence committed by a man ever whom, at the time, they had no control. The proposed new tenant was a man of irreproachable character, and if the request was now granted the owners were willing to surrender the licenses of two houses at Parr—the Blacksmith's Arms and the Live and Let Live. The Peel Arms would be used as a high-class restaurant, where dinners, teas, and other refreshments could be obtaiued,and not as one of the modern gin palaces, which were considered so ob- jectionable in large towns.—Mr. Owen, the applicant, and Mr. Alfred Wilcock, owner, gave formal evidence in support.—Mr. Thomas Pringle,rag,ged school missionary, Opposed the application on the ground that there were already four or five licensed houses in the immediate neighbourhood,and if the additional license was granted the drinking facilities would te increased and he should be hindered in his missionary work. He had found that out in years gone by. and he was proving it every day.—Mr. Brown suggested that mere matters of opinion could not be evidence.—The Clerk said that evidence as to the number of licensed houses was being given.—Mr. Pringle said that drink was already hinder- ing him in his work.—ln answer to Mr. Brown, he said he did not think any of the licensed houses in the neigh- bourhood were used as restaurants.—Mr. Brown : You can take it from me that they are not. I :ake it from the tenor of your remarks that you think there are too many licensed houses generally in St. Helens.—Mr. Pringle: I believe there are too many in this particular neighbourhood.—Mr. Brown: If two licenses were taken away from Parr, would it not be a good thing for that part of the town ?—Mr. Pringle : But not for this locality. Mr. Brown : Then your pillion- throphy only extends to your own particular loca- lity ? Mr. Pringle: In this instance. The Rev. William Tingle, pastor of the Primitive Methodist Chapel and Schools, Westfield-street opposed on similar grounds In reply to Mr. Brown, he said he had only been living in the town for six weeks--Mr. Browne: And after that lengthy experience you don't know the character of the houses? The Rev. W. Tingle: No.—Mr. Brown: Have you ever been in one? The Rev. W. Tingle: No, I have not.—Mr. Browne: Do you consider that the same mis- chief arises from a well-conducted restaurant as from an ordinary public-house ? The Rev. W. Tingle: Well, it depends whether they are well conducted.—The Chair- man intimated that the bench would give their decision after hearing the other applications. Alderman T. C. Wilcock, for whom Mr. R. W. H. Thomas appeared, applied for an off-license for the Phcenix Brewery, Packer's Hill-road, Sutton.—Mr. Thomas explained that Mr. Wilcock already held a wholesale license for the premises, and as he proposed to enter into the bottling business be desired to have a license for selling beer in less quantities than he was at present permitted. If the application was granted he would enter into an undertaking not to sell less than one dozen bottles at a time—Alderman Wilcock gave formal evidence, and said it was not intended to do any" jug" or private business of that kind. There was no opposi- tion to the application. Thomas Jenkins, represented by Mr. .1. P. Mearns, applied for an off-license in respect to the provision shop at 75, Charles-st. Mr. Meams said that a great deal of building was going on in the locality, and during the last two months so less than 47 houses had been erected. The nearest licensed house was 300 or 400 yards away.—The Rev. W. Efolrnyd, minister of the Central Baptist Church, Hall-st., opposed the granting of the license as he thought the district was sufficiently supplied already. His spiritual work would be very much hindered by the placing of another licensed house in the neighbourhood.—ln reply to Mr. Mearns, he said he was opposing the application both on his own behalf and on behalf of his congregation. The feeling of his congregation was unanimously against the proposal. The Bench retired, and were away a quarter of an hour. The Chairman then intimated that the applica- tions by Mr. Owen and Mr. Jenkins would be refused and that by Mr. Wilcock, respecting the Phoenix Brew- ery, would be granted on condition that not less than One dozen bottles of beer were sold at the time.

div.head: RHYMES FOR THE PEOPLE.
div.p: RHYMES FOR THE PEOPLE.
No. 4.—THE BARMAN. 0 hard indeed is the BaWnan's lot,

Poor servant of Beer and Gin; He may be out of the fold of grace, But who cares, or asks him in The parson supports the liquor trade, And praises the Liqumr Lords ; But for the serfs in the " Tied " brigade He has neither looks nor words. And the men who say,. ".Thy Kingdom Come,"
And by cheques would heathens —save, Pass over the darker souls at home, . _

And over the Brewer's slave. Nor is it his lord that grinds him most In liquordom's cruel way, But some working-men whose aim and boast Is an eight-hours working day. For sixteen hours out of twenty-four, In a loathsome atmosphere, They tax his strength, and his patience more, In meeting their calls for Beer. From room to room he must rush along With the foul and madd'ning, swill, While his ears are stunn'd with drunken song,

And disorder louder still. And sometimes, too, when he fain would try To allay the wrangling mob, A bruised limb or a blackened eye. Vi'ill reward the thankless job. On the Sunday morn, in coach and pair, '` Beer" rolls to the house of God; But his weary henchman seeks fresh air, Or rests in "the land of Nod." And when evening bells to warship call, He resumes his "Sentry Go." To supply strong drink to great and small, For the Law will have it so. For six blessed hours of Sunday night, He reaps of the worker's spoil, And turns them out in a wretched plight, Unfit for the morrow's toil. And these things are done that "Beer" may rise, And shine in the Church and State; Accursed indeed by poor men's cries, But blessed by rich and great! We urge a Strike: 'tis a proper thing, A power in this Christian age: E'en holy priests have a holy" Ring" To uphold. their cloth and wage. Then Barmen Strike, with a solid stroke, For a life like ether men : Yea, tear off the Brewer's horrid yoke, And By from the Brewer's den. For his swills are poison drugs conceal'd In the Drink shop's flashy things; And 0, what a crop of death they yield, Wherever his Signboard swings'
MYRA.

div.head: SHOCKING WIFE MURDER IN CI7MBE RLAND.
div.p: SHOCKING WIFE MURDER IN CI7MBE RLAND.

On Monday at the Whitehaven Police-court, Georp Bruce, collier, Sandwith, near Whitehaven, was charged with murdering his wife on the 26th inst., by fracturing her skull with a garden spade.— Constable Beattie stated he found the body of Mary Jane Bruce, prisoner's wife, lying in their garden at Far Preston How. She had a large wound on the right side of her head. He appre- hended the prisoner at High House, Sandwith, and on charging him with murdering his wife, prisoner replied. "Oh, it is a bad job. I did it. It was all through jealousy." Prisoner was remanded.

THE EXAMINER,
SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 3, 1892.
THE proceedings of magistrates Licensing at Brewster sessions are naturally Reform. .

directing public attention to the need of reform in our licensing laws. It is felt to be a most anomalous thing in these days of repre- sentative government that a matter which so largely affects the well-being of the masses should still be left to the, control of men who cannot be said to be in any way representatives of the masses. It is a matter of course, therefore, to state that one of the chief clauses of the licensing bill which the present Government are pledged to lay before Parliament will provide for some representative body having the direction of licensing business. There are some who argue that such powers as are now exercised at Brewster Sessions should be handed over to Town Councils and County Coun- cils; but it seems to us that the duties of those bodies are_ithady_sufficiently responsible and complex with-out an addition of a most re- sponsible and most complex kind. The issues at stake are so large, socially, morally and materially, as to warrant the appointment of a special board, as has been done in the matter of education. This Licensing Board would be limited and directed in it operations by the At of Parliament which brought it into being; and it is about time that the people of this country entered upon a discussion of the new bases of operations. It is not sufficient to say that the ratepayers must have the benefit of Local Option; that is essential, but some- -thing, in addition; will-have- to be settled as to the principle upon which the number of licensed-houses shall be Leduced. It is gener- ally conceded that one licensed house is fully sufficient for eiary 1,000 of the population. This was the proposal which was, we believe, em- bodied in the Bill prepared by Mr. Bruce in 1871. The reduction would necessarily be gradual; and due notice would be given ; but there would be no such thing as expendingmillions of the ratepayer's
or taxpayer'smoney in compensation. At present there are 124,000 public-houses and beerheuses in the United Kingdom; and upon the basis of Ito 1,000 inhabitants the number would be reduced to 40,000.

But what about those that are left? Are they to he the more firmly entrenched in their monopoly, and reap profits which, relatively to the number of houses, will be enormously increased? These are questions which are now being frequently put, and the issues which they involve require to be care- fully considered. Whilst we believe that drunk- enness will be largely reduced by largely reducing the number of licenlied houses, we are still of opinion that something more requires to be done. If the drink trade in the fixture is to become more and more of a monopply,why should not the State, or the Municipality, have the benefit of the profits of that menopoly,instead of letting them be pocket, ed by individual brewers? And,, what is of even More moment, why slipald not the whole business be managed in such a way as to discourage drink- ing to excess? These are laudable objects,and they caa. be secured if the 'people of this country make up their minds to deal with the drink traffic on what is known aa the Norwegian system. This means, that in each town, licensed houses, after being reduced in numbers, would be managed by Companies who would receive 5 percent. and no more for the money they had invested, while the profits' would be applied as the Municipal. ity or State might direct. In Norway the profits are applied in ming pecuniary • • ak

grants to the funds of deserving charities, benevo- lent societies, philanthropic institutions, or other objects of public utility and benefit, which are dependent for their existence on the voluntary support of the public alone." It is a modest estim- ate that in towns like Warrington and St. Helens the net profits of the liquor trade are £50,000 annually. But there would be less profit when there was less drinking; and if it be assumed that the amount realised would be only half the sum named, say £25,000 a year, it will still be seen that it would provide an annual fund which would be the means of enriching and beautifying the town with p:cture galleries, parks, baths, libraries, and other noble institutions. How much better all this than allowing a Greenall, or a Walker, to become "rich beyond the dreams of avarice," and at the expense, too, of the degradation of the community! The chief merit of the Norwegian system—and we cannot too strongly emphasise it—is that, whilst it proves so profitable, it tends in m remark- able degree to lessen drunkenness by lessening in every way the temptation to drink to excess. As an ounce af fact in such a matter is worth a ton of theory, we hasten to add that in Norway, under the operation of the new system, "the consump- tion of spirits was,between 1876 and 1887,reduced 50 per cent." Surely a similar ftesult is worth striving far in this country. Ignorance is, we suspect, the parent of indifference in this matter; and, by way of assisting in the removal of both, we should be glad to open our columns to the discussion of this important subject. If there are lions in the path, let them be faced, and, if need be, fought.
THERE has been another meeting The . of the shareholders of the Manches-

ip Canal. - ter Ship Canal Co., and another report of the state of the work; and the cry is still that more money is wanted. The three Millions advanced by the Manchester Corporation are swallowed up, and it is now obvious that some- thing like two millions more will be required. There are explanations, in abundance,of the causes •of the extra expenditure; but the shareholders have got tired of these explanations, and are get- ting dispirited if not despairing. The outlook for them is certainly a dark one at present, as the interest upon borrowed m oney will of course have the first claim upon the revenue to be derived from the underaking. Still, there is a grain of comfort in the statemmit of thE Chairman at the meeting, on Tuesday, that he had "never less despaired of the ultimate success of the Ship Canal than at the present time." This means that, notwithstanding the fact that the cost will be more than double the original estimate, nothing has happened to inter- fere with the original prospects as to revenue. On the contrary, the growth of traffic in this part of the country continues to be great, and there are signs in abundance that the canal will be made ample use of for traffic purposes. The construction of the new railway across the coati try, with its terminus at Warrington, is in itself evidence that there are investors in other parts of England who have faith in the under- taking as a highway of commerce. With regard to the difficulties which have still to be encountered, there is at least this to be said, that the original Board of Directors has the benefit now of the experience of the able and energetic men who have been added to the Board, as representatives of the Corporation of Manchester. Granted that the requisite money will be provided—and Man- chester has gone too far in this direction to turn back—it is still just possible that the Canal will be open for traffic by the end of 1893. , Amongst the difficulties which involve uncer- tainty as t the ultimate expenditure may be mentioned the cost of dredging the estuary por- tion of the canal in front of Runcorn Docks. It would seem, too, that the London and North- Western Railway Company, either from negligence or design, are interfering by their delays with the completion of the railway deviations. Indeed, the opinion is abroad that the Railway Company have shown themselves troublesome, ratter than helpful, to the Ship Canal Company; so much so that it was hinted at the meeting, that, unless a change took place, some of the Ship Canal share- holders, who are merchants, might take it upon themselves to retaliate upon tbe Railway Com- pany. Reference was made to Warrington and Salford as tmvns at witich additional works had to be made, when the Canal was completed; and the Chairman remarlied that these towns might take upon themselves the power to complete these works in their• boroughs upon certain terms and conditions. It has been sug- gested by Mr. Mo Nits, CAI, that Warrington docks might be constructed by the Corporation of Warrington, or that a trust might. be formed for that purpose. Already the matter has been placed before the members of the General Purposes Committee, but nothing has as yet been decided upon. Need we say that it will be necessary, in the interest of the ratepayers, to proceed with the utmost caution? In the first place, all requisite information and estimates must be procured, and the project must be thoroughly discussed by every section of the community, before any decision is come to as to what shall be done. Warrington cannot afford to make any mistake in a matter of this kind, in view of the large expenditure which must ere long be incurred in the widening of Bridge-street. Still, if it can be demonstrated that it would, in the long run, be to the interest of the ratepayers of Warringten to have these docks in their own bands, they will, it is to be hoped, be equal to the occasion. This much is certain, that the Ship Canal Company must not be permitted to set aside their undertaking to com- plete the docks in Warrington within three years of the opening of the Canal.

Charles Wilson, alias Peters, was remanded at Edinburgh Police Ccurt, on Wednesday. on a charge of being in possession of jewellery for which be could not satisfactorily account. He attempted on Tuesday to pawn part of the jewellery in Edinburgh, and was banded over to the police. • •• The marriage of Miss Frances Kean, second daughter of Mr. M. Kean of Mercer-et., Newton, with Mr. Samuel George Walton, D.D.S., of Middlesboro', was solemnised at St. Peter's Church. Newton, on Tuesday afternoon, the Rev. J. W. Johnstone, being the officiating clergy man. There was a large number of spectators in the church, and the bride looked very pretty in a dress of grey velvet, with hat to match. Her bridesinaids were Miss Florrie Kean and bliss Annie Naylor, who were attired in dresses of cream cashmere and bats to match. Mr. E. Leyland acted as best man, and the bride was given away by her lather. The presents are fairly numerous, amongst them being a handt some silver cruet presented by the choir of War- grave Church, of which the bride was a member. The newly wedded pair left Newton later in the' evening for Saltburn, where the honeymoon will be ,spent.

div.p: RUNCORN TONIC SOL-FA CHOIR. The annual general meeting was held in Ellesmere- street schoolroom on Monday evening last and there was a good attendance of members. From a musical point, the season has been one upon which the society may con- gratulate themselves,but from another important point of view" finance" it is to be regretted that every concert has proved a loss to the society amounting in all to about £l2. This season,however,the society intend to make a bold bid for the patronage they have long been so welt deserving of. It has been decided to give Judas Maccabreus and the Messiah for the first and second concerts respectively. Thanks were voted to the officers and committee for their past services, upon which the officers for the coming season were elected as follows :—Conductor, Mr. J. Holford ; secretaries Messrs. W. Cooke and W. Gaudy: treasurer, Mr. J. Newall; libarian, Mr. R. W. Newall. Committee: Ladies, Messrs, Leathwood, Stubbs, Newall, Massey, Paull, and Marlow. Gentlemen : Messrs. C. and J. Leathwood, Borrows, Ainsworth, ' T. Parry, and E. Worrall. Rehearsals commence on Monday evening next. Particulars may •be found in our advertising column.

w------- NARRqW ESCAPE FROM DROWNING AT WIDNES. Cn Tuesday two children, named James Harper, aged one year and sine months, of Witt-road, Widnes, and Annie Cook, abcut three years of age, residing at 6, Witt-road, very narrowly escaped being drowned in an old pit on some waste land situated off Moor-lane. The two children, in company with another little girl, were playing near the pond, when Harper and Cook acciden- tally slipped and fell into the water. Fortunately Superintendent Keighley was standing in Moor-lane at the time, and,bearing thechild's cries, asked a boy named George Under wood,son of Mr. James Underwood, grocer, of Witt-road,to /amend ascertain the eause,little suspect- ing that anything of a serious nature had occurred. Underwood ran at once and found the two children struggling in the water. Without divesting himself of his clothing he pluckily jumpell into the pond, which fortunatelyisnot very deep, and rescued both children, and carried them to their respective homes. Superin- tendent Keighley followed,when he saw the nature of the affair, and assisted to restore animation in the case of Harper, who did not regain consciousness for some time. His ycung friend fared much better, and seemed to be more frightened than hurt.

- - HORTICULTURAL SHOW AT WESTON POINT. The first annual exhibition in connection with the Weston Point Horticultural Society was held on Satur- day afternoon, in the Church Schoolroom. A short time ago a few gentlemen; in order to encourage emulation among the residents of the village in the growth of flowers and vegetables, decided to form a society, and tne following officials were appointed :—President, the Rev. J. H. Wilcockson, M.A. ; Committee. Messrs. Beresford, Reece, Cowley, Robinson, Andrews, and R. Rosenberg; hon. treasurer, Mr. S. Rosenberg ; and hon secretary, L. Rosenberg, jun. The exhibition although notbn a very extensive scale, was encouraging to the promoters. A large number of beautiful plants were sent for exhibitiononly, by the Rev. J. W. Wilcockson, Messrs. R. Morris (Runcorn), Thomas Berrington Wm. Beckett, Cowley, Beresford, L. Rosenberg, jun.,Edward Mills, and R. Cookson. Altogether there was a very nice collection. During the afternoon selections of music were played by the Salt Union Brass Band, under the conduc- torship of Mr. Samuel Prince; and Miss McLean gave an effective rendering of "A Summer Shower." The prizes were distributed by the Rey. J. H. Wilcockson, as follows :—For best light fuchsias, Mr. James Saddler, Mersey-view, Weston Point ; collection of six greenhouse plants, Mr. T. Robinson, gardener to the Rev. J. H. Wilceckson ; best sticks of celery, Mr. William Savage, Weaver Cottages, Weston Point ; best begonia, Mr. S. Beresford, Clark's-terrace, hand bouquet, first: , Mr. Stonehouse, Hale ; 2nd, Mr. T. Robinson. In the indus- trial section, in which prizes were offered by Mrs. Wilccckson, for garments, Ste., the successful competitor was Miss Carrie Fabb.

div.head: NEW MAGISTRATES FOR ST. HELENS.
div.p: NEW MAGISTRATES FOR ST. HELENS.

_ Councillors John Forster, Henry Martin, and James Burchall, of St. Helens, have received an in- timation from the Chancellor of the Duchy that he is prepared to attach their names to the roll of magistrates for the borough on receiving their con- sent. These gentlemen have for many years taken an active interest in all public affairs of the town, and their elevation to the bench will be a popular recognition of their services. CLOSE OF THE DEE SALMON' FISHERY.

The season of salmon fishing with trammel! and draft nets closed in the Dee on Wednesday. The fishing nets has been altogether disappointing. Salmon have been scarcer both in the Estuary and at Chester, although one or two fish weighing about thirty pounds each have been taken recently. The average run of fish this year has been unusually light; in fact, the great majority of the salmon caughtliave been under eight pounds in weight. UMBRELLAS HECOTERED.—J. and W. DUTTON, Sankey-st., Warrington.—Adv. INQUEST AT EARLESTOWN. At the Railway Hotel, Earlestown, on Wednes- day morning, before Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner, an inquest was held on the body of Peter Woods, 56 years of age,who died at his residence, 61 Houghton- at., Earlestown, on Saturday. From the evidence it appeared the deceased was employed at the Bold Collieries, where he commenced to work on Wednes- day fast week. On the following day whilst en- gaged in sawing a piece of timber with a circular saw, the timber by some means was thrown back with great force, and striking the deceased in the stomach caused serious internal injuries., He was at once removed home, and attended by Dr. Handy- side, but despite every attention, he died on Satur- day, as stated. A verdict of "Accidental death" was returned. UMBRELLAS RECOVERED. —J. and W. DUTTON, Elankey-st., Warrington.—"lds. TICE ROME IRON TRADE.

There is still little alteration of note in the Eng- lish iron market. In the Cleveland district business is fairly active and prices are firm at an advance cf 9d. on the week. The (ilacow warrant market is more active; but transactions are confined to Scotch warraets. Scotch makers' irons is in less brisk demands ; but rates are firmly upheld, and in the case of several brands are higher, owing to scarcity of supplies. In manufactured iron little is doing, and shipplates, girderplates, boilerplates, arid angles have been reduced 2s. 0,1. in the Cleveland district. Tinplates are in fair sale, but at very low prices. The steel trade exhibits little activity, and, as la finished iron, lower quotations are recorded in the north of -England. Shipbuilders are depressed, and engineers are indifferently employed. The coal trade is rather quiet.—lron. UMBRELLAS RECOVERED.—J. and W. DUTTON, Sankey-st., Warrington.—Adv. DEATH OF DR. MCDONNELL OF WIDNES..

Dr. McDonnell, of Mersey-road, ‘Vidnes, died at his residence on Saturday last at the comparatively early age of 41 years. He had been ill for some months past, and he was confined to bed for three weeks immediately prior to his death. The deceased gentleman was widely known and respected in Runcorn and Widnes.and his early death is univer- sally regretted. Educated at Glasgow and Edin- burgh Universities for the medical profession he commenced his career as assistant to one of the leading practioners of Wigan, and after a stay of two years he took a similar position with Dr. Robin- son,of Runcorn. Three years later he commenced a practice on his own account at Widnes, and speedily became popular by reason of his cleverness and urbanity of manner. For some years past he had been in partnership with Dr. McCambridge. In religion the deceased was a•Catholic,and took an active interest in the affairs of St. Patrick's Church, with which he was connected, and by his decease they lose a generous and consistent supporter. He had represented hie co-religionists on the School Board for the past three years. His mortal remains were committed to the grave at Appleton Church yard on Monday afternoon, in the presence of a large concourse of people gathered to pay their last res- pects to his memory. The Rev. Dean Finegan con- ducted the burial service. The funeral cortege , consisted of a hearse and eight coaches. Lavin Tennis.—GAELAND. ironmonger, Bridge-st.. Warring- ' ton. _ _
iH-E- CLARKE ASPINALL TEMTERANCE .NIRMORIAL FUND.

As the outcome of the scheme, the Liverpool Dio- cesan Church of England Temperance Society ate about to appoint four additional police court mis- sionaries to labour in the following districts :—I. Liverpool city and county. 2. Southport, birkdale, and Orrnskirk. 3. Warrington,Widnes,and Newton. 4. St. Helens borough and county and Prescor. In response there were 76 applications. A sub-commit- tee representing the various districts reduced the number to twelve. The appointments will be made at a meeting of the Diocesan Executive to be held shortly. Amongst the selected candidates are four Church Army officers, and several navvy and canal missionaries,Stc..who are very highly recommended. The Memorial Fund will be kept open for some time to give an opportunity to intending sub- scribers. Upwards of forty Justices of the Peace have already shown their appreciation by subscrib- ing. Mr. James Mercer, the oldest and most expe- rienced member of the present staff of the Police Court and Prison Gate Mission, will, in October, re- move to the Bootle Borough Court, which he will attend every morning instead of two or three morn- ings of the week, according; to the present arrange- ments. At a public meeting held in connection with the Mission, at the Town Hall, Bootle, a short time ago,the Mayor (Mr. John Vicars) expressed the wish that one of the society s missionaries should attend the Bootle Borough Court every morning.
THE ACCIDENT AT BANK QUAY STATION, WARRINGTON._
From inquiries made at the Infirmary last even- ing we learn that the Widnes woman, named Ryan, who was severely injured at Bank Quay station last evening week is progressing favourably.

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN
AT RUNCORN.
BY AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT.
That the meeting of the Runcorn Musical Society on Tuesday augurs ill for the future of the Society; that indeed it appears highly probable that its existence will cease.

That the Society should come to this abrupt and untimely end is deeply to be regretted, because it has provided in the past concerts of the highest class, which have been thoroughly enjoyed by hundreds.

That the threatened termination may be avoided if the members would sink altogether the little petty differences that have existed, and lose the memory of them, and assured of more enthusiasm ampngst the members,and more practical assistance in the work.

That the whole question is to be discussed at a meeting to be held on Tutsday evening next, and it is hoped that not only will there be a full attend- ance of members, but that the vice-presidents will will turn up in large nnmbers and give their assist- ance in arriving at a wise decision.

That I hear there are a large number of cases of typhoid fever in the town: the number mentioned is 20; but the officials of the Board of Commis- sioners made no report on the subject at the meet- ing this week, and we are left in the dark as to the real facts of the case.

That no wonder we have fever in our midst. In- to Flalton Brook the sewage of about 20 houses drains at Halton, and there is evidence to prove that boatmen on the Bridgewater Canal are in the habit of filling their water kegs from this po:luted stream, and that even a farmer in the district is put to the necessity of using it when his own sup- ply from the pump is cut off from any cause. That there is no surer method of causing disease than drinking impure water, and this subject ought to at once receive the attention of Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority in whose district the brook is situated.

That the election Of five Commissioners on Thurs- day was the quietest that has taken place for many years past, and was in striking contrast with last year, when all was bustle and excitement from the opening of the poll to its close.
That Mr. Speakman occupied the position which was popularly assigned to him—the head of the poll. It shows that his name has lost none of its power to conjure votes.

That the surprise of the election is the low posi- tion occupied by the other retiring members, as there was generally considered to be no fear of their return to the positions both gentlemen bad worthily tilled.

That although there *ere no avowed temperance orpublican candidates in the &id, it is of course well known that both Mr. Lea and Mr. Leach are staunch supporters of the blue ribbon cause, and that Mr. Hough was the candidate of the Licensed Victuallers Association.

That the temperance folks affirm that the result shows that King Bung is not the all powerful monarch his suoPerters claimed him to be, and that many years will roll before the Board is wholly composed of followers of "the trade" •
That a man is no worse for being a teetotaller and no better for drinking ale, and that votes will be recorded for a good man whatever his views on these subjects.

That if the Legal and Parliamentary Committee, whom Mr. Humphreys pointedly charges with pass- ing idiotic resolutions, were consulted on th matter, they would say that neither pop nor ale had anything to do with the constitution of the Board.

That there was universal condemnation of the antiquated cumbersome and nonsenical election machinery by which the 'Commissioners are elected, and that the sooner there is a time fixed for the nomination and withdrawal of candidates and the ballot is introduced and the better.
That thP Commissioners might help this forward by petitioning the Local Government Board on the subject.

That there was at least one incident at the elec- tion worth recording. A free and independent voter went into Dr. Morgan's booth, and the clerk in charge commenced to fill up the voting paper according to his express desire. The names of Lea and Leach were inscribed, and then the man pre- pared to attach his signature to the bottom of the form. He was pressed to allow the names of Dr. Morgan and Mr. Hough to be inserted, but he de- clared "them are ray men," and would not permit any other name to be written. That was spoiling the Philistines with a vengeance.

The Committee's arrangements for the work of the next session are in a forward state. Several improve- ments and extensions have been introduced. The art classes will occupy two nights instead of one; the machine construction and building construction classes will be held on separate nights, under special teachers ; a new class in applied mechanics will be commenced, as well as one in physiography, and those in theoretical chemistry. electricity and magnetism, sound, light, and heat, and French classes will be resumed. The dress- making class will be conducted by the same teacher. Tne usual announcements will appear very shortly.

A shocking outrage was discovered on Tuesday morn- ing at a farm near Bagnall, Staffordshire the tails of five shorthorn heifers having been docked and the throats of two:milch cows cut. At Brentford, on Tuesda.y, Cornelius Smith, aged twenty-five, was committed for trial on a a charge of causing the death of William Smith, his brother, in the course of a fight.

Near Agrarn, in Hungary. the body of a girl of 17 has been found on the railway. The inquest showed that the head was cut off with a knife and the mutilated body laid on the line to avoid suspicion being cast on the murderer.

If that were so had the Board any power to prevent it.— The Surveyor said the houses had drains into a tempor- ary cesspool. This Committee recommended; that a horse hose and implement cart be procured and that the teader of Messrs. Shand, Mason and Cu., London, to supply the same for the sum of £32 be accep:edl.co include a pair of carriage lamps and a pair of sealiiig ladders. That Bray's lamps (2 lights) be substituted for the lamps now in use at the following places :—ln Bridge-street, at the end of Ellesmere-street; in High-street at the following places—Royal Hotel, Churai Mission, W. E. Lea's, end of Vicar-street, Parr's Bank, end of Loch-street, New Inn, J. H. That a hydrant be fixed in the slaughter house 3 arci forjitishing purposes. Mr. Hankinson moved the adoption ot.the minutes and remarked that thegas manager had informed the Com- mittee that Bray's lamps would be more economical than increasing the number of lamps—Mr. Bisbmwn seconded the motion.—Mr. Lightburn said on Saturday night in one lane in the town there were only tdx out of eight lamps lighted, and he thought they ought to have some means of-checking the lighting of these lamps so that they might know they were getting value for their money. In order to secure efficiency in the Fire Brigade they ought to have periodical tests. THE LIGHTING OF SALISBUNY-ST., &C. . _

Mr. Humphreys said he had that morning had placed in his hands a memorial from the inhabitants of &Bs- bury-st., Byrom-st , Picow-st.' Chaucer-sr., with respect to the want of light there, and lie had been asked to pre- sent it to the Board, and he now did so. The memorial stated there were 125 dwelling-houses in these streets many of which had been tenanted tor over live years during which the streets had been allowed to re- main in total darkness nig:it ,L ter night. The memorial state 4 that the petitioners did not wish to harrow the minds of the Board enumerat- ing the number of accidents that had occuried through such a state of tlinigs ; if the Board wool I take steps to lemi tly the matter they would confer a great boon upon the petitMners. The petition was signed by about 50 of the inhabitants —The Surveyor said the Gas Company had no mains in the streets ; they were grim; to put theta in, but they did not say when.— At a later period in the proceedings the Se,retary said in October, 1890, a resolution was passed that lamps he fixed in these streets, and a reauest was immediately sent to the G4i; CO. to lay mains. He had since then sent three or four letters to Mr.Ft ith on the matter,and he had also waited on him three or four times. In the spring Mr.Frith said they could riot lay the mains at that time, but he pro- mised that they would be laid at the back end.—Mr. Humphreys saki Mr. Frith was reported to have said that he had never been asked to lay the mains at all in respect to some of the streets.—Mr. Fisher said the Board ought to be exonerated from all blame : if any one was injured the Gas Co. and not the Board were to blame.—Mr. Humphreys : Is it possible that we may have the town in darkness at the will of the Gas Co. ? The Law Clerk said they would have a remedy against the Gas Co. In this instance the streets were private, and until they were made and adopted, the Commissioners were under no obligation to light them unless they choose.—Mr. Hum- phreys said it was high time this matter should be faced. It was not surprising that those who paid rates should object strongly to being left in darkness.—Mr. Speakman said the Gas Company seemed to simply ignore their request. It had been the custom of the Gas Com- pany to put mains in before the streets were made,and it did seem hard that they should go to the expense of making streets and then the Gas Company could come and break them up. The Gas Company oaght to attend to a reasonable application at once o say they could not do it.—Mr. Taylor: I move that the Gas Company be written to.—The Secretary : I wrote again yesterday.— Eventually the matter was left in the hands of the High- way Committee.
FINANCE.
The Finance Committee reported that the receipts for the month amounted to £613 23. 4d., and accounts amounting to £455 Bs. 3d. were recommended for pay- ment —Passed.
LW! BOAT SATURDAY.

The Secretary read a letter from the Manchester and Salford Life Boat Saturday Committee asking the Board to organise a Life Boat Saturday in Runcorn district. Mr. Speakman approved of the object to which he had subscribed for many years. He moved that the letter be referred to the Logal and Parliamentary Com- mittee for their report.—Mr. Lightburn in seconding the motion said he knew no place in the Kingdom that ought to support the Life Boat cause more than Runcorn.—Mr. Humphreys said he had not a rap of confidence in the Legal and Parliamentary Committee. They passed a most idiotic resolution some months ago in which they said that all matters of this kind which were not directly within the cognizance of the Board should not come before them at all, and they must now stultify themselves if they cleat with this. For this reason he moved that the letter be referred to a Corn- mittee of the whole Board.—Mr. Lightburn said it was a stretch of the usual license of courtesy to say any Committee were acting in an idiotic manner.—Mr. Humphreys: I said the resolution was idiotic.—Mr. Lightburn said that was passing the bounds of pro- priety.—The amendment was not seconded, and the motion was carried.
