div.head: RUNCORN MAN DROWNED AT FRODSHAM
div.p: A RUNCORN MAN DROWNED AT FRODSHAM

On Sunday afternoon,about four o'clock, the body of a man unknown was found in the river Weaver, at Sutton. ID wee otemdiirag Laprish ira ,ho w lAST, and the deceased is supposed to have walked into the river. It appears to be the body of a man aged 40 years, who was five feet eight or nine inches in height. He had brown hair, a moustache, but no whiskers. The body was respectably dressed in a plaid coat and vest, with striped trousers, and a red striped shirt, and blue woollen underclothing, with low shoes. In his pockets were found a rail- way ticket from Frodsham to Runcorn, issued for the 8.27 p.m. train on the 24th inst.. a silver lever watch, with curbed chain, .£1 12s. 44d. in money, two pocket knives, a pipe, tobacco pouch, box of matches and a silk handkerchief. The inquest was held at Aston Arms, on Monday night, and a verdict of " Found Drowned " was returned. The body was identified as that of William Fletcher, aged 37, labourer, St. Helens, son of Mr. William Fletcher, Oaktnere-et., Greenway-road, Runcorn. The deceased visited his relatives at Frodsham on the 24th ult., and intended to return home in the evening. He purchased a ticket for Runcorn, but got into the wrong train, and' on finding out his mistake he left the carriage at Halton. He then started to walk back to Frodsham to catch the 10 p.m. train thence to Runcorn. The night was very dark, and it is supposed that he tcok a wrong turn- ing and got into the river. His watch was stopped at a quarter-past nine. The deceased should have been married to a young lade belonging to Liver- pool on September 10th. lle was a teetotaller. His remains were interred in the Church of England portion of the Runcorn Cemetery on Wednesday afternnon. Upon the coffin were a number of wreathe from sorrowing relatives and friends.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF IMPROVEMENT
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF IMPROVEMENT
COMMISSIONEIt S. ANNUAL ELECTION.

.. The annti-tif election of five members to Runcorn Board of Commissioners took place on Tnursday. , The. Market Hall in Bridge-street was the place of 1 polling. There were five vacancies to be filled up, ail! of the returning members three only offered themselves for re-election, viz. Messrs. C. Speak- man, A. J. Once, W. Hankinson. Messrs. W. Tim- mins and EL White retired from the contest. At one time it was thought that no contest would take place, but at the eleventh hour Messrs. T. Lea, W. ' Leach, A. Hough, and D. Mangan submitted their addresses to the electorate, and an election became certain. Messrs. P. Speakman, H. Once, and W. Hankinson, those who lied served the ratepayers in the past, again asked the electors for their suffrage In addresses in which were mentioned schemes of great importance to the town, and which they promised to support. The arrangements for polling were the same as last year. The system of voting.is quite open, but Mr. F. Wiswall, the returning officer, had provided &booth, numbered" 2," in which the elactors might fill up their papers without being overlooked by the prying eyes of the candidates' henchmen, anal he system worked as well as the cumbersome and an- tiquated style of election would permit. rle polling place was the Market Hall, and whilst the returning officer appropriated one of the offices to his use, the candidates hail engaged Several of the stalls for the headquarters. There was an almost total absence of squills, awl it was generally agreed that the election was one of the -q.detest that had been held for many years past. Assisting the returning officer (Mr. Wiswall), were • Messrs. F. A. Lake, E. Marshall, M. Barker. J. D. Jones, and W. Sutton, and keeping miler in the Hall-were Messrs. J. Percival, W. Garrett, and E. Austin. . .

At half-uast four, Mr. Wiswall announced that the following votes had beearecorded so far as they could ascertain : P. SPEAKMAN, C.O 585 T. LEA 515 W. LEACH 497 DR. MANGAN 440 He stated that. these gentlemen were certainly elected, but the figures for the other three candi- dates were so close that they would not be an- nounced until there had been a recount. . . .

_ Mr. Speakman, who was received with applause, said he was very pleased once more to appear there as their representative. (Hear, hear.) It was a long time since they first gave him their suffrages, and so lung as his health permitted, and they felt inclined to support him as their member, he was ready to serve them. Ile stood particularly on that occasion because he loved his native town, and they had in Runcorn a great many things to do, and they required men of experience to do them. Runcorn was proverbial for its low rates, and efficiency, and rates should be kept down so that they could succeed in bringing capitalists into their midst. They might be styled an oid-fashioned town so far as the way in which that election was conducted, but he hoped the time would not be far distant when they could deliver their consciences in the ballot boxes. (Applause.) He would do the best he could in the future, as in the past, to promote their interests. • He had very great pleasure in proposing a hearty vote of thanks to their Returning Officer and his colleagues for the efficient way in which they had carried out the election. He was proud to do this, because Mr. Wiswall was one of themselves, and he was glad to find him in I the honourable position he now occupied. Mr. Lea seconded the proposition. He thanked the ratepayers heartily for the honourable position in which they had placed him, and said he would endeavour to the best of his ability to do nothing to forfeit the confi- dence they had reposed in him. (Applause.) Mr. Leach thanked them heartily for electing him a member of the Board of Commissioners. He hoped there were other working-men who would qualify them- selves for that position. He hoped the day was far dis- tant when he should lose their confidence. He had espe- cial pleasure in supporting the proposition, because Mr. Wiswall was an old fellow-workman. (Applause.) The motion was unanimously carried. Mr. Wiswall expressed his obligations to all present for their kindness,and said the ratepayers were welcome to his services, for themselves and for the benefit of the town. The recount took place at the Town Hall, yesterday morning, and at noon the Dumpers were published as follows : SPEAKMAN T.' LEA 513 W. LEAC EI DR. MANGAN 446 W HANRINSON 424 H. J. GRICE A. HOUGH 3/39 _ . _
The first five were declared elected. The poll was very small compared with last year, when about 1,350 polled. This year only 840 recorded their votes.

The mechanics, fitters, pattiarnmakera, itc., employed by the Ebbw Vale Iron and Steel Company are out on strike for an amendment of the sliding scale. A Toronto telegram states that the secession movement in the Canadian branch of the Salvation Army is grow- ing, and that the, outside districts are &ginning to be affected.

div.head: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held on Tuesday, Mr. f. Sutton Timmis presiding, and there were present, Rev. Dean Finegan, and Father Clarke, Messrs. H. W. Deacon, C. E. Barlow, S. Quinn, and a: H. Denby (clerk).

div.head: DEATH OF. DR, MCDONNELL.
div.p: DEATH OF. DR, MCDONNELL.

The Chairmatrreferred to the death of -Dr. McDonnell, remarking that they would all feel his loss. He proposed that a vote of condolence be sent to Mrs. McDonnell.— Dean Finegan seconded the motion, which was carried.

div.head: DISTRICT EDUCATION COMMITTEE.
div.p: DISTRICT EDUCATION COMMITTEE.

This ComMittee reported that during the month of July (two weeks) there were 12 applications for payment of fees, which were recommended to be paid in ten cases. 173 parents appeared before the Committee for contravention of the Education Act, and 19 were pro- secuted before the magistrates and 18 committed. One case was withdrawn.

DRAWING EXAMINATION. In moving the adoption of the minutes of the School Management Committee, Dean Finegan said the draw- ing examination was held in June, and out of twelve depagments, he had earned the " excellent" grant and two" good" which was very satisfactory indeed.

div.head: FINANCE.
div.p: FINANCE.
The Finance Committee recommended the payment of accounts amounting to £677 4s. 11.—Approved.
STATE-AIDED SUPERANNUATION.

The Clerk read a circular letter from the National Union ot Teachers, who asked the Board to sign a memorial in support of state aided superannuation for teachers.—Dean Finegan said he wished to see some provision made for their teachers, and Lie was greatly in favour of the proposal. If there was any cl ss of people that deserved superannuation it was h teaciiers in elementary schools. He had therefore great pleasure in moving that the Chairman sign the memorial on I-ehalf uf the Board.—The Chairman agi eial with the Dean. He thought that there was no occupation so laborious as teaching in an elementary school, and he should have great pleasure in signing the memorial.—lt was accord- ingly resolved that he do so.

div.head: SCIENTIFIC TEXPeRANCE.
div.p: SCIENTIFIC TEXPeRANCE.

A letter was read from the Livci:po—ol Band of Hope and temperance Union asking for Permission for Mr. J. J. Jakeman to give a " single Scientific" temperance address at the schools during school hours some time dur- ing October.—The subject was referred to the School Management Committee.

div.head: FRODSHAM.
div.p: FRODSHAM.

T.WRIVSING SR.SRICINS The annual licensing sessions far the Frodsham section of the Eddishury Division was held on ‘Vednesday, at the Frodsham Police Station. The magistrates present were Messrs. C. Reynolds, A. Thomas, and R. Reynolds.,

div.head: REPORT: DECREASE OF DRUNKENNESS.
div.p: THE REPORT: DECREASE OF DRUNKENNESS.

Superintendent Meredith submitted his report for the Frodsham section of the Eddisl.ury division. It showed that there were 17 licensed victuallers, eight beersellers, and one other who sold off the premises; total 28; which gave an average of 258 of the ppulatiou to each license. No licensed victuallers or beersellers bad been proceeded against during the year; and last year one beerseller was proceeded against but not convicted. The number of persons convicted for drunkenness was 43 against 105 last year, being a decrease of 62 persons. He objected to the renewal of the license of the Volun- teer Inn, held by Thomas Morris, on the ground that a complaint had been received that the licensee kept a disorderly house. The unopposed licenses were then renewed. THE VOLUNTEER INN.

On Wednesday, Mr. Fletcher, solicitor' objected on behalf of the police to the renewal of the license of the Volunteer Inn, Frodsham, on the grounds (1) that the house was of a disorderly character or frequented by persons of bad character; (2), that the house • was not duly qualified as by law required ; and (3), that the house was not necessary for the requirements of the neighbour- hood. Mr. Fletcher said the grounds of objection on which he most strongly relied were the two first. He sOlould be ab!e to show that the house was frequented bf persons who had repeatedly been convicted for drunkenness, by poachers, and persons of low class. He was surprised that the other ground of objection had not been submitten before—namely; that the house was not duly qualified. An inspec- tion would at once prove that the house was abso- lutely disqualified by law from holding a license. IThe annual value to let, apart from the license and any I land held with it (except a garden used by the guests), must be at least £ll in ths case of a house qualified to receive a license ; but this place was merely a small cottage, with three rooms downstairs and three above, not worth more than a rental of £8 a year, and there was to garden immediately adjoining it. The house was assessed at the poor rate at £lO 55.-212 gross, and £l2 ss. with the license and the garden included. It possessed no accommodation for travellors, and was nothing more than a mere dram-shop for navvies and -thers.—Evidence was then given in .opposition by

police oflicers.—The Bev. ii. B. Biog.', vicar of Frodsham, said he had once or twice 'been in the house, which he considered was worthsabout £8 a year. The house hid for a long time had a bad character:— Mrs. Pooley, a neighbour, said that the noise, singing and drunkenness on Saturday evening was simply in- tolerable.—Mr. Pugh, barrister, - Birkenhead, for the appiicant, said he should prove that the house was .licenged beforo 1869, and that during the whole of that period there had never been a conviction against the tenant. This fact was worthy of much more considera- tion than such a statement as Mrs. Pooley's. As to the annual value. lie shou:d prove that it was now much in excess of that required by law. Evidence was then given as to annual value and the character of the house, after which the justices said they had decided to renew the license.

div.head: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.
div.p: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.
The toonthly meeting of this Council will be held on Tuesday evening -next at the Town [Jail. Amongst other matters the Council will consider the following recommendations of Committees.

div.head: THK HOUSING OF THE WORKING CLASSES.
div.p: THK HOUSING OF THE WORKING CLASSES.

The Sanitary Committer have passed a resolution that the Town Clerk be itistructed to take the necessary proceedings under the Houses of the Working Classes Act, 1890, for the closing of the under-mentioned houses, all of which has been reported by the Medical Officer of Health to be unfit for human habitation, viz. : —Nos. 2 to 28, Erwood-street, and Nos. 1 to 27, Erwood- street. The same committee recomniends that a sub- committee of the following members be appointed to consider the report pf the Medical Officer of Health under the Housing of the Working Classes Act, and in con- junction therewith to consider the question of provid- viding Artisans' Dwellings :—The Chairman, Alderman Sutton, Councillors Browne, Flood and Hepherd.
TUE BOROUGH SURVEYOR AND THE LONGFORD DEPOT.

The Borough Surveyor (Mr. T. Longdin) wrote on the 314 August to the Sanitary Committee as follows "Kindly allow me to ask your relief from any further engineering wark in connection with your depot, Long- ford, as I find the increase of work in my department, caused by the extension of the borough and the rapid growth of the town, requires all my available time. With the exception of a few minor matters, the work carried out under the Local Government Board's sanc- tioned loan is almest complete, and I think I may justly say that the machinery and plant is doing what it was designed for. Thanking all the members of the Com- mittee for the kindness I have always received at their hands in the elucidation of a difficult problem." In regard to this letter, the Committee have passed the fol- lowing resolution :—" That the Committee wish to ex- press their high appreciation of the very valuable ser- vices rendered by Mr. Longdio, during a period of many years, in the construction and enlargement from time to time of the plant at Longford Depot; and for his general supervision of the works, which be leaves in a perfectly satisfactory condition."
SANITARY PRECAUTIONS.

The Paving and Sewerage Committee have passed the following resolution :—" At the request of the Sanitary Committee, the necessary arrangements be made for applying the smoke test to the sewers and drains in the following cases : 1. At every house in which a cage of enteric fever or diphtheria may have occurred. 2. Whenever the Medical Officer of Health is of opinion in any other came than the foregoing that a smoke test is desirable. SCHOOL ATTRNDANCH COMMITTEH.-RESIONTATION OF A

MEMBER. The School Attendance Committee recommended that the resignation of Councillor H. Roberts as a member of Committee be accepted. The Committee have likewise passed the followings resolution :—" That the Clerk again call the attention of the managers of the Public Elementary Schools to the advisability of their giving notice, previous to the next examination, of the require- ments of article 30 of the new Education Code, so as to entitle children desirous of going to work to be examined for labour certificates." TER SCHOOL OF ART. The Museum, Sm., Committee have passed the follow- I ling resolutions rhat the Borough Treasurer be re- quested to pay the sum of £2OO to Mr. William Owen, Treasurer of the School of Art, in completion of the transfer of the School of Art to the Corporation," and " that the Technical Instruction Sub-Committee be directed to make arrangements for carrying on the School of Art." The Committee also recommend that Mr. W. Owen be added to the Technical Instruction Sub-Committee.
_TES NEW BETHS.
The Baths Committee recommends that the tenders of Messrs. Thomas and Taylor, of Stockport, to supply and fix the whole of the engineering work for the new baths, at £6OB 2. 61, be accepted.

Intense indignation is being felt througtout Canada consequent on the inhuman treatment inflicted on the crews of three Canadian sealers which were seized by a Russian man-of-war off Copper Islands. The British Government is being urged to demand an explanation.
'TEEING'S HEAR") AND SEEN

AT WARRINGTON. • The old Public Hall Company finally wound up its business this week, but an attempt is to he made to provide Warrington with the now much needed concert or assembly hall. Mr. W. D. Jeans is taking an active interest in the proposal, and plans have been prepared for him by Mr. P. Si!cock. A meet- ing of people interested in the scheme will probably be held in a short time. Warrington must have a hirge Public Hall ; it is indispensable.

I see that the Mayor of Manchester has received a letter from a Belfast mechanis, who enclosed a postal order for twenty shillings as a token of his sympathy with the shareholders oi the Manchester Ship Canal, and his admiration of their enterprise. The writer suggests that other working-men throughout the country should "go and do like- wise "in order that the shareholders may have some reward for their outlay. I am afraid he will not find many who will "follow suit." It is im- possible to get up any enthusiasm about subscrip- tions to ensure a dividend.

Is there any etiquette applicable to committees of the Corporation? lam led to ask this question by a little incident which has taken place lately in connection with the Watch Committee. That committee acting, of course, on behalf of the Cor- poration, is now entrusted with the duty of licens- ing theatres and such like places of entertainment, and it is in cohnection with the licensing of the " Royal Court Theatre' (late Public Hall), that the incident I refer to happened. The representative of the Royal Court Theatre applied to the Watch Committee on the 2nd June for a license. The committee meeting was pretty well attended, there being present Aldermen llarrisori, Chandley, Fran- comb, Platt and Councillors Heaton, and Cannel!. This full committee considered the application, and decided to gmut the license on the same condition that they had granted the license to the Theatre Royal in Scotland-road, the condition being that a license to sell liquors should not also be applied for. The representative of the Royal Court Theatre, as, of co urse,he was perfectly entitled to do, thought he would like to take time to consider the matter before accepting the condition, and he took time.

On the 30th June there was another meeting or o....u.Aluttle, Mit MIA h, .. it was a wall meeting. There were present only the Mayor, Aldermen ...Sutton and Harrison, and Councillor Cannel!. The application again came forward, and was granted without any condition being attached to it. Now, to say nothing of the unfairness of granting to one theatre a privilege and a source of profit which is denied to another, does this little incident not show the necessity for an understand- ing being come to amongst the members of Committees. If there was such an understanding, one would not hear, as in this case, of a sparsely- attended committee passing what had been deliberately rejected a short time before by a largely-attended meeting. Nobody wants to see Corporation business conducted according to the principles of the "artful dodger." Applicants to committees should not be encouraged to time their appearances just as the committee was supposed to be favourable, no matter how small in number. There is no reason to say that anything that sort was done in this case, but still, in its results the case is eminently calculated to "encourage the others," as the French would say.

I was told the other day that the cholera is par- ticularly fond of visiting places where there are plenty of smells. If tnat be so, lam afraid there is a possibility of its finding Warrington a hospit- able abiding place. Just as the town has a variety of industries so its odours are multifarious. I think that, under certain climatic conditions, a blind man might know his whereabouts in Warrington by the evidence of his vlfactory nerves. There is for instance, the Mersey-street smell, the Dial- St. smell—and so on in great variety. But in addition to the smells which have found a local habitation and a name, there are the peripatetic kind, which accompany a familar vehicle owned by the Cor- poration. A few days ago in passing along Orford- lane I was disposed to think that that district is entitled to the honour of having the champion smell of Warrington. lam not going to say that that is due to the proximity of the intercepting depot. That might have something to do with it, but not everything. Indeed there was not one smell but many. It was a concatenation of smells,from which all the pleasing odoura bad been carefully excluded.

I am informed by an insurance agent in the town that there are a large number of men and women in Warrington who cannot read or write, although their ages are such that they ought to have had the advantages of the Education Act. It is commonly asserted that there arevery few people now-a-days who cannot both read and write, but the supposi- tion, as the state of things I hare mentioned shows, is another of those pleasant fictions, with which we are continually deluding ourselves, and which come - to be believed implicitly through being frequently repeated. It appears that the Insurance Com- panies share in the certainly excusable delusion, for my informant tells me that his company are quite incredulous as to the fact of insurers being un- able to append their names to the papers he has to submit to them. If there are so many adults in Warrington who ought to have received proper school education, but have not, one would assume- that in all probability there are a good many child- ren in the town who are in the same unhappy con— dition. I understand that this is the case. There are, it appears, a great many children who ought. to be on the school register, but never get on to it, and consequently are never looked after by the educational officials.

Of cOurse, in a town where there is a strong desire not to adopt the School Board system there is an equally strong temptation not to look so care- fully as is necessary after children's education, lest , there should have to be additional accommodation provided for, and an argument be thus supplied in favour of establishing Board Schools. But it seems to me that a forcible argument in favour of that policy is being furnished by the existing state of things. In these days of general education chil- dren suffer a much greater hardship than formerly through not being properly instructed, because the competition they have to contend with in after life, and the reproach of being uneducated are greater• than they used to be.

The Salvation Army in Warrington have got a decided acquisition, namely that of no other than a real live member of the legal profession. He is a new Corner to the town, from London, and his name is surgestive of something which lawyers are cer- tainly sometimes the agents in promoting, but of which iu popular imagination they are not sup- pesed to be particularly enthusiastic promoters. This gentleman, however, is distinctly and unmis- takably a Salvationist soldier, and may be seen occasionally taking part in the processions of the local corps about the town; and right proud is it, I dare say, of having such a member,regarding him no doubt, as a host in himself. The legal Salvttion- ist made his first appearance as an advocate at the police court last Saturday.

I do not exactly admire some of the methods of the Salvation Army; they are, to say the least, eccentric. and I could never fancy myself becoming a member of it, but it has done a great amount of g, ood and in the way of practical•Christianitymiore good than many churches, and rdo not think the new W arrington solicitor need have any slur cast upon him for his connection with it. Indeed, his pluck in identifying himself so prominently with such an organisation shows a real grit in the man that cannot be praised too highly in these days of flabby temporising with everything that is "res- pectable" and popular. I like the individuality of the thing.

div.head: LO W TON.
div.p: LO W TON.

TaE AIIGUST HOLIDAYS.—As in previous years, the last zaturday and Monday in August was in Lowtou and Pennington recognised as a holiday amongst the ' inhabitants. The Pennington Mill weaving shed and the Pennington Spinning Company's mill ceased opera- tions on the Friday evening, and commenced on 'files- day morning. On Saturday Mr. H. Draper, of Lowton, t)ok a party of about 20 in waggonettes to Frodsnam, and also a party to Runcorn. Ia both cases the outing was somewhat marred by the rain which came down at intervals during the day. The railway companies issued cheap tickets to various places of resort, and a good number availed themselves of the opportunity. A trip was run on the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire Railway to Geethorpes, and was fairly well patronised.. In the afternoon, Mr. W. Worsley conveyed a party - from Lowton to Worsley, where the annual show of-- flowers, Itc., took place on that day. On the Monday, rain fell for the greater part of the day, and made pic- nicking rather unpleasant. Work was commenced on Tuesday morning.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

11IORE DAMAGING OF TELEGRAPH INSULATORS. At the Daresbury Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, Richard Bretherton, a young man, a journeyman butcher resid- ing at Latchford, was charged with attempting to damage some telegraph insulators on the 9th inst., at Appleton.—P.C. Bratt deposed that he saw the defend- ant, in company with a number of small boys and he and the lads were all throwing stones at the telegragh wires. Some of them struck the poles and some went through the wires. As soon as they saw witness they stopped throwing. The defendant told him they were trying which could throw the highest, and afterwards said he was throwing at a sparrow.—bout two hours previously one of the telegraph clerks called upon wit- ness and complained of so many insulators being broken. —The district telegraph engineer stated that 49 insula- tors had been broken in the neighbourhood in a short time. They cost Is. each, not including the time and railway fare of the man who had to put them up.—The defendant said he only and none of the boys threw, and he only threw a bit of soil at a sparrow.—He was fined 10s.

div.head: SHOOTING HOMING rIGNONS.
div.p: SHOOTING HOMING rIGNONS.

At the Warrington Boroueh Police Court yesterday James Cottam of Hawley, had been summoned by James Burgess, Wellington-st., on a charge of killing one hom- ing pigeon and wounding another belonging to the corn- plainant.—Mr. Jenkins, who represented the defendant, said homing pigeons were very valuable birds, and frequently owners suffered much through their being shot, being quite unable to discover who had shot them. In this case he had consented to his client paying 50s. damages, and on his behalf offered a humble apology for shooting the pigeons, and he would never repeat the offence, though at the same time he had to say that the pigeons were flying with his own, and he did not shoot them in malice.—Mr. Longton, who represented the prosecutor, said he admitted that there was no malice in the matter, and the prosecutor merely wanted compensation for loss. It was desirable that it should be known that homing pigeons could not be shot in this manner. It was neces- sary that the practice should be put down, especially as these birds were invaluable for naval and military pur- poses, for which they were trained. He accepted the terms offered and withdrew the summons.

div.head: MINOR CASES.
div.p: MINOR CASES.
%%ARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT.

SA:TlMM—Before Alderman Burgess (in the chair),Mr. . L. Voisey, and Mr. John Geddes. FRAUDULENT ENLISTMENT.—David Gilmore was charged with fradulently enlisting by stating that he had not been previously in the Army.—Colour Sergeant Clayton from Orford Barracks, proved the case, and the prisoner was sent to gaol f3r a month. _ _ . .
MONDAY.—defore the Mayor (Alderman Greenall) in the

chair, and Alderman Francomb. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—Thos. Ridger was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Knutsford-road, on Saturday night, aud also with threatening Wm. Ridger, his brother. As the latter did not appear the seoond charge could not be proceeded with. A constable said the man was very drunk and disorderly and threat- ening his brother with a steel. Re was fined ss. and costs.—Thos. Burns, drunk and disorderly in Bett.rmar- ket-street, en Saturday night, ss. and costs.—William Dooley was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Old-road, on Saturday night, and John Daley with assaulting P.C. Cooper 20 on the same occasion.—Cooper said a young man complained to him about Daley assaulting him and he was proceeding to get his name and address, to summon him, and Daley struck him in the face. Dooley was drunk and very noisy. Daley was fined ss. and costs, and Dooley 10s. and costa.— Sarah Wilkinson, drunk and disorderly in River-road,on Saturday night, ss. and costs.—Patrick Baldwin was charged with being drunk and also with assaulting P.C.'s Monks and Turner, in Tanners's-lane, on Satur- day night. On P.C. Turner trying to induce him to go home as he was (trunk and noisy, he assaulted him, and he had about a dozen people on him all at once. P.C. MDnks corroborated. 20s. and costs, or a month's hard labour.—Ellen Cooper, drunk and disorderly at Arpley wharf, about one o'clock on Sunday morning, was discharged on promising to leave the tostn.— Michael Donlan, in the Crown and Sceptre-yard, shortly after two o'clock on Sunday morning, ss. and costa.— Catherine Benson, in Buttermarket-street, about ten minutes to one that (Monday) morning, who was re- cently prosecuted for cruelty to her children ,was warned that if she was not careful she would be so prosecuted again, and dismissed on promising to leave the town. ARMY DESERTION.—Fred Thompson for being a deser- ter from the Welsh Fusiliers in May last, having enlisted on the 15th of that month and deserted on the 17th, was sent to Strangevvays jail to await an escort. FIGHTING. —James Green and Martin Dolan, for fight- in, in Florsemarket-street, were each bound over in .£5 to keep the peace six months, and Dolan had also to pay easf a. CRIMNEY ON Firm—Thomas Lawrenson, was fined is. for having his chimney on fire. LODOING-HOUSO OFFENCES.—Mary Clarke, lodging- house keeper, was summoned on the charges of haying omitted to sweep the floors of her house before 10. a.m. on the 23rd inst., and of having also omitted to remove solid and liquid filth from the premises before 9 a.m. on the same date. She pleaded guilty and was tined ss. .
DRUNK IN CHARGE OF A HORSE.—Mathew Maden, drunk in charge of a horse and cart in Sankey-street on the 20th inst., wals fined ss. and Costs. TUESDAY.—Before Mr.„R. Garnett (in the chair) and
Mr. Owen.

INDECENCY.—Mary Ellen Smith and Catherine Doherty were charged with indecent behaviour, and were sent to gaol for a month. DECLINING TO PAY.—For not having paid the amount due on an order previously made by the court, John Plunkett was sent to gaol for a month. SCHOOL CASES.—Mr. George Riley prosecuted, on be- half of the School Attendance Committee, several pa- rents for not sending their children regularly to school. The following persons were fined :—Martin Carey, Jas. Coleman, Peter Farrell, William Farrington, Peter Gar- land, James Hill, John McDonnell, Thomas Moody, John Naylor, Thomas Robinson, and William Traynor. The son of Thomas Bracegirdle was sent to the ship "Clio." WEDNESDAY.—Before Councillor James Fairclough (chairman) and Alderman Wright. ASSAULT WITH A ROLLING PlN.—William Keighley, factory hand, living at 16, Hine-street, was charged with assaulting, on Tuesday afternoon, Elizabeth Pritchard, his sister-in-law, wife of James Pritchard, with a roll- ing pin, on the head.—The Chief-Constable said the defendant and his wife were quarrelling and the com- plainant went between them to prevent violence, and was struck .—The complainant said she heard a little girl screaming murder across the street and she ran across and found the defendant had her sister in a corner in the house. lie" clicked" hold of a rolling pia and split her head open with it. She did not strike him.—Maggie Keighley, the little girl, said she came in and found the complainant, her aunt, bleeding. The defendant kicked witness's mother in the chest. She did not see her aunt hit him.—P.C. Jones said he found the complainant in the street with a wound in her head two inches long, which he was informed the defen- dant had caused with a rolling-pin. He took her back

to the house and bathed and bandaged up her head, and then took her to the 'bus to be conveyed to the Infir- mary. He took the defendant to the Police Station, and on being charged he said, " It's all right : she struck me first."—The defendant said she came in and struck him with the rolling-pin, and he took it from her and struck her with it. His head had been bleeding all night.—He was fined 10s. and costs, or 14 days. A MIDNIGHT PROWLER—Luke Tilley was charged with being a convicted thief, and also with being found on the enclosed premises of Dr. Adams at 25 minutes past twelve that morning. A constable said he was coming down Bewsey-road and he saw the defendant and an- other man leaving the premises. The other man ran away. Witness found Dr. Adams's surgery window in- secure.—The Chief Constable said there was not a more dangerous man in Warrington than the prisoner.—He was sent to gaol for 14 days. _ . .

THUESDAy.—Before Alderman Sutton (chairman), Coun- cillor James Fairclough, and Captain Ridgway. ASSAULTING HIS MOTHER.—John McDonough, appre- hended under a free warrant, was charged with assault- ing his mother on the 30th of August. The complainant said the defendant had shoved and knocked her down, but manifested great reluctance to give evidence, although the previous day she had begged the magis- trates hard to grant her a warrant, being apparently in the greatest terror of her son.—The Chairman said it was evident that the complainant had come therewith the intention not to prosecute, but the Bench were satis- fied that an assault had been committed, butadvised the complainant not to come there again with such equivo- cating evidence. They fined the defendant 103. and costs or 14 days' imprisonment. UNSEEMLINESS IN THE STREETS.—A woman named Smith, of Naylor-it., and another named O'Dowd, were charged with unseemly behaviour in Mersey-st., the previous night, and sent to jail for 14 days' hard labour each—Catherine Brown, 19th appearance, was charged with like conduct in Bank-st., that morning and a man named Morris, a labourer, with aiding and abetting her. Brown was sent to jail for a month with hard labour, and Morris was fined ss. and costs, or seven days.—The Chief Constable complained that in other places the fares of such characters were paid by the prison authorities to Warrington when they represented that they were go- ing there ; though many of them did not belong to Warrington.—The Chairman thought that ought not to be, and he did not know how -authorities could have power to do so.—The Chief Constable : The Discharged Prisoners' Aid Society, sir. FRlDAY.—Before Alderman Wright (chairman) and Mr. L. Voisey. MAGISTERIAL UNPUNCTUALITY.—There were no magis- trates present at court until ZO minutes past 10, when Alderman Wright made his appearance, and immedi- ately after Mr. Voisey entered. ABSENCE FROM Saroor..—Fanny Smith, of Hollinfare, was charged by Frederick Wright, school attendance officer for that district, with not sending her two child- ren to school. She was fined 55. NON-MAINTENANCE IN A REFORMATORY. James Birchall was charged by Inspector James with non-con- tribution for the maintenance of his son in a reformatory and was ordered to pay is. 6d. a week. CRUELTY TO A HORSE.—John Simpson. Appleton Thorn, was charged by Inspector Dowty, R.S.P.C.A., with working his horse while in an unfit state, on the 17th August, on the Fair Ground.—The Chief Constable remarked that this was a man who was once brought up for smashing a lamp, and when a constable wanted his name he said " Get into the cart and I will give you the name "and then switched up the horse and carried him to Appleton. (Laughter.) He was fined 103. and costs, £1 Os. 6d. in all. _ _ .

DAMAGH BY BOYS.—Chas. Nicholls, 78, Longford-st., Edward Littlefair, Peter Garland, Thomas Heath, and Wm. Dutton, all of Watkin-st., John Higham, 14,Silver- st., and Joseph France, Watkin-st., all boys, were charged with wilfully damaging turnips the property of W. Thompson,Avenue Farm,Orford. Some of the lads, it appeared, pulled up the turnips and handed them over the hedge. They were fined ss. and costs each, and sen- tenced to be detained in the cells till 6 o'clock the follow- ing night. ASSAULTS.—Wm. Allen, 13, Crosley-st., was charged with assaulting Mary Jane Owens,6, Orchard-st., on the 26th of August. He had to pay costs.—Ed. Oakes, 10, River-rd., was charged with assaulting Thos. Knight, 9, River-rd., his father-in-law, on the 30th of August. Mr. Browne appeared for the prosecution. He stated that the defendant's wife was ill, and the complainant allowed her young daughter to go and keep her com- pany. The defendant struck the girl with a knife, and she ran home frightened. The complainant, went to him for an explanation, and the defendant immediately assaulted him. Oakes had to pay the costs, and was bound over to keep the peace.—Margaret Wheeler, 79, Lower Bank-street was charged with assaulting Annie Lee, 81, Lower Bank-street. The defendant had abused the complainant because she thought she had given certain information to the inspector of nuisances.—The defendant was bound over to keep the peace.
WARRINGTON OCCASIONAL COURT. MONDAY.—Before_Mr. James Tinsley.

DAM (Cilis7G TURNIPS—AIfred Field was cilarged with doing damage to turnips, belonging to William Bennett, at Poulton, on Saturday.—The evidence showed that the prisoner was seen gathering turnips by the prosecutor, who handed him over to P.C. Fleming.—On promising to go to Manchester,:the prisoner was discharged.

DARESBURY PET l'Y SESSIONS. TuFsray.—Before Messrs. J. C. Parr, H. Neild, and W. Long. Dnornr AND DISORDERLY.—George Johnson and Win. Bate, at Preston Brook, on the 23rd inst., were fined 2s. 6d. each.—Edward Thomason, shoemaker, at Whitley, on the 30th ult. The police officer who proved the charge said the defendant was shouting very much. —Defendant I was shouting same as I do many a time —cub-hunting. (Laughter.)—There was much specula- tion as to what he meant by cub-hunting, and nothing more could be got out of him than that he had been cub-hunting, except that he had been doing that for many a year.—The case was dismissed. CHARGES OF ASSAULT.—Joseph Green, farmer's teams- man, was charged with assaulting John Warburton, farmer, Cartledge-lane, Grappenhall, on the 27th of July and John Warburton was cross-summoned on a charge of assaulting Green on the same date. Mr. Browne appeared for Warburton and Mr. P. Davies for Green.— John Warburton said on Sunday afternoon the 24th of July, his son Arthur came into the house and complained of certain conduct to him by Green. Witness went out and asked him what he had done to the lad, and he said " Nowt," and told him with an oath to go in to his calf. He came up to him put his toe against witness's foot, and put his face up to complainant's mouth and struck him on the side of the head. Witness did not to his recollection call him a scamp and a rogue, or strike him. Witness could not say that he had been reported to Mr. Mortimer and Mr. Mclver for shooting partridges. He would not:say that he had not. —Arthur Warburton deposed to Green misbehaving to him, and to witness complaining to Mr. Warburton.— Sarah Warburton, wife of John, corroborated as to the alleged assault on her husband. She denied that her husband knocked Green's hat off.—Edward O'Brien also corroborated, and said Warburton shoved Green to defend himself .—Patrick Clark said he saw Warburton lift his hand to Green.—Mr. Davies called William Johnson, employed by Mr. Warburton, why said the boy had a sheep dog, and Green complained about the dog, and started tickling the lad and pulled his brace undo ne, and he complained to his father, who appealed to witness, and he said nothing had been done that was any harm. Green said he had done " nowt," and Warburton called him a liar and a scamp. They got close together, and Warburton shoved Green and knocked his hat off. Then Green knocked Warburton's hat off, and no more blows were struck. Green told Warburton to go in to his calf.—By Mr. Brown, War- burton told Green if he had done nothing to the lad there was an end of it, and Green said there was not, and threatened to punch the lad when be caught him. —By Mr. Davies: He did not suppose Green would have hit Warburton if Warburton had not struck tirst.—Thos. Craigen and Mrs, Ainsworth said Warburton was the aggressor.—Joseph Green denied this, and corroborated Johnson's account as to what he did to the lad.—Mr. Davies said the summons against Green was a matter of spite because he had reported Warburton for shooting partridges.—The Bench after some private consideration, bound Green over in £5 to keep the peace for three months, and dismissed the case against Warburton. CHARGE AGAINST MR. FARR'S GARDENER.—DILATORY Snrmrcit OF SMAMONSES. Roderick Elphinstone was charged with being drunk and disorderly at Stockton Heath, on the 6th August. The defendant being gardener to Mr. Parr, who had presided during the pre- vious business, that gentleman now left the Court, the chair being taken by Mr. Long. Two constables gave evidence in support of the charge. Mr. Browne, who de- fended, said he had often complained there about the manner in which summonses were served by the police. Summonses were served weeks after the offence occurred and after a defendant had no chance of getting up a case. The offence in the present case was committed on the 6th of August, and the summons was not served on the defendant until the 27th. He tMr. Browne) did not think this was right.—Several witnesses were called who denied that the defendant was drunk.—The Bench dis- missed the case, the Chairman expressing the hope that the state of things as to the service of summonses of which Mr. Browne complained, would be remedied.— Superintendent Atherton promised to see into the matter. OFFENDING CYCLISTS .--Frederick Upton,of Macclesfield, for riding a bicycle at 10 p.m., without a li,e,ht, was fined 2s. 6d., and Henry Manley and William Johnson. both of Penketh for riding bicycles on the footpath at Walton, on the 23rd ult., were fined ss. each, SLEEPING DRlVERS.—ratrick Hannon asleep in charge of his lorry on the 29th of August at Appleton, 2s. 6d. Andrew Wilson and Reuben Wilson for similar offences, at Stretton and Walton respectively, were fined, the former ss. and the latter 10s.—Samuel Johnson for a like offence at Whitley was fined 2s. 6cl. RIDING WITHOUT RElNS.—Frederick Platt, of Little Leigh, charged with riding without reins, was dismissed. KEEPING A DOG WITHOUT LICENCE.—John Warburton, farmer, Cartledge-lane, Grappenhall, was charged with / keeping a dog without a licence on the 16th of August. Mr. Browne defended, and, P.C. Millington having given
evidence against the defendant, called his brother and son who stated that they had drowned the dog on August 15th. The case was dismissed.

div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 3, 1892.
CRICKET.

Secretaries of Cricket Clubs are requested to note that reports of matches played on Saturday must be sent to the head office, Bewsey-street, Warrington, not later than ten o'clock on Wednesday morning.

WARRINGTON V. LIVERPOOL.—This match, which was set apart for the benefit of A. Clark, the respected pro- fessional wicket-keeper of the Warrington Club, was in- terfered with by rain to such an extent on Saturday, that only 35 minutes' play was indulged in, when the game was abandoned. It was to be regretted, as a large number of speetators had assembled. Warrington won the toss, and took up the defence, Messrs. R. Smith and J. J. Crosfield being the first representatives,the two pro- fessionals, Shoutbridge and Creber being the bowlers. Runs came but slowly at first, but eventually J. J. Cros- field got the first-named fast bowler nicely to the bound- ary, and, four more runs resulting from the same over, he was shunted for E. C. Hornbv. The score gradually rose, and no impression could be made on the batsmen, runs coming more freely. The light became terribly bad with the score at 33. At this total a double change was resorted to, H. B. Steel and A. L. Melly going on. The total had only reached 43 when the rain came down in real earnest, and after waiting nearly an hour, the match was abandoned at a draw :

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND
ATHLETICS.
CRICKET.

The season is expiring in the midst of a brilliant dis- play of cricket fireworks. Lancashire's defeat of Notts and the magnificent hitting of the Somersetshire cracks will render the close of the present season memorable in the annals of the national game. The past week was crammed with good cricket. Surrey has once more secured the honour of the Blue Ribbcn, partly by its own splendid play and partly by the default of Notts, which has broken down just at the moment when the coveted prize was fairly within its grasp. There will be much lamentation at Trent Bridge, and many vain regrets that the Nottingham players in their anxiety not to be defeated were obliged to be content with that draw against Gloucester which a little self-denial would so easily have converted into a victory.

The performances of the Somersetshire cricketers stand out in bold relief. They have defeated Middlesex by 70 runs,and against Yorkshire they made the highest score of the year. Messrs. Hewitt and Paleiret were the heroes of the encounter with the Tykes, the former achieving the excessively rare honour of an innings of thore than 200 runs, and the latter coming a splendid second with an innings of 146. A reference to the averages will show how magnificently these two Varsity players have maintained their reputation as the most" exhilararating " batsmen in England.

Mr. Palairet has been declared as the" coming man" in cricket, and the Oxford captain apparently intends to justify the selection of him as the successor, in batt- ing, at all events, to Mr. Grace. The match with York- shire was, unfortunately drawn in consequence of the vagaries of what in this country is called weather, but already 891 runs had been obtained for the loss of 20 wickets. Somersetshire have now to meet Sussex, and the result of the encounter will in all probability ensure tkem the third place in the contest for the championship.

Another great scoring match was that between Kent and Sussex, in which 874 runs were scored for the loss of 29 wickets. Mr. Le Fleming, a famous footballer and hurdler, who has been too often absent from the Kent team, scored 131 runs in three boors; but his perform- ance was overshadowed by the double century of Mr. G. Braun, for Sussex. It was one of the finest perform- ances of the season, and places Mr. Brann amongst the exceedingly select few who have attained the distinction of scoring a "century" twice in the same match. The Kentish men would undoubtedly have won the match if relentless time had not interposed, and they must be credited with a very fine display of cricket.
In the matches against Somerset and Yorkshire the champion played splendid cricket, and his scores of 89 and 61 have materially improved his position in the averages.

Shrewsbury still heads the season's averages for first- class matches, his figures being 4200. for 30 completed innings. We cannot, however, overlook the unpleasant fact that his last four essays with the bat have realised but 18, 0, 16, and o—a crab-like rate of progress which may end in his being speedily overtaken. Although the famous Notts professional enjoys premier position at the present he no longer possesses the largest aggregate. Hewett with 1,299 runs has a slight advantage in this respect, and as this gentleman has still opportunities of tatting against Gloucestershire and Sussex, whose bowl- ing is not too deadly, it is quite on the cards that he

may yet depose Shrewsbury. As Stanley Scott and William Gunn have each passed into a total of four figures for,the season, six batesmen have already scored over 1,000 runs in 1892, and four of these are amateurs. As Gilbert Grace and Walter Read are also likely to score 1,000 are the curtain is rung down in September, it must be confessed that the amateurs have covered themselves with glory during the past three months.

Lockwood, who has been the most successful bowler in the Surrey eleven, occupies the first position in the companion table of averages for the present campaign with 138 wickets for 13.44 runs each. Still he is closely pressed by Mold, who obtained twelve Notts wickets for 100 runs. This has helped him, and his record is now 120 wickets for an average of 13.63. As Briggs has also dismissed 124 men for 13.74 runs each. Lancastrians will be delighted to see their two chief bowlers among the first three in the country.

It is stated that about £l5O has beers subscribed in Notts for presentation to the county cricket team, in order to mark the enthusiasm the eleven aroused by; their earlier performances this season. A cloud may possibly o'ershadow the gathering, but Notts people should remember that good sportsmen are not too elated by success nor too cast down by defeat. That a sum of £l5O can be raised in Notts for this purpose shows that the love of cricket has not entirely died within the confines of the county.

div.head: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.
ANNUAL INSPECTION.

In November next the Widnes Local Board will turn over to the Corporation then to be formed, an estate such as few, if any, towns of a similar size can boast, and the members on Thursday last week made their last annual inspection of the property. The " last inspection" was announced twelve months ago in the expectation that ere another year had rolled by, the town would have been elevated into a full fledged borough, but the circumlocution of the London Authorities caused this hope to be unfulfilled, and the Local Board remained in power. However, this occasion was positively the last on which the Local Board would take a survey of the valuable property of the ratepayers,and the follow- ing members and officials put in an appearance at the Town Hall at 11 o'clock :—Messrs. B. Brown, J. Tilley, D. Wright, J. Midwood, R. Cook, J. Taylor, 0.1. Neil, T. Owns, J. Bench, H. S. Oppenheim (clerk), J. (;raik (assistant clerk), I. Carr (engineer), J. S. Sinclair (surveyor), and W. Lowe (nuisance inspectot). Two waggonettes from the livery, stables of Mr. J. H. Lee were in attendance, and the drive through the sur- rounding country, which the inspection renders neces- sary, was made in fine weather, for which all concerned were duly thankful. The West Bank Promenade was tho first place visited. Here through the excavation of rock along the foreshore by the Ship Canal Co., the " scour "of the tide had been much increased, and the foundations of the promenade were being undermined by the action of the water. Negotiations took place between the Local Board and the Company, who even- tually agreed to contribute £l5O towards the cost of re- pairing the mischief caused. At the time of the visit Messrs. Roberts Bros., whose tender of £2lB had been accepted, were engaged in placing round the base of the promenade a concrete belt, in the shape of a footpath 175 yards long, five feet wide, and varying in thickness from lit. 6in. to 31t. This is the scheme of the Surveyor, Mr. Sinclair, and when the footpath is completed it will form a pleasant promenade, besides arresting the des- tructive effects of the waves of the Mersey.

THE ACCIDENT HOSPITAL. which is in the neighbourhood,was found to be a picture of cleanliness and order, and upon this the matron, Miss Warburton, was complimented. Seven of the ten beds in the institution were occupied. It was observed that extensive alterations were being made in the gar- den, where a couple of convalescents were basking in the sun. Formerly the garden sloped rapidly to the river ; the surveyor is now having it made into two terraces, which will be planted with shrubs, and a rookery will be formed. Again entering the convey- ances

THE GAS WORKS were quiekly reached, and great interest was mani- fested in the processes carried on. The new purifying house was in complete working order, and it was gratify- ing to learn that a much purer gas was now distributed, in consequence of the improved appliances. In No. 1 retort house half of the retorts are fitted with the Dinsmote patent, and are heated by regenerator furnaces, adapted by Mr. Carr, which have resulted in a great saving of fuel. It was mentioned that during the past month the illuminating power of the gas had averaged about 20 candles. The tar plant, ammonia soda works, engine houses, stores, &c., were visited, and everything found highly satisfactory. The producing power of the works is 1,000,000 cubic feet per day of 24 hours, while the average consumption is from 300,000 cubic feet in sum- mer to 600,000 cubic feet in winter. During the past year the profit on the works was about £3,000, although 1 the price of gas is only Is. 10d. and 2s. per 1,000 cubic feet. There is not a gas works in England making so small a quantity of gas where the price is anything near so low, and just across the river at Runcorn the gas consumers have to pay 3s. 24. per 1,000 cubic feet. These facts are striking testimony to the admirable management of the Gas Committee, of which Mr. Brown is chairman, and to the ability of Mr. Carr, the engineer. After a short drive

THE FEVER HOSPITAL at Halton View was reached, and this most useful in- stitution was found to be in admirable order. Miss Milburn, the matron, informed the members that out of the 28 beds, six were in use, five by typhoid fever patients, and one by a scarlet fever patient, and all were convalescent. The grounds were looking very bright and fresh, and apparently the chemical gases seldom reach the snot. Re-entering the conveyances there was a pleasant drive through the ancient village of Farnworth to rex Hill, where the covered reservoirs are situated. The large one, which is one of the largest in the world, has a holding capacity of 10,0007000 gallons, and was nearly full, the depth registered being 19ft 3in. The small reservoir has a capacity of half a million gallons. There is a total storage at Pex Hill of nearly a week's supply for the town. The view from the Hill was much admired, and regret was expressed that the place was not easier of access to the townspeople. The gardens are well kept by caretaker Platt. Refresh- ment having been partaken of, the drive was continued

div.head: STOCHSWELL PUMPING. STATION,
div.p: STOCHSWELL PUMPING. STATION,

where there was nothing new to chronicle.' Everything was in capital order. It was satisfactory to learn that during the past four years the water had maintained its height at 901 t. from the ground, although, during this time,more than double the quantity of water previously pumped had been brought to the surface. This would indicate that there is an almost inexhaustible supply of water at this place. The engine is capable of pumping 1.1 million gallms per day. _ _

NETHHRLNY PUMPING STATION. Another brief drive brought the party to Netherley Pumping Station. Here most important additions have been and are being made. Two bore holes have been sunk, an engine house built, and at the time of the visit men were at work putting down the engine and neces- sary machinery for pumping. TRH ENOINS ROUSE _ _ _ .

has been built by Messrs. Henshaw and Sons, of Liver- pool, from the designs of Colonel Ellison (Messrs. Ellison and Son, Liverpool). The original buildings at Nether- ley were built 12 years ago from the plans of Colonel Ellison, which were accepted in public competition, and so satisfactorily have those buildings proved both in design and in quality of work that the Board had no hesitation in asking Colonel Ellison to prep ire the designs of the new structure. The new building is in the Gothic style of architecture, to harmonise with the rest of the buildings ; and altogether they make an im- posing block. It is constructed of selected grey brick. with red brick and stone facings. The roof is worked into towers at both ends, this arrangement being made in order to all the• pumping trees to be drawn out through the roof withottt injury to the building. The ceiling is a very handsome one of varnished pitch pine. The interior is worked with a deep dado of Ruabon red bricks, with piers of the same, material, and a frieze carrying the beam upon which the beams are supported from the travelling crane. The wall is built in panels ' with coloured flats. This building has cost £1,600, and several members expressed astonishment at the low amount, one gentleman remarking that they could not get chapels built at that prive. Altogether the buildings at this station have cost £7,ooo,including the workmen's cottages.

TILE ENGINES and pumping machinery have been supplied by Messrs. Hathorn, Davey, and Company, the eminent firm of water engineers, of Leeds, and they ware being fixed under the superintendence of Mr. Briggs, their chief foreman. The amount of the contract is £5,600. The engine is a horizontal compound condensing engine, which is a new type for this class of work- It will pump from two boreholes 20 feet apart ; each borehole is 30 inches diameter to a depth of 200 feet, and 18 inches diameter for a further depth of 200 feet in Number One borehole ; and is further 400 feet in Number two bore- hole. The suction of the pumps extends 200 feet down each borehole. On risin!,r to the surface the water flows into a tank, whence it is forced to the reservoirs at Pex Hill by a double-acting piston force pump. The engines and pumps are expected to be finished and ready for working in their work time. There would appear to be - -

div.head: NO FEAR OF A WATER FAMINE. _
div.p: NO FEAR OF A WATER FAMINE. _

At -present 11 million gallons per day can be pumped at Netherley, and the new engine is expected to pump an additional 2/ millions per day; so that with Stocks- well, the Board will be able to provide five million gallons per day for the use of the district. As the daily conumption is only three million gallons per day at the present time, this supply should be quite ample for many years to ume. There is a fine reserve supply of water at Belle Vale, where the members found water running out of the borehole in a constant and voluminous stream.

div.head: TEA AND TOASTS.
div.p: TEA AND TOASTS.

This concluded the inspection,and the party were then driven to Ohildwall Abbey Hotel, where they partook of a knife and fork tea. In addition to the members, Col. Ellison and Mr. Briggs Were present. Mr. Brown pre- sided, and Mr. Oppenheim occupied the vice-chair. After tea Mr. Oppenhehn read the following extract from a letter he received from Mr. F. H. Gossage,J.P.,

- CHAIRMAN OF THE BOARD - who has unfortunately had to have an operation per- formed upon his eye. Writing from Wiesbaden on the 22nd inst. Mr. Gossage said :—" Will you please ex- press to the members of the Board at the annual inspec- tion how very much I regret not being able to be present. I think the Board is to be much congratulated on the progress of its business during • this the last twelve months of its existence. lam glad to say my eye is making steady progress, although it is slow, and I fear I cannot calculate on being back at Widnes under an- other fortnight."—Mr. Brown said they were very sorry that Mr. Gossage could not be among them but were glad to hear that his eye was going on satisfactorily. He suggested that the Clerk should write to Mr. Gossage to that effect, and the suggestion was unanimously agreed to. At a later stage Mr. Brown proposed

- "SUCCESS TO THE NSW WORKS." He said it had been a pleasure for the members to go round the works, and he thought they had every reason tote satisfied at the way in which they had found everything. He also thought that the Committee had I acted wisely iq accepting the practical suggestions of Mr. Carr in regard to the new engines. They had departed somewhat from the style of the engines at the other wells,and were pumping direct froth the boreholes, thus doing away with a considerable expense—the sav- ing would probably amount to £lOOO. He was pleased to bear his testimony to Mr. Carr's able and energetic management ; and they were also fortunate in having the services of Messrs. Hathorn, Davey, and Co. to con- struct their engines. rhe building spoke for itself, and they were glad to have Col. Ellison among them. They regretted the absence of their Chairman, and also that Mr. Samuel Sadler was prevented from attending by a very severe affliction, from which he was happily recovering.—The toast was duly honoured. Col. Ellison proposed the health of the Chairman, to whom he referred in eulogistic terms. He also thanked the Board for the confidence they had reposed in him in allowing him to make the addition to the buildings he designed sotneyears ago.—Mr. Carr, in .supporting the toast, said that the Gas and Water Committee had always had the advantage of having an energetic and practical chairman. The reservoirs at Pox Hill reflected great credit upon the engineer who designed them, the committee which carried the work out, and the contrac- tor who erected them. Those reservoirs would stand I for generations, and he thought it was only right that I they should remember the people who had gone befcre them and done such splendid work. If the committee in erecting the reservoirs had followed a cheese- paring policy, and only built them one-quarter the present size, they_ would not now have been Isufficient to supply the wants of the town, as the I storage capacity and pumping machinery would not have been sufficient to tide them over breakdowns and I other difficulties. To Igr. Gossage, Mr. Gaskell, and IMr. Brown, who had been backed up by strong commit- tees, their thanks were due for the practical way in which the works had been carried out. (Hear, hear).— The toast was drunk, and acknowledged by Mr. Brown, who thanked the members for their confidence, remark- ing that his idea of public work was to do honest and sound work independent of any criticism, only striving to do the right and satisfy his conscience. (Applause.)— Subsequently, Mr. Beech proposed the toast of the "Chairmen of other Committees," coupled with the names of Mr. D. Wright and Mr. Midwood, who both responded. Mr. Wright proposed the health of the officials, and the Clerk and Surveyor responded.

div.head: RUNCORN VOLUNTEER SHOOTING CLUB. VISIT TO THE ISLE OF MAN.
div.p: RUNCORN VOLUNTEER SHOOTING CLUB. VISIT TO THE ISLE OF MAN.

The above Club, on the occasion of tilt battalion camping at Douglas at the beginning of this month resolved to have a match with the resident corps, but this was frustrated owing to the Manx Volun- teers being in camp at Stronsall during the same week, Arrangements, however, were subsequently made for a portion of the club to re-visit the Island for the purpose of having a shooting match. On Friday afternoon Colour-Sergeants J Mort and J. Poole, Sergts. W. H. Harvey, J. W. Woodland J. A. Rushton, and R. ' Cooper, Lance-Corporal Neild, and Bandsman J. Gitteus, proceeded to Douglas. By the kind permission of the , Isle of Man Steam Company, saloon passes were granted at steerage fares. The passage was very rough, and calculated to unnerve shooting men. The troubles of the voyage, however,were soon forgotten on landing, for there they received a hoarty welcome, and were pro- vided with a substantial' meal. Next morning, the weather proving propitious, a start was made by wag- gonettes to Castletown, which was reached about noon. Shooting was promptly commenced, and ended in a victory for the visitors by 138 points, the total being 554, and the Isle of Man 418. The range at Castletown is very pleasantly situated, being open to the sea, but both teams found it exceed- ingly difficult to put on tall scores, as a very strong wind was blowing from the right. It has been said that "every bullet has its ' but if, as is to be pre- sumed, the bull's eye was the destined billet on this occasion, certainly a considerable number failed in their destiny. Colour-Sergeant Mort's magnificent score at 500 yards of 34 out of a possible 35 was a notable excep- tiop, and elicited well-deserved applause from his op- ponents' team, which consisted of Lieutenant Dearden, Sergeants S. Maden, J. Nicholls, and Acheson, Corporal Corkhill, and Private Rivers, Duggin, and Moore. After the competition a first-class dinner was partaken of at the Castle Hotel, provided at the expense of the home team. Several hours were spent in a convivial manner. The company returned to Douglas, reaching there about 10 o'clock. Sunday being church parade in connection with the Isle of Man Volunteers, the contin- gent from Runcorn accompanied them to service in accordance with the pressing invitation of the Major. The Runcorn team got on board the steamer on Sunday at midnight and reached home about eight o'clock on Monday mocning, thorougtily satisfied with their pleasant outing. The members of the team speak in high praise of the kind and genial manner in which they were treated by their confreres in the Island.

div.head: R.UNCORN, WESTON, AND 11A.LTON WATERWORKS CO.
div.p: R.UNCORN, WESTON, AND 11A.LTON WATERWORKS CO.

The annual meeting of the shareholders of this company was bald on Monday afternoon in the Public flail, Runcorn, for the purposes of declaring a dividend, electing a director, appointing an auditor, and for reducing the number of directors from six to five. The chair was occupied by Mr. John Brundrit,and there were also present ;—Messrs. John Simpson, William Whittaker, and William Hayes (directors) ; and W. F. Salkeld secretary. The report a the directors stated that the reonnue showed a balance of £997 4s. 1.1d.' including £242 7s. 3d. brought from the previous half-year, out of which the directors recommended a dividend of five pounds per centum per annum, payable on and after the first day of October, which wbuld absorb £750, leaving a balance of £247 4s. lid, to be carried forward. The machinery and plant were all in very good order. The Chairman, in submitting the adoption of the report, stated that everything was going on most satis- factory. The Directors had lately entered into provi- sional agreement with the Manchester Ship Canal Co.' who wanted a large supply, and this would be provided from the Liverpool Corporation pipes. This, according to Act of Parliament, would require the sanction of the shareholders, at a meeting to be specially convened for , the purpose, and any remarks thereon he reserved until that meeting, which would be called in the course of a few days. With regard to a .special supply of water to Ruocorm it might be known that the Runcorn Commis- sioners had approached them,, but negotiations had not arrived at that position, when It was possible to lay be- fore the shareholders anything bf a tangible character. If anything came of the proposal they would receive the earliest possible intimation. There bad been an increase of 87 in the number of houses to be supplied, making the following totals :—Runcorn, 4,264; Weston, 365; and Halton, 145; or in all, 4,744. Everything was going on in a highly satisfactory manner. Mr. Whittaker seconded the proposition, which was carried. Mr. Hayes prAposed, Mr. Simpson seconded, and it was resolved, that the number of directors be reduced from six to five. ' On the proposition of Mr. Whittaker, seconded by Mr. Hayes, it was decided that Mr. Thomas Bankes, of Weston, be re-elected a director. Mr. James Collier was re-appointed auditor to the company. On the proposition of Mr. Whittaker, seconded by the Chairman, a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. W. F. Salkeld, secretary, and his assistants.

THE CHOLERA.
CASES IN LONDON AND TIIE COUNTRY.

Fresh cases of cholera in London were reported on Tuesday to the Local Government Board. The sufferers were passengers in the steamship Peregrine, which ar- rived in the Thames on the 29th inst. from Hamburg; but they got to their homes in the City-road before the symptoms manifested themselves. It is stated that Eugene McCarthy, a house wrecker, residing at the White Horse, 90, Fetter-lane, was taken into St. Bartholomew's Hospital on Monday suffering from symptoms of Asiatic cholera, and that he died there the same night. A claolera patient was removed to the floating hospital at Grimsby on Tuesday, although the case is not sup- posed to be of the Asiatic type. The man Walworth, who died at Bolton from Asiatic cholera, was buried on Tuesday, the interment being carried out under the surveillance of sanitary authori- ties, every precaution being taken to prevent Contagion. The house has been taken charge of by the authorities, and is being thoroughly fumigated. Dr. Lissamaii,whi; has had considerable experience of the disease abroad, certified the case as one of true Asiatic cholera. The schooner Helene, which arrived at Gravesend in tow of a Dover tug about midnight on Tuesday. was found, on being inspected by Drs. VVhitcombe and Col- lingridge, to have two cases of cholera on board. The vessel was at once placed in quarantine.
SUPPOSED CASES IN LIVERPOOL.
PRECAUTIONS ON AMERICAN LINERS.

The various Liverpool steamship companies are taking every possible step to ensure the complete disinfection of the emigrants, of whatever nationality, who are pro- ceeding to America by their vessels. The United States consular authorities in this city have received very stringent instructions from the American Government as to the steps to be taken, and under these instructions no emigrants are to be allowed to embark in American- bound steamships unless their clothes and effects have been subjected to a thorough process of steam disinfec- tion.

At the Southhill Hospital, Liverpool, the four patients who are said to be suffering from cholera are receiving the most unremitting attention from the hospital staff, and from Dr. Hope, the assistant medical officer, whose zeal in coping with or providing for every possible con- I tingency that may arise is praiseworthy in the extreme. The Press Association learns upon inquiry at the Local Government Board that over 100 passengers arrived from Hamburg on the 28th ultimo in the steamship Peregrine and dispersed at Harwich, from which port the City-road patients, one of wham has since died, travelled by train to London. Every effort is being made by the authorities to trace these passengers. A number of them have already been traced, and official communications have been sent to thesanitary authorities of the districts to which they belong. Three suspicious cases have been removed to the hospital at Falmouth from the steamship Clement March, which left two of her crew in the hospital at Hamburg. A suspicious case has alio been placed in the hospi tat at Tynemouth from the ship Garona which was also the source of a case now being treated at Middles- borough. It was learned upon Inquiry at the London Hospital that the two infants who were removed there on Tues- day in the belief that they were suffering from cholera died on Wednesday. During their illness the doctors stated that the symptoms were not those of cholera, but of acute cliarrlicea, and the post-mortem examination proved that they died from the effects of acute diarrlicea, there being no symptoms of cholera present. Great anxiety exists at Cardiff in reference to the cholera epidemic. The precautions taken against the introduction of the disease are considered by many to be altogether inadequate. The German named R,...senbaum, who was reported on Tuesday to be suffering from cholera in City-road, London died on Wednesday irtSt. Bartholomew's Hospi- tal, London, whither, together with his wife and chil- dren, who are\also suffering from choler, he was re- moved for the purpose of isolation. The family arrived from Hamburg on Monday,having been on the Continent on their holidays. A telegram from Sheerness, on Wednesday night, states that the cholera cases there are going on favourably. The Helene is undergoing thorough disinfection. The Swansea port sanitary authorities have decided to charter a steamer, for the purpose of inspecting all incoming vessels. Two other seamen from the steam- ship Harrington were removed on Wednesday to the infectious diseases hospital, suffering from choleraic , aymptoms. RAVAGES ON THE CONTINENT.

At Berlin on Tuesday there were altogether about fifty suspected cases of cholera in the Moabit Hospital. Of these three were certified to be Asiatic cholera, but of these patients two had come from Hamburg. There were no deaths, and there was no sign of alarm among the population. A serious disturbance occurred at Weis- senses, a suburb of Berlin, on Monday night at a place of entertainment, arising out of the appearance of a per- formnr. wl,o had come from Hamburg. The police ordered him to leave and, tried to stop the performance, but the crowd prevented them from doing their duty till they had been reinforced. There was a notable decrease in the epidemic at Hamburg on Monday, but it was feared that owing to the return of hot weather the im- provement would not be -naintained. The cases num- bered on Monday 139, and the deaths 43, according to the local authorities. The disease is now nearly as pre- valent in the suburbs, and about ten places in Schleswig- Holstein are now infected. At Antwerp there were 22 cases and four deaths on Monday, and 10 cases and one death on Tuesday. There was one case at the Hague and one case and one death at Brussels. At Havre 71 persons were seized with choleraic symptoms on Monday, and there were 17 deaths. The official returns for St. Petersburg show that on Monday there were 156 cases and 41 deaths. According to a Rome correspondent there have been some sporadic eases in various parts of Italy. Only one case in the Austrian Empire is reported, that of a latter sorter at Pilgen, who had handled postal matter coming from Germany. The Austrian police have suppressed a Vienna paper which reported that the pre- cautions taken on the Bohemian frontier were insuffi- cient. The Portuguese Government has declared the port of Gravesend to be infected. ALARMING NEWS MOM HAMBURG.

HAMBURG, WEDNESDAY—The situation, far from showing the improvement so confidently anticipated yesterday morning, is becoming worse and worse. There are now 400 dead bodies lying unburied in the military drill shed. It is sometimes a matter of great , difficulty to obtain the papers of identification required for the interment of the dead, as whole families have perished. Many businesses, Including grocers', bakers', and butchers', shops, have been closed by the police owing to cases of cholera having occurred among the employes and salesmen. The epidemic now tends to spread to the suburbs and the villages around Hamburg. The Prussian Ministry of War has sent orders to the garrison lazaretto at Altona to supply 500 beds to the Hamburg hospitals. The offices of the registrars of death are now kept ,open until ten in the evening, and will also be open on Sundays. HAMBURG, WEDNESDAY ( LATER', . —During tne 24 hours ending midnight yesterday the ambulances carried away 508 patents, and 268 died, or a total of 776, against 650 on the preceding day. HAMBURG, WEDNESDAY EVENING—The Chamber of Commerce has undertaken the formation of a relief committee for the alleviation of the distress which has been caused by the epidemic. Cases of cholera are now becoming more frequent amongst the middle and upper classes. BERLIN, WEDNESDAY.—The official cholera return is- sued by the Berlin Board of Health, states that 425 fresh cases of cholera and 219 deaths occurred at Ham- burg yesterday. In Berlin three persons were seized with the disease, and one died yesterday. At Madgeburg there were three cases and one (leath. There were also two cases at Lubeck tc-day. A t Altona eleven cases, not 15 as at first reporte ccurred on the 28th inst., and 20 cases and eight ,aths on the 29th. Isolated cases are reported fro,, „ne district of Stade, from five localities in the dist, of Schleswig, from seven in Mecklenburg-Schwerin,and from two in Saxe-Altenhuro. GRON/YGEN, WEDNESDAY.—A man who had arrived here from Hamburg died of cholera yesterday. Measures have been taken to arrest the spread of the disease. COPENHAGEN, WEDNESDAY EVENING.—TIIO man who contracted cholera from conveying to burial the remains of the person from Hamburg, who died of cholera at Aarhus (Jutland), has died of the disease.
