div.head: TIT BITS
div.p: TIT BITS
THE SCOT ABROAA,

A story was told during the Crimean war of the , disappointment of an Englishman who went out to the East as an interpreter, and whose ruling Passion was a hatred of everything Scotch; but, strolling through the camp with a Turkish °Meer, ' and abusing the Scotch to his heart's content, to 1,31,4 astonishment Hassan Bey, the Turk, broke out, tell ye whaat, ;na mon, gin ye daur lowse Yere tongue upon My country like thaat, I'll gVe ye a cloot on the lug that'll mak' it tingle fra this till Ilallowe'en 1" The thunderstruck Englishman stammered out, "Why, my good man, I thought You were a Turk !" "And sae I am a Turk the ma braw chiel," said the angry Glasgow Mussui.nan "but my faither's auld leather breeks be'er travelled farther than just fra Glasgow to GreLlock and back again; but when I gang hame— as I'll do or its lang—l'll just be Wuily Forbes, son 0' auld Daddy Forbes o' the Gorbals, for a' that's come and gane " Presently a splendidly dressed Ilengarian came up, and said to the Turk, oily, men, there's a truce the noo for twa hours—just come wi' me and we'll hae a glass o' whisky thegither." It was the ssme with a Russian officer, until the Englishman exclaimed, "Bless heart, is everybody on earth a Scotchman ? Perhaps 1 am one myself without knowing it."' Lut when the Russian General Tarassoff exclaimed, " Eh, Donald Cawmell I are you here ?" and Ibrahim Pasha burst forth, simultaneously, " What, Sandy Robertson I can this be you ?" the Englishtnan beret forth. "It's all over Turks, Ru:sians, Hungarians, English—all Scotchmen I It more than I can bear! I shall go home ! there's nothing left for ine to do here. I sin out as an • interpreter, but if all the nations of Europe talk nothing but Scotch, what use can I be ?" This seems very droll, but it is not more droll than real. We believe it is Sir Archi- bald Ali:on who mentions how, when Marshal Keith was combating the Turkish forces Under the Grand Vizier, the two generals came to conference with each other; the Grand Vizier came mounted on ta•camel, in all the pomp of Eastern magnificence; the Scotch Marshal Keith, Who originally came from the neighbourhood of reterhead, in Aberdeenshire, approached on horseback. After the conference the Turkish Grand Vizier said to Keith that he would like to speak a few Words in private to him in his tent, and he begged that no one should accompany him. Mar- shal Keith accordingly went in, and the moment they conferred the Grand Vizier threw off his turban, tore off his beard, and running to Marshal Keith, said, "Oh, Johnnie, foo's a' wi' ye man?" and he then discovered that the Grand Vizier of Turkey was a schoolfellow of his own who had disappeared about thirty years before from a parish school near Methlick. And we remember to have met with an anecdote of a Scotchman from Perth, who had penetrated into ,some far interior of Asia—we forget where; he fled to see the Pasha or Bashaw. He was intro- duced to the comely man In his tent. They gathered up their knees, and sat down upon their carpets. They drank their strong coffee and smoked their hookahs together in solemn silence; few words at any rate) passed between them, but, We may ;rust, sufficient for the occasion; but, ...When the man of Perth was about to leave, the &aka also rose and following him outside the 'eagood, said, in g:el strong Doric Scotch, "I kenned verra well in Perth; ye are just sae an sae." Li.ae Perth man was astonished, as well he might ?e, until the Pasha explained, as ,he said, "I'm I.tat a Perth man mysel' I " Ile had travelled and bad become of importance to the Government there. Ile was an illustration of the übiquity of his race,

div.head: PEASANT AND THE EMPEESIRt
div.p: THE PEASANT AND THE EMPEESIRt

A Persian emperor, when hunting, perceived & !ell' old man planting a walnut-tree, and advancing rvards him, asked his e. The peasant replied: lam four years old." An attendant rebuked a.ini for uttering such absurdity in the presence of the emperor. You censure me without cause," replied the peasant; "I did not speak without retlection, for the wise do not reckon that time Which has been lost in folly and the cares of the World ; I, therefore, consider that to be my real age which has been passed in serving the Deity and discharging my duty to society.' The emperor, struck with the singularity of the remark, observed : "Thou canst not hope to see the trees then art planting come to perfection." "True " !,laswered the sage; "but since others have planted -gnat we might eat, it is right that we Should plant for the benefit of other." " Excel- lent !" exclaimed the emperor, upon which (as Was the custom when any one was honoured with "no applause of the sovereign), a purse-bearer Presented the old man with a thousand pieces of ; on receiving them the shrewd peasant 'Jade a low obeisance, and added: "0, king I Other men's trees come to perfection in the space af forty years, but mine have produced fruit as 8"n as they were planted." "Bravo I" said the nlonarch, and a second purse of gold was pre- aented, when the old man exclaimed: "The trees of others bear fruit only once a year, but ine have yielded two crops in one day. " De- htful I" replied the emperor, and a third purse gold was given, after which, putting spurs to 41ie horse, the monarch retreated, saying: ' Rev- erend father, I dare not stay longer, lest thy wit Could exhaust my treasury."

div.head: LOST ANGEL.
div.p: A LOST ANGEL.
AN OLD ARTIST'S STORY.
It was in an old' artist's studio that I saw the picture called "A Lost Angel." Near it hung a head which was catalogued "A Cherub."

In these two works the extremes of human expression were depicted. ;rho larger, in fact, merited the name bestowed upon it. The smaller seemed too sweet for anything but heaven. A mother might have said: "Thus my child —must look in Paradise ;" but it was almost impossible to believe that such a divine creature actually .existed. on earth.

"Every one sari something like that," said the old artist whose work it was. "I saw that face in Florence, years ago. A mallet and child at together at the dam of. the little vine.wreathed stone house. The woman was sweet simplicity itself. The child far more beautiful ,that that attempt to reprnduce its features. Ifelt that I should, never again have so angelic a model, and advancing, requested the mother to allow me to sketch her child.

"'I will pay you I said. Do you think you can persuade him to be quiet?' "She gave rue a bright smile of assent. "'Yes,' she' answered. 'Little 'Sider shall pose for the Signor Artist. It is time he began. He must earn his bread as a model. It was his poor father's business before he died. He was said to be the handsomest model in Florence. They painted him for their lovers; and little Isidor re- sembles his father.'
." His mother, also,' I said. "She laughed, but answered in business-like fashion:

"'Oh, I'm well enough ; but they only engage me when they need peasant women. lam not line like my poor husband; besides, youth is quick to go. Hold up your heaclf Isidor. Show the Signor Painter that you know how to pose.' "The little Italian instantly threw himself into an exquisite attitude. His eyes uplifted, his car- mine lips slightly apart, an ineffable sweetness in his eyes. "'Tell me, then, if I am right,' he said, after a moment, and I nodded an affirmative. Instantly he seemed to have forgotten the Nixed and to be listening to the harps of the angels. One might have fancied that he would vanish like a beauti- ful dream. He seemed too fair, too holy for earth. I painted him with rapture, but at my second sit- ting decided to make a larger portrait than I had at first intended. I presented my first Sketch to kis mother, who received it with delight, and fast- ened it to the wall on which a gilded crucifix and • a print of the Virgin already hung, and I worked many days over my picture. When it was com- pleted I paid my model's mother liberally, gave little Isidor a handful of small Italian coin that made him feel as rich as a king, and departed, sOrry to turn my back on the quaint stone house, the kindly, handsome woman, and the beautiful boy. "Wherever I carried my little angel,4 people exclaimed over the beauty of the face. I think no woman ever saw it without crying out upon the moment: What a lovely child l' I often thought of the boy. In all the years that followed I never forgot him. They were many, for lam an old man now. I was twents-five when I left the little stone house, with the mother and her beautiful boy stand- ing on the high steps under the shadow of a great vine that clung to the old wall. I was sixty when I saw it again—a man with his life behind him. I had achieved some fame; my name was well known, but I was no longer a bright-haired, light-hearted young fellow, with all life's prizes to win.

- - "One or two graves lay across the path I had trodden; many dlsillusions. I thought of the man who had painted little Isidor almost as of some other whom I had known and been fond of. "I stood before the house where little Isidor had lived with his mother. It seemed unchanged. A vine grew over the door, springing, doubtles, from the same roots. The door was fast locked, and in any case it was foolish to fancy that those two dwelt there st4ll. I walked away, and wrapped in a reverie, stumbled over the toes of an old friend, who was a government official, and who seized me by the arm with a light Italian laugh. "'Well met,' he said. "I thought of going to find you. There is sothething in the town which an artist like you must see. It will not be on exhi- tion long, for it is a fine specimen of the genus rascal, and he will be executed in a few days. He is a bandit—a murderer—everything that is horrible. He has cut bff the ears and fingers of his prisoners and sent them to their friends, with intimations that if a certain ransom was not paid, this was only the beginning. "'He was captured at last on a visit to his sick mother, whom he seems to have been fond of. "I went with him. The proper ceremonials were accomplished. As an artist, who wished to transfer this doomed Italian to canvass I was permitted to pass into his cell. " Campani,' said my conductor, "this is a gentleman—an artist who would like to sketch your head, He is a celebrated artist. Your face will be in all the great salons. You will pose for him—wilt you not?' " I have a talent for that,' said Campani, with the air of a monarch receiving ambassadors from a foreign court, and shall rejoice to oblige the Signor Artist. I will look as terrible as possible. The signor, as an artist, will comprehend my motive. The signor will kindly not perpetuate the scars upon my face, which I do nut wish handed down to posterity, as without them I am remarkably handsome.'

"Instantly he assumed an expression for which I have no words, and, with a word of thanks, I fell to work. As the head grew beneath my fingers I found that he was right. The scars and his ex- pression alone made him hideous. His features were perfect. His hair glorious. "• I like it,' he said approvingly, pocketing the money I gave him. Bring me some wine and some cigars, you there! I will drink the signor's health. No thanks. It is a pleasure to pose once more for a true artist.". " Great heavens I' said my friend, as he exam- ined the picture in an outer room. You have made a lost angel of our great brigand, Campani.' . _ .

"I never added the scar. I felt that the brigand was right in his request, from an artistic point of view. "A few days afterward he was executed. "An improvisatore repeated the story of his life in the twilight streets, and women crossed them- selves as they listened. A singer sung an im- promptu song to his guitar, in which the murder, of a lovely English lady by the cruel Campani was vividly portrayed. A man at a corner sold fragments of his garments as charms against bul- lets, and drove a EiTvitiftra7de. The air was full of Campani. Leaving the crowd, I wandered away to the quiet portion of the city, where stood the little stone house where I had sketched the angelic Isidor. Usually peace lay upon it, and its old vine might have shadowed the cell of a hermit. _ _ _
"NOW a crowd surrounded the door. "On its outskirts I saw my own servant, Antoine.

"He bowed and spoke: '"There is something the signor should see. It is the house of the mother of the brigand, Campani. There he was captured. Within is his portrait when a child. I give the signor my word.. that it is angelic.' "'I will see it,' I said. _. . .

" I joined the crowd and paid my bit of silver to a greedy old crone, who gathered the coin into her apron. Two candles burnt in sconces near the object of interest, and, as the peasant, who had been before me, crossed himself and retired, I saw, banging beside a gilded crucifix over the head of the little bed, my own litt)e sketch of the baby, Isidor.

"'lt is like him,' said the old hag at the door. That was my son, Isidor Campani, at the age of five. He was like that, only lovelier. A great Signor painted it. His father was the handsomest man in Florence.'"

AT a zunctay enoot service a clergyman was explaining to a number of smart little urchins the necessity of Christian profession in order properly to enjoy the blessings of Providence in this world, and to make it apparent to the youthful mind he said—" For instance, I want to introduce water into my house. I turn it on. The pipes and faucets and every convenience are in good order, but I get no water. Can any of you tell me why I don't get any water ?" He expected the children to see that it was because he had not made a con- nection with the main in the street. The boys looked perplexed. They could not see why the water should refuse to run into his premises after such faultless plumbing. "Can no one tell me what I have neglected 2" reiterated the good man, looking ot the many wondering faces bowed down by the weight of the problem. "I know," squeaked a little five-year-old. "You don't pay up l"—Lippincott's Magazine.
THE EXAMINER, SATURDA Y, SEPTEMBER 3, 1892

div.head: DEBTORS AND CREDITORS.
div.p: DEBTORS AND CREDITORS.

The cemmon feeling respecting debtors and creditors is very erroneous, and, as is common with popular fallacies, it imposes with double force upon the young and inexperienced. Debtors are repre- sented in all works of fictioe, and in the ordinary language of a large portion of society, as a set of amiable, unfortunate, and most inte4sting persons: Creditors, on the other hand, as an unmingled generation of etecrable wretches, with a hardness of heart that Would not disgrace the executioner, and indeed only one remove from another stony class of men, the much misrepresented gaolers. Now, the person who writes this article has known many debtors and creditors, and he can say that, in by far the most cases, the latter were the better class of men. He alludes, of course, nest° commercial men at large, who are in their own persons, in general, as much of the one thing as the other, but to cases where the creditor is a tradesman, and the debtor a customer; that is, where the debt is not incurred in the intercourse of business, but for the personal use and benefit of the debtor. In these eases, so far from the creditor being an unfeeling and relate les,s;tryaut, as he is generally reresented, he is only the indignant victim of the imprudence or guilt of the debtor. The latter may be as amiable and interestin g person, for we of ten find these charac- teristics united to consummate folly and disregard of the right of others. But the young must beware how they set down debtors, in a class, as purely esti- mable and entitled to sympathy, while they at the same time lock upon creditors •as only ruthless yJersecutors, worthy of the bitterest execration. They may depend upon it that no notion could be more erroneous, no error more apt to be fatal to them in their course through life. They must be in- formed that to incur debt for their own gratifica- tions, without the itbi:ity to discharge it, is just an- other thing for selling themselves as sieves to their creditors. After deing so, they are no longer en- tirely free; part of themselves becomes the property of another, and thus they lose the respect of the world, which cannot see one man indulge in enjoy- ments at the expense of his fellow, without thinking of him very meanly. The incurring of debt for per- sonal gratification is odious for many reasons. In the first place, it violates that rule of nature which appoints every man to work for himself, and only enjoy as he works. It also tends to occasion the rain of innocent persons. Creditors are not in- variably rich, as one would suppose them to be, from reading novels. They are more frequently poor, industrious persons, who, in losing money by their debtors, are apt to be made debtors them- selves, and thereby ruined: In fact, the case stands generally thus :—An idle or extrava- gant person procures support for his bad appetites, and is enabled to show himself off as a very fine fellow, at the expense of a humble-minded honest trader, who confines himself constantly to his busi- ness, and forbids himself almost every indulgence, In order that he may be able to pay everyone to whom he is indebted, and discharge all the othet duties of a good citizen. Now, if young people will bring their naturally generous feelings to bear upon this point, they will see that the debtor, and not the creditor, is alone worthy of execration. And they may be assured that where creditors show a severity to their debtors, it is generally either merited by the latter, or is dictated by a justifiable considera- tion of the danger into which they are thrown-by the non-payment of the money which is their due, , and Which they may be owing in their turn to some other person. In every ride there are, exceptions; but it is necessary to guard against the breaking down of great rules by allowing for trifling exceptions. Because good men sometimes incur debt, and become insolvent, through no fault of theirs, we must not infringe upon the majesty of the great maxim, that debt ought to be paid, and that its non-payment is an evil. Young people, if they wish to prosper in the world, will do well not to excuse all contraction of debt for the sake of the few who contract it innocently. They must have impressed forcibly upon their mines, that every pleasure in which they indulge themselves, without the reasonable prospect of paying for it, though it be but to the amount of one Fenny, is a step in error, and apt to be the beginning of their destruction. They must have it impressed upon their minds that no man of good feelings can enjoy the least comfort, if he be not conscious of working for, or being honestly come irto the possession of, fully as much as he spends. To persist in living beyond our incomes is to live a life of nishonesty, and to subsist on the industry of relatives, as is sometimes the case with the idle and the dissolute, is worse Still, for it involves an excess- ive meanness of spirit, ingratitude, and, hard heart- edness—thus adding depth to the crime, and will be sure to be visited some day with feelings of anguish and remorse.

A predominating error among the ;junior classes of society, is a disinclination to wait for a short time till they be enabled to compete in the enjoy- ment of luxuries with others they see around them, and who it is more than probable have toiled long and painfully before they arrived at their present apparently prosperous condition. This impatience of reaching a certain height in the ladder of fortune, without taking deliberation to mount a number of preliminary and difficult steps, cannot, indeed, be sufficiently reprehended where it occurs, as it leads to that fatal resource of incurring debts never to be paid, and that supposed harshness of creditors, which a disordered process of reasoning brings into view. I would here tenderly admonish the youthful part of the community to refrain from indulgences they can- not honestly command. Let them believe one who has had some experience, when he tells them that there is not the least cbance of the world running away from them; that the present generation of grown men will not consume all earthly enjoyments but will leave a boundless variety of every thing which can please the senses, or gratify an honour- able ambition. They need, therefore, be in no hurry whatever, and take time to build their fortune on a firm and secure basis. The rising generation cannot lay these things sufficiently to heart. They cannot be sufficiently taught, that suffering under the con- sequences of imprudently incurred debts does not necesssa.rily make them heroes—is not entitled to un- mingled sympathy, no more than a robber at the gallows is a martyr; hut that, while pity is perhaps due to them, as to all who err in this frail world, the larger share of sympathy ought to be bestowed on their unfortunate victims, the creditors, whose families may be suffering from their criminal follies, and who are apt to be by far the better and honester men.

SYRIAN HOSPITALITY.—In the travels of John Carte in the East, the following example of Syrian hospitality occurs, and was accepted, as well it might, by the author and his friends, with emotions of lively gratitude :—" We entered the populous town, and instead of making our way as usual to the caravanserai, we resolved to trust to the hospitality of the natives. After winding through several narrow, dirty, and precipitous streets, we at last had the pleasure of alighting at the door of a ' dwelling, to which a flight of steps conducted us. The household was a large one; several young and good-looking women formed part of it, who re- ceived us kindly, and set about in earnest to piepare the supper. The only objection to the luxury of this warm divan was, that all the mysteries of the cooking were obliged to be performed within the settle at the cheerful fire, over which, in intense earnestness, bent the forms of our Syrian hostesses, their dark eyes fixed not on conquest or mischief, but on an excellent omelet, and one or two other preparations. The tresses of their dark hair dropped at times so tear the blaze, as to threaten the destruction of that richest ornament of womaa. It needed not the strong fatigue of that day's journey, the drizzling rain, and the desolate town without, to enter with strong relish into the scene and its tempting accompaniments. ,The repast was at last ready; we would fain have shared it with the fair preparers, who had so well received the hostless stranger; but they declined, and stood calmly and silently gazing at the good will with which their viands were devoured. Their figures were slight and very well made, the complexion pale, but the features lively and expressive, with those insepar- able features, the raven hair and the dark eye."

Tim evil consequences of our crimes long survive their commission, and like the ghosts of the mur- dered, for ever haunt the steps of the malefactor. MoriAn principles are social-and universal. They form, in a manner, the party of human kind against vice and disorder, its common enemy. THERE is one thing calculated to develop or. he latent pedestrian ability a woman has in her, and that is, to be caught in a shower with her best bonnet on and no umbrella. ONE of the most ingenious processes which has lately come into vogue is that of giving to iron a silver surface, by first covering it with mercury and then silver by the galvanic process. THE liberty of using harmless pleasures will not be disputed ; but it is still to be examined what pleasures are harmless. The evil of any pleasure is not in the act itself, but in its consequences.

div.head: ?Letter to the Otittor.
div.p: ?Letter to the Otittor.

THE DISINFECTION OF DWELLING-HOUSES. Sir,—At the present time when we are visited by a serious outbreak of smallpox and scarlet fever, and with the cholera bacillus looming unpleasantly near us, the question will often arise as to the best means of disinfect- ing a room. The usual plan, and one recommended in the "Times "of last Saturday, is to burn sulphur on a tray, the windows and doors being closely shut. I should like to remind your readers that when sulphur burns a dioxide is formed which is n9t by itself a good disinfectant, and that it is of very little use to burn sul- phur in this manner. It is only when combined with water, forming sulphurous acid, that it becomes a dis- infectant, and though of course a small quantity is formed from the moisture naturally present in the at- mosphere it is altogether insufficient for the purpose. The best plan is to sprinkle the walls,ceiling, and floor with water, and to evaporate in a pan over au oil stove, or other convenient apparatus, water to the extent of three or four time 3 the weight of sulphur burned, and let the chinks,especially those near the floor, be carefully stopped. If chlorine is used instead of sulphur the same principle holds good. Water must be present.— Yours &C., . FREDERICK G. RUDDOCK, F.I C. Analytical and Consulting Chemist. Ist September, 1892.

div.head: UUNCOILY PARISH CHURCH.
div.p: UUNCOILY PARISH CHURCH.

Sir,—lf any former resident of Runcorn, after an absence from the town of a few year§,suddenly returned and paid a visit to the Parish Church, he would prob- ably be much struck by the improved appearance of that noble building and its immediate surroundings. He would notice that the ivy which formerly clung to the walls, at the risk of seriously damaging the fabric, had been all cut away. He would observe that the walks had been newly covered with gravel, and that the grass in the churchyard had been recently cut, and removed. He would also observe that the roof scented in go d repair, and upon inquiry would learn that it had been overhauled about a month ago, when the loose slates were fastened. Without having to exercise his judge- ment very much, he would be convinced that the paint on all the iron railings, and the iron work attached to all the church doors was not more than about 12 months old. Upon entering the church he would also find that many improvements and additions had been made since his last visit,and he would not.:e at a glance that, while pains had been taken to beautify the interior of the building, the comfort of the worshippers had not teen lost sight of. In short he would no doubt come to the conclusion that no one (pessimists and habitual grumb- lers excepted) would be likely to complain of the condi- tion of either the exterior or the interior of the sacred edifice.—Yours, Scc., .

div.head: PARISHIONER.
div.p: PARISHIONER.
RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

Sir,—ln the report of the last meeting of the Runcorn, Rural Sanitary Authority it is stated that Mr. Aaron gave notice that he would move the re-appointment of Mr. Farrington as Inspector of Nuisances at an increase of salary of £2O. Now, sir, I ask you, seeing that farmers are the heaviest ratepayers of the Authority, whether this is a fit and proper time for an Increase of salary to any public servant? Have they obtained such a good price for their produce up to the present, or are their prospects so very bright for the future, as to warrant anything of the kind ? I think not ? But, sir, I have watched the proceedings of Mr. Aaron at the Board and I have come to the conclus- ion that he is of that class" who rush in where angels fear to tread." I hope that every guardian will appear in his place, and vote against this increase of salary as uncalled for. Certainly it is another argument in favour of the ratepayers voting against the triennial election of guardians. I se l nothing has been done to fill up the vacancy caused by the death of Mr. Kirkham in the representa- tion of Weston. I suppose they are satisfied with Mr. Aaron. I think I have shown he is a host in himself of a certain kind ; but I certainly cannot congratulate the ratepayers of Weston on the economical tendencies of their representative.—l am, Sir, yours truly, September Ist, 1892.
EXAMINER.
MR. PEERS EMERGES.

Sir,—At last Mr. Peers is about to address himself to something practical. Emerging from the citadel of the unknown where we last left him, he steps forth to pat you on the back as a token of his admiration of "your -advocacy of the cause of humanity (?) in the treatment of animals."

Mr. Peers is rarely behind-hand in imputing motives. I had my own reasons for writing to you last week. Be is good enough to admit that, apparently, I have some acquaintance with the verses of Shelley, but thinks I show an entire ignorance of the man himself. Mr. Peers is welcome to such an opinion. A perusal of his letter, will convince anyone that whatever be his knowledge of Shelley, or of his writings, he is careful not to betray himself. Your correspondent is about to take up cudgels on be- half of the illused of the animal kingdom'. lam quite with him on such a matter. But lest he should fall accidentally into a species of pliarisaism, allow me to suggest that he has no sort of a monopoly of tender feelings by virtue of his being an evolutionist. The con- trast between the two parts of his letter is very marked ; so much so that many readers would at once draw the inference—perhaps the one Mr. Peers intended should be dz awn—that, while Mr. Butler as a Methodist was the supporter of" the crude imaginings of an age of ignor- ance and crass credulity," Mr. Peers as a sceptic de- voted himself to the alleviation of animal suffering and to the betterment of the human race. This is a good illustration of the method pursued by my friend. How- ever,if Mr. Peers will turn tea copy of the " Examiner " for January 16th, he will find there a leader by the Editor on the " Horrors of Sport " ; and if he will refer to the issue of Jan. 30th he will find a letter signed " Olding B," advocating the rights of the dumb crea- tion. If he requires any further information he may turn to" Sunrise" for August 13th. The amiable desire of your correspondent to see ma tenderly turned inside out by the poet Shelley is des- tined never to be gratified. In the first place, poets can- not turn anyone inside out, and, secondly, Shelley has been dead these seventy years. Perhaps Mr. Peers being neither a poet nor a thinker feels himself equal to the task—one cannot say. But he has certainly had the opportunity. And he may have again if he so desires. Any letter written by Mr. Peers is very racy reading. He certainly manages to infuse an appearance of wit and brilliancy into his writings. I take what the ordinary reader would consider a most effective retort, and, isolating it, ask Mr. Peer or anyone else to show me its relevancy. [" But Stay ! Great men are generally misunderstood by their generation says Mr. Butler. What a solace for talkative medrocrity !"] Is there the slightest connection between my statement and Mr. Peers' retort ? Yet it looks well and sounds better. I am afraid that Mr. Peers' armoury is complete with sounding words and showy sentences.—Yours truly, W. H. BUTLER. Wilderspool. •
MB. JOILN DIGNUM V. EVOLUTION: EVOLU- TION V. MR. JOHN DIGNIIM.

Sir,—Looking over a back copy of the " Examiner " I came across an article entitled "Mr. John Dignum on Evolution." This had escaped my notice at the time, but now, after our periodic attack of political fever is over, I propose to say a few words as to this most mis leading extract. First let me say that I have a most sincere respect for Mr. John Dignum despite his con- scientious onesidedness. I may say also that Mr. Dignum very kindly sent me a copy of his little brochure, but it is not with his pamphlet I fall out. Whatever *Tors may be in this will find decent burial there. But , the case is very different when these errors are restated in a public journal. I do not propose to go through the very dogmatic (and like most dogmas erroneous) state- ments of this extract. Take one or two as a sample of the rest. He has ten indictments against Evolution. Take 5-6. "No single fact of transmutation of one

species into another has ever been recorded in all history —a fact admitted by Dawin himself-6. The testimony of the rocks is entirely against it; as there are no inter- mediate forms between species and species left us,which must have been in myriads of examples, if this theory were true."

Here we have a notable example of the folly of nega- tive argument. Mr. John Di,gnum has never seen some- thing—therefore it cannot exist ! The man who never saw ice or felt the frost, has a difficulty in believing in its existence—but the hard fact is there navertheless,and no amount of denial will remove it. I have never had the pleasure of meeting Mr. John Dignum in our Museum ; otherwise I might have introduced him to one specimen which would have given 4 fiat contradiction to his most baseless assertion that "there are no inter- mediate forms between species and species." Here our author is surely kicking against the pricks. A creature that is at once a feathered lizard or a toothed bird is surely a transitional form, and a cast ot a fossil showing this may be seen in the bird-room of the Museum. Let Mr. Dignum de—as I have seen another scientific gentle- man do—go down on his marrow bones before this beau- tiful but ecclesiastic relic and make full confession and recantation. _

As to the "myriads of examples" which ought to have been left us according to our critic. I may say that transitional forms not being so well adapted to their environments would quickly become extinct after leaving the modification to their descendants. If these latter were better fitted to survive than the parent form they would speedily replace the less fitted form. Now, Mr. Dignum argues from the absence of transi- tional forms against evolution, so I, more reasonably I think, may justly maintain, the total breakdown of the creation theory from one known example of transition form. But we have not merely one but many such ; a toothed bird from the chalk and this feather- tailed flying lizard-bird, to say nothing of the fossil un- gulates—that splendid series of transitional forms— rhinoceros, hippopotamus, tapir, and the horse. These are facts which no amount of denial will explain away. Assuredly there can be no honour accrue to the Power that wrought all these wonders to say that He did it in a way that His works directly and flatly contradict! But it is the old, old tale the Book before the Maker. Truly the letter killeth. JOHN PEERS.

div.head: "AN EYE TO THE FUTURE."
div.p: "AN EYE TO THE FUTURE."

Sir,—Mr. Robert Davies at the licensing sessions on August 25th said :—"They (Messrs. Greenall, Whitley, and Co.) had no interest in the sale of spirits, and it was Rot to obtain an increase in the sale of beer that the present applications were being made. They had an eye to the future." Quite so, are they selling about ten barrels per week in the whole of the licenses they pro- pose to give up? If they are given up, the whole of that trade will go into their other houses near. They expect to do some 30 barrels per week in the two new licenses granted them ; so it would seem they are very kind and generous. Did the licensing committee believe them ? Now, I would offer a suggestion to Messrs. Greenall, Whitley, and Co. who want to do so much for the public. Buttermarket-st. is very narrow, and wants widening like Bridge-st. Let them give up the licenses and also the sites upon which they stand on one side of Butter- market-st., viz., the "Fox," " Crown and Sceptre," " Curriers' Arms," "White Bear," and " Rope and Anchor," for the two new licenses in Bewsey-road, and Battersby-lane. Then half the property required for the widening of that street would be in the hands of the Corporation. This would be giving something to the public. The two new licenses given them in Bewsev- road and Battersby-lane, with the monopoly they c&rry with them, are worth the whole lot from a brewer's point of view. 'lley also ought to compensate the exist- ing license holders in those districts for the trade they will take from them, on the basis of the Tory com- pensation scheme of the late lamented G evernment.— Yours, &c.,
A WARRINGTONIAN.
WARRINGTON LICENSING SESSION.

Sir,—ln looking over the results of the new applica- tions of the new licenses one is struck with the want of common fairness and justice in the results, viz., in the granting of two new licenses to Messrs. Greenall and Whitley and Co. for Bewsey-road and Battersby-lane, totally ignoring all the licenses already held in those dis- tricts, and giving a monopoly to Greenall, Whitley, and Co. to build two new gin palaces where they will be able to reap all the large profits arising from beer being consumed on the premises, and the sale of spirits, &c., by retail. Simply for what? Because they are the owners of a class of licensed property that they and the public can won do without, and by the giving up of which there will be no loss either to themselves or the public. It is strange that a lot of business men, with such clear beads as the licensing comtnitte profess to have should attempt to barter with something they don't understand. What right has a brewer because he has three houses in one street (where one house could do all the business required by the public in a legitimate way) to expect that he should have them transferred to a new district (mark you where that brewer has none, but some other brewer has) to improve the one left, making it worth more than the three put together in value , before the removals ? The property left can then be ' converted into shops that will bring considerably more revenue than they did as public-houses. Should the new licenses be confirmed by the full bench the licenses of the "Bear's Paw" and " Fox " will be two of the most valuable ever held in Warrington, as they will be put in d,stricts where it is an impossibility for anyone to compete with them on the same terms. We will examine the trucking of this great and would-be infallible licensing committee, who should study justice to other license holders as well as to Messrs. Greenall, Whitley, and Co. The "Crown and Sceptre" will absorb the " Curriers' Arms," simply In a sense robbing the In- land Revenue of the value of a license duty. This is nothing but a paper gain to the public. The" Fox "and the "Bear's Paw" trade will still be done by other houses belonging to Messrs. Greenall, Whitley, and Co. The " Black Horse " and " Whiteßear " are two beerhouses that, I have not the slightest doubt, the brewery com- pany would only be too glad to be without, from all ac- counts, and one member of the trade says he would not own them on any account. The off-license in Catharine- st., I presume, is to be be one of the two in Huyle-st., which I understand they don't own,and this immaculate licensing committee don't know about, as in their deci- sion they talk about giving up an off-license in Catharine- st. I have yet to learn that there is an off-license in Catherine-st. ; and how Messrs. Greenall, Whitley, and Co. will give up what there is not, is a riddle to me. Perhaps this great committee may try to create one for the occasion.

We hear a good deal about the licensee being too thick in Buttermarket-street, but by putting new licenses in Bewsey-road and Battershy-lane, on the sites belonginr to Messrs. Greenall, Whitley, and Co., they will then be quite as thick in those districts as in Buttermarket-st. Take Bewsey-road site. First, there is a license at the corner of Hoyle-street and Bewsey-road, so there is only Hoyle-street between it and the new license. Lower down in Hoyle-street there is another license immedia- tely adjoiniug, and Messrs. Greenall, Whitley, and Co's. new hotel, and a third at the corner of Pierpoint-street and Bewsey-road, just two dwelling-houses and a coal yard between it and the proposed hotel. Now there is 'also another license a few yards down Pierpoint-street, making four licenses, which mean that this new license is to be planted in the midst of four existing licenses which are quite sufficient for that portion of the district. In Itattersby-lane there is a license at the corner of Sharp-st., and :Battersby-lane ; just Sharp-st. between it and the proposed new gin palace. On the other side there is a license at the corner of fireball-st. and Battersby-lane about 30 yards off. It is very kind of Messrs. Greenall, Whitley and Co. to want to come here, as Mr. Bolton (in his evidence) stated that he took the precaution to secure the right of selling in Ti acres. His licenses were in existence in Battersby-lane long be- fore Messrs. Greenall, Whitley and Co. made an appli- cation for a license in that district. The inhabitants of Battersby-lane dread the time when this new gin palace will be completed,as it will attract all the barracks rowdies and the class of women who follow them, mak- ing an extra policeman necessary to preserve order. If the district were polled there would not be 20in favour of it. ONE WHO HATES JOBBERY.

div.head: FARCICAL PHILANTHROPY.
div.p: FARCICAL PHILANTHROPY.

Sir,—At the gathering of "the seven " in the Warrington Police Court, last week, an attempt was made to cure Warrington of some of its curses. Of course Mr. Robert Davies in his usual bland way must commence by introducing the trade, as a "legitimate business,' but when in the name of Messrs. Oreenall Whitley and Co. in entered upon a cal- culation of" give and take" the whole thing was too ludicuous to be taken in earnest. Even had the veteran Sir Gilbert himself—hovering over the grave—sent a messenger to say he was anxious " to alter the com- plexion of Buttermarket-street " and do away with some of the "dens of iniquity" he had granted there, one would have received it as an indication that his thoughts were in the right direction. But whoa a firm, Messrs. Oreenall, Whitley, and Co.,wych may—so far as the name is concerned—mean anybody or nobody, with- out personal responsibility, when this conglomeration, in the person of Mr. Davies' says, "if you grant us a license in Battersby-lane and one in Catherine-street, we will give up six public houses," and then pleads the case by iterating and reiterating" it. is not for the increased sale of beer," we shall have "no pecuniary advantage," "no emolument is looked for," why, sir, on the face of it there is something which looks very much like foolery and claptrap. There was honesty and candour in Mr. Bolton's appli- cation ; he admitted that a brewer wanted all the " houses "he could get. Mr. egar said—" We do not

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 3, 1892.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 3, 1892.

wish to insult the bench by offering a bribe, but if you will grant us this we will give up three other licenses as well as Messrs. Greenall, Whitley and Co. We do not wish to blink the fact that this for us will be a good business speculation." The offer of Messrs. Greenall, Whitley and Co. may seem very plausible,but,as Mr.Chorlton pointed out, two houses will be worked at very much less expense than six. Taking the managers alone, if they get £lOO each per year, that will be a net gain of £4OO, though probably a respgctable hotel keeper would ask for more than the manager of a place like the " Fox." Mr. Davies said if you grant our application the " Fox" will go, the Bear's Paw " will go, the " White Bear" and the "Black Horse" will go, indeed the whole six will go—perhaps because they don't" go "—and the con- gested condition of the town's centre will be relieved. But, sir, these places will "go " i.e., they will be cleared out whether this offered bargain be accepted or not. The near future will not tolerate them. I know there are men of position in this town who look upon these and the like as necessary evils, that they are resorts for prostitutes, and bad characters and that it is a good thing for the town, but to have licensed brothels would be better. But the day has gone for such blind and immoral opinions to find favour with any but every small portion of the community. These places are already doomed ; the proprietors know it, and I trust the magistrates who are doing their utmost to wipe a 1 terrible disgace off the town will not be hoodwinked by a promise that decrepit buildings and vanishing busi- nesses shall be forsaken for new pastures to be desolated and desecrated by erections which may be more beauti- ful achitecturally but none the less ruinous in their effects upon the population. Each member of. the bench occupies a tremendously responsible position ; duty binds upon them the neces- sity of getting to know all they can about the trade and itswork. I cannot but think there must have been a vast amount of ignorance, or the license for "iThe Lion" would not have been renewed without restrictions and conditions. Nearly a year ago Messrs. Walker and Sons' —another irresponsible mass —submitted plans to a small bench of magistrates, showing what they called" slight alterations "to be made. The plans have been carried ' out, but it would be difficult to imagine more extensive alteration; to say nothing of the increased facilities for drinking in" The Lion" yard—by which the market people have been robbed of their waiting room and must now sit in the vaults or the archway—a private door in Bridge-st., has been converted into a flaring gin palace entrance, and up " Ship Yard " an entirely new door opened. Many gentlemen in the town consider that un- justifiable advantage has been taken of the Licensing Committee, and would have put in a protest at the Brewster Sessions, but personal interests prevented any being willing to appear as witnesses. Had the facts of the case been fully known to the magistrates, I feel sure they possess such a sense of " justice " that the license of " The Lion "would not have been renewed without a promise from Messrs. Walker and Sons that they would close the" Ship Yard" entrance. The following facts may be useful in the future :- 1. The Ship Yard entrance cannot be necessary as "rho Lion" has so many other doors close by. 2. It is preposterous to expect the police to give such a place proper supervision. 3. Some years ago the "Ship Inn "—from which the yard takes its name—exactly opposite this new entrance was closed by the magistrates. 4. A person living in "Ship Yard" told me the neigh- bourhood was bad enough before, but since that door was opened it is a very hell. 5. Another inhabitant of the yard said "it has turned every house into a urinal." 6. Four weeks ago in "Ship Yard," at one o'clock on Sunday morning, ten panes of glass were smashed in a drunken squabble. The woman and her daughter liv- ing in the house are too poor to have them put in, and ever since the widow has had a windowless home.

Who is to protect the poor from having their homes made vile and their lives hellish through these drink shops ? It is all very well for Mr. Davl3 to tlay he Nfr.ltd not object to live next door to a public-house, and for Alderman Wright, .LP., to plead in Court on behalf of his tenants—without their consent—that a public-house might be erected close to their doors ; but when you think of their own residences such declarations are a hollow mockery. The people living in "Ship Yard" have as much right to claim protection of the Bench as any living in the most respectable parts of Warrington. If nothing more can be done now in "The Lion" case, sanely it is a legitimate thin.. to ask that a rail may be placed up each side of the dangerous steps of this " Ship-yard entrance to enable the little child- ren with cans, and the men and women who frequent the place, to get up and especially down without break- ing a limb. At Liverpool last week in consequence of structural alterations at the North Western Railway Hotel not having first been submitted to the Licensing justices, they postponed the renewal of the license, and the Chairman remarked • " You think because you are a big Railway Company you Can do what you like. We cannot discriminate between rich and poor." Had the magistrates of Warrington known the facts of the case, I cannot but think some such course would have been taken with " The Lion" license.—Yours, PRO BONO PUBLICo, THOMAS ROSS. 2, Palmyra Square, Warrington, Aug. 30th, 1892.

The subject of our portrait sketch this week is Lord Newton, better known in this neighbourhood as Colonel W. J. Legh, of Lyme Hall, Disley—and father of the Hon. T. W. Legh, M.P., for the Newton Division. Lord New ton was born at Ratcliffe Hall, Leicester, on the 19th December, 1828, and is there- fore in his 64th year. He was .ducated at Rugby, and in 1848 he joined the 21st Royal Scots Fusiliers. He served through the Crimean Campaign of 1854-5, ard was present at the battles of Balaclava, and In- kermann and the Siege of Sebastopol. He is in pos- session of the Crimean medal with three clasps,and of the Turkish medal for the campaign. With the rank of Captain, he retired from the Army in 1855. In 1856 he married Emily Jane, third daughter of the Rev. Charles Nourse Wodehouse, Canon ot Norwich. -There are four children -issue of the marriage living, viz: Thomas Wodehouse Legh, M P., born 1857, Gilbert Legh, Lieutenant in the 2nd battalion Grenadier guards, Dulcibella Jane and Mable Maud Legh. In 1858 Lord Newton joined the Lancashire Yeomanry hussars, and having com- manded the regiment for live years, retired in May, 1 ' 1885, with permission to retain rank and uniform. Since January, 1873, he has been Honorary Colonel of the 4th Cheshire Rifle Volunteers. On the death of his elder brother, Thomas Burnaby Legh, in 1855, he became heir presumptive to

TELE LEGIT ESTATES, and in May, 1857, he came into possession of the estates on the death of his uncle, the late Thomas Legh, of Lyme. The estates are situated in the counties of Cheshire and Lancashire, and comprise Lomething like 8,000 acres in each county. To show how the estates came into possession of the Legh family, it may be stated that the township of Lyme, which is part of the Cheshire estate, con- tains about 4,000 acres. Formerly it was part of the Macclesfield Forest, and was granted by letters patent dated January 4th, 1398, from Richard 11.,t0 Piers de Legh, and Margaret, his wife (only daugh- ter and heiress of Sir Thomas Danyers, of Bradley and Appleton, Chester), who at the battle of Cressy, rescued the standard of the Black Prince, and took prisonlr the count de Tankerville, chamberlain to Pretsali Ring. Fr 4!.ci uvices, Piers de Legh was allowed a grant of 40 marks per annum, until he should receive a grant of land worth £2O per annum. In 1398 the grant of Lyme (then valued at ..£2O per annum) was made in substitu- tion for the grant of 40 marks. Piers de Legh, son of the above, fought at the battle of Agincourt in 1415, and was then knighted. By his marriage with Joan, daughter and heiress of Sir Gilbert de Haydock, of Ilaydock, Lancashire, he acquired ex- tensive estates in that neighbourhood. Their son, Peter de Legh, was engaged in the battle of Wake- field, December, 1460,where he was knighted. Their grandson, Piers, married in 1467. Ellen, daughter of Sir John Clifton, by his wife Katherine, sister of the first Earl of Derby. In August, 1482, he was knighted at Iluttonfield, near Berwick-on-TweeA. It will thus be seen how the Lyme and Ilaydock estates, now the Legh estate, came into the posses- sion of the Legh family.

LYME HALL, THE RESIDENCE, is built of stone, in the form of a quadrangle. The earliest portion of the building dates from the bcginning of the fifteenth century, but large ad- ditions were made in the early part of the 17th I century, the new portion being of the lonic order of architecture. These additions were carved out by Giacomo Leoni, a noted Italian architect of that day. Other additions have since then been made. The stables are also of stone and of a quadrangular form, and have been built by the present represent- ative of.the Legh family at a very large outlay. In the park are herds of red and fallow deer, and up to a very recent date it contained a herd of wild cattle similar to those at Chillingliam. From con- tinuous inter-breeding, however, they have become extinct.

T lia plus, which is very extensive, is a favourite resort for pleasure-seekers from the large manufacturing dis- tricts in its vicinity, and during the Easter and Whitsuntide holidays, is visited by many thousands of people daily. The Lancashire estates comprise the important and valuable collieries at Haydock, and a large area of land at Warrington, together with the Newton racecourse. The "Barony of New- ton and Fee of Mairerfield," of which Lord Newton is the lord, comprises 17 townships lying between Wigan on the north and Warrington on the south. The Lancashire family residences (Haydock Lodge and Golborne Park) are now let. Lord Newton is a deputy-lieutenant for the counties of Lancashire and Cheshire, a patron of three Church livings,mas- ,ter of the Lyme Harriers, and a member of the Jockey Club. In Parliament he represented South Lancashire from 1859 to 1865, East Cheshire from 1868 to 1885,and unsuccessfully contested the Hyde division of Cheshire in 1886. In 1887 he made an °E'er of a piece of land to the Newton Commis- sioners for a park, but the idea of a park being re- tr..ed by the ratepayers, he gave in substitution a p'ece of land for a public hall, and £5OO towards its erection.

Tim Flag BRIGADE.—On Saturday afternoon the Lymm Fire Brigade, under the superintendence of Mr. Moston, captain, turned \out for practice. The bell was rung at three o'clock and the men, after assembling at the Local Board offices, proceeded with their engines to the Dam, where they stayed for a short time. They afterwards practiced in the villaga,and their manceuvres were watched by a large number of people.
