div.p: CADISTIEAD.

MBE's BII3LE CLASS.—A popular service, in connection with this class, was held in the Wesleyan Chapel, on Sunday afternoon, There was a fair attendance. The speakers were Mr. W. H. Kelshaw k Bridgewater-street Mission, Manchester). and Mr. J. C. Elder, and these gave capital addressee. Solos were well sung by Miss M. Johnson, Mr. J. Wright, and Mr. Kelshaw. The leader of the class is Mr. J. Wood, and the secretary,Mr. Grubb. There was no collection. THA MEHTING.—On Monday evening, a tea meeting was held in the schoolroom, Lord-st., followed by a meeting in the Wesleyan Chapel. At this meeting the Rev. B. Yates, who will depart this week for his new circuit, gave a financial, statement of the beautifying fund. The total amount raised was£346 15s. 2d. The meeting was addressed by Mr. Wood and Mr. Walton. The Rev. B. Yates was presented with a handsome dressing-case by MicA,. Gatenby, on behalf of the choir and orchestral band. The rev, gentleman duly acknow- ledged the present. Solos were sung by Miss M. A. Toft and Miss Johnson. There was a good attendance.

div.head: CROFT.
div.p: CROFT.

INDUCTION OF THE Naw RACTOR.—On Monday after- noon. the Rev. Henry Isaac Wadeson, M.A., the newly appointed hector of Christ Church, Croft, was formally inducted the living by the Rev. Canon Penrhyn, rural dean, the Rector of Winwick. The events not being publicly known, only the rev-, gentlemen, the church- wardens (Messrs. William Priestner and Richard Turner) Mrs. Wadeson, the Misses Penrhyn, and several members of the congregation were present. The new Rector, having received the keys of the church doors from the churchwardens, unlocked the south-east door, and entered the church, after which he ascended the belfry and tolled the bell. He then returned to the door and admitted those present, when they proceeded through the church to the vestry, where the documents of the induction were signed by the new Rector, churchwar- dens, &c., and the proceedings terminated. It is expected that the Rector will read himself in at the after- noon service on Sunday next. FLOWER SHow,—The first annual flower show was held at the Joiners' Arms Hotel on Saturday, when prizes were offered by the proprietor, Mr. S. Daxon. There was, however, only a small number of entries, though some of the specimens exhibited were very fine ones, considering the season. The exhibits were staged in the large clubroom, which was well adapted for an exhibition of this kind, and the tables had been nicely arranged for the exhibits by Mr. S. Daxon, the proprie- tor, the staging of the exhibits being effectively carried out by Mr. A. Dixon. The judges were Mr. William Butters, head gardener to Mr. S. S. Brown, C.C., of Golborne ; and Mr. Thomas Jolley, gardener and nurseryman, of Hermitage Green, Croft, whose decisions gave general satisfaction. There was a fair attendance during the time the show was open on Saturday and Sunday. rhe following is a list of the prize-winners in the order of merit :—Specimens of cut flowers. Three roses, distinct :1, Fairhurst ;2, S. Daxon. Three double dahlias, distinct: 1 and 2, T. Dixon. Three pompon° dahlias, distinct: 1, T. Dixon. Three single dahlias, distinct : 1, S. Daxon. Three cactus dahlias, distinct :1, E.. Monks; 2, S. Daxon. Three asters.dis- tinct 1. S. Daxon; 2, E. Monks. Five stocks (spikes), any variety ;1, S. Daxon; 2, T. Fairhurst. Bouquet, any variety ;1, S. Daxon. Three window plants (con- fined to persons not having a green house), including single and double geranium and pelargonium : 1, M.' Dixon ;2, E. Monks. One double fuchsia; 1, E. Monks. One calceolaria ; 1, E. Monks.

div.head: MARRIAGE OF LORD GREY; DE RITT.HYN.
div.p: MARRIAGE OF LORD GREY; DE RITT.HYN.

The marriage of Lord Grey de Ruthyn, of Walton Rail, Lytham, to Miss Isobel Foster, thughter of Mr, James Foster, of Craneborne Hall, Windsor, was solem- nised on Thursday, at St. Peter's Church, Cianley Gard- ens, London, in the presende of a large and distinguished gathering. Among the guests were the Duke of Nor- tolk, the Marquis of Bute, the Marchioness Ailsa, the Earl and Countess of Loudoun, the Cbuntess of Guild- ford. The bride who was given away by her father, wore a costume of white cluehesse satin with a train and flounces of fine old Brussels point and tulle veil.

div.head: MR. LEGH, MP.. AT GATtSWOOD.
div.p: MR. LEGH, MP.. AT GATtSWOOD.

Lady Gerard, ruling councillor and dame presi- dent of the Garswood Habitation of the Primrose League, gave a garden part) in Garswood Park, Ashton-in-Makerfield, on Saturday afternoon, and, despite the unfavourable weather, it was largely attended by associates of the League and the prin- cipal Conservatives of the Newton Division. The band of the Lancashire Hussars was present, and, under Bandmaster Batty, discoursed a choice selection of music. Lord and Lady Gerard received the guests, and amongse those present were Sir Humphrey and Lady De Trafford and Miss Franklin, the Hon. T. W. Legh, M.P., Mr. T. Pearson, J.P. (chairman of the Newton Division Conservative Association), Major Reif (ex- ruling councillor) and Mrs. Relf, Commander and Mrs. Royse, Mr. R. Stone, Dr. and Mrs. Street, Mrs. Webster (ruling councillor of the Sutton Habita- tion), Mr. and Mrs. Wood (Newton-le-Willows), Mr. W. Valiant, and Mr. Rowe (hon. secretary). Addressing the assembly, Mr. Ugh said he felt that he was surrounded by so many friends that he cs•uld not refrain from expressing to them his gratitude for the magnificent support accorded him at the general elec- tion. It was to his supporters that he was specially grateful, but if there were any of his opponents present. ' lie hoped they, would accept his condolence upon the de- feat which was inflicted upon them on that occasion. (Laughter.) He should always feel indebted to his sup- porters for their great exertions on his behalf, and he now promised to serve them to the best of his ability. He felt the honour they had conferred on him all the more because, despite the adverse influences which were at work, the Conservative majority in that division had been increased. In that respect they had not only seta good example to the Conservatives of Lancashire, but to the country at large, and their victory was all the more valuable because it was not obtained by reckless pro- mises. He had pursued a straightforward course, and while expressing the hope that he might long represent that consti.,uency, be heartily thanked one and an for the magnificent support accorded him at the recent elec- tion. (Cheers.)—A miscellaneous programme of amuse- ments was provided, and at the close Lady Gerard was heartily thanked for the entertainment provided.

The•lpswich magistrates on Wednesday extinguished a public-house and a beerhouse license, considering that they were no longer required. A number of men were remanded at Lambeth Police Court, on Wednesday, on a charge of having committed extensive long Orm _frauds in -different parts of the country. As Mrs. Troode, wife of Colonel Troode, of Stratford, Exeter, was walking with another lady to the meet ot the Dulverton Foxhounds, a wasp became entangled in her hair. Its efforts to free itself so startled Mrs. Troode that she fainted. She recovered, but immediately ex- claiming to her companion," 1 am dying," sank back dead.

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL.
EXPECTED TRAFFIC.

Whether or no they are over sanguine time alone will show, but it is beyond doubt that the pro- moters of the Ship Canal expect big things in the way of traffic when—there is much meaning in that little word—the waterway has been cut and made navigable. At this time, when shareholders in the concern, and especially those who are of comparatively bumble means, are sorely troubled about the rapid way in which their money is dis- appearing, it may be comforting to them to point to what the promoters expect to secure in the way of traffic when once their difficulties are over.

It does not require more than a cursory review of the proposed dock accommodation of the canal to make you feel sure that the promoters entertain little if any doubt as to the extensive custom they anticipate becoming theirs when the canal is made. At the Manchester end alone there will be a length o". quays of over five miles, a quay acreage of 132 acres, and a dock water area of 114 acres. These figures, of cuurse, include Salford. Already births are being allotted to regular trading lines, it being officially on record that applications have been made by nearly all the regular lines running from this city. At Manchester a jetty will be set apart exclusively for the fruit trade, and there will be other jetties at Salford to accommodate trade from North America and East India. Then again,there are the proposed docks at Warrington, the existing ones at Runcorn, as well as traffic facilities at Ellesmere Port and other points. The railway companies, it is claimed, are preparing to obtain communication with the canal, which will also be tapped by the new line to be made from east to west. Much stress is laid on the enormous industrial population of the northern and midland counties, with which the canal will be connected by railways and other smaller canals, and it is anticipated that large in- dustries will be established on the banks of the canal that will develop trade still further, altogeth- er in addition to the through traffic between , Manchester and the ocean. Within a radius of a dozen miles from the Exchange at Manches- ter there is a population of over 2,000,000 and a ' map published in lleywood's Guide shows the ' proximity of a much greater proportion of this population to Manchester than to any other port. A triangle traced on the map, formed by way of Stockport, Preston, and Leeds, through giving an area of only 713 square miles, has within its radius a greater manufactnring population than any area of equai size in the world. It is hoped that a orofitable trade will come from these manufacturing centres, and it is further claimed that an area of 7,500 square miles, with a population of 7i millions, can be served by the Ship Canal with equal, if not better facilities than at present exist. From Board of Trade re- turns, it appears that the output of coal in a radius nearer to the canal than it is to any other ocean steamer port is greater than the total output of Northumberland, Durham, and South Wales com- bined. The coalfields of Lancashire and South Yorkshire, the saltfields of cheshir,), the chemical works of South-west Lancashire, and the COal, iron, and pottery trades of Staffordshire are looked upon to provide a steady return, and a good deal is ex- pected from the construction of the Lancashire, Derbyshire, and East Coast Line, which will place the canal in direct communication with the west. The maximum charges upon the canal are only about one half of the cost of carriage between the ship at Liverpool and Manchester, reducing, it is said, the cost of transit by 50 per cent. As is well known,the opened portion of the canal is now earning something, as also is the Bridge- water Navigation system, but it is only "a drop in the bucket when compared to the expenditure , that la going on. In August, 1887,the company ac- quired by purchase the undertakings of the Bridge- water Canal Company and the Mersey and Irwell Navigation, and thus became possessed of a large series of basins, docks, and warehouses at Runcorn. They have also become the proprietors of a fleet of powerful steam tugs, which tow seagoing vessels. The port mentioned has seven wet docks ands. grid- iron, 150 ft. by 40ft., and in time the Ship Canal will enable vessels to enter the docks at any state of the tide. It is estimated that on an average 60,000 craft yearly ascend or descend the Mersey estuary by this sea gateway, and the imports and oxports, coastwise and foreign, show an average of about 500,000 tons. The principal exp.srts consist of salt and coals, but the imports are of a more miscellaneous character. In addition, there is a large barge , traffic between Runcorn, and, among other places, Widnes, Garston, Ellesmere Port, and Liverpool. Roundly speaking, some 800,000 tons of merchan- dise are yearly conveyed on the Bridgewater canals undertaking between Manchester and this city. This undertaking, now being profitably worked by the Canal Company, has a total effective mileage of over 43 miles. It, includes the Bridgewater Canal, originating at Manchester, and having its terminal at Runcorn; the Worsley and Leigh Canal, starting at Stratford and finishing at Leigh; the Preston Brook Canal, a continuation of the Bridgewater Canal to the Trent and the Mersey; the canal from Runcorn to Weston; and one originating at Throstle Nest, Manchester. The various inland navigations that are in direct communication with this system of canals,which practically means in communication with the Ship Cinal, give a large tonnage, and traverse the industrial district of which Manchester is the centre. These inland navigations I include the Leeds and Liverpool, the Weaver, the Shropshire Union, and about a dozen others. The Shropshire Union undertaking is an amalgamation of canals, and is leased in perpetuity to the London and North-western Railway Company. It has a total effective mileage of over 200 miles and on the main line is in communication with Wolverhampton and Birmingham. The Weaver Navigation has its commencement at Winsford, and, by way of North- wich, passes through The centre of the salt district. It terminates at the Weston Point docks, after run- ning a course of 20 miles' those docks being situated on the line of the canal. The exports of salt amount to about 1,000,000 tons yearly, and various chemical products are also exported. From the various avenues of trade mentioned, the Canal Company expect a profitable traffic, in addition to the exten- sive traffic movement of the Manchester district itself, and hope to be able to pay interest on bor- rowed capital and a decent percentage to the share- holders before the lapse of very many years after the opening of the canal.

div.head: WARRINUTON AND THE SHIP CANAL.
div.p: WARRINUTON AND THE SHIP CANAL.

1 At a meeting of the General Purposes Committee of the Warrington Corporation, held on Monday afternoon, a conversation took Ogee as to the con- struction of the Warrington Docks. The opinion seemed to be generally held that there was not much likelihood of the docks being made within a reasonable time by the Ship Canal Company. The Corporation have power to construct the docks if they felt disposed to do so, but no decision as to the desirability or otherwise of the Corporation un- dertaking the work was come to.

div.head: WARRINGTON BANK R U Y.I2CY COURT.
div.p: WARRINGTON BANK R U Y.I2CY COURT.

FRlDAY.—Before Mr. Ridgway, registrar_ Rs. Tnos. LAWLESS.—Thomas Lawless, fishmonger, Corporation-street and Market Place, came up for his adjourned examination. There were no questions of importance put to the bankrupt, and the examination was further adjourned till the 23rd inst. RE. EIENRY BENT.—Henry Bent, farmer, Burtonwood, came up for his preliminary examination. His gross liabilities are £834 es.Bd.,and the deficiency £294 138.1 d. The official receiver's observations on the bankruptcy 'are I_—The bankrupt filed his own petition, and at the date of the receiving order there were four County Court summonses pending against him, and other County Court actions had been commenced; and a distraint for rent had been levied. Since 1887 ,he has been a tenant 0 Hall-lane Farm, Bnrton- wood, which he entered without capital. He admts that he first knew of his insolvency about 2years ago, though nearly all his present liabilities are mainly for loans ; the remainder are for goods. The bankrupt admits that he kept no books of account whatever, and alleges that in conseqtv-,nee he is unable to account for the deficiency beyond Ovine estimates of the losses he has sustained by the failure of crops, by the death of live stock, and by the forced sale of his property and effects in bankruotcy.—The bankrupt was subjected to a lengthy examination by Mr. Patter, the assistant official receiver, and in the course of this he stated that after finding himself insolvent he continued business be- cause he thought hesaw his way cl ar to paying off his creditors and if he had had an average crop last year •he could 'have done so, but the crops were damaged by the weather both that and the previous year.

A young man named Rogers became entangled in the machinery at Mr. Williams's leather works, Romsey, on Monday morning, and was killed. A suicidal mania is prevalent at Trieste, and in the past ten diys 16 persons have takf n their lives. Most of the suicides were due to love affairs or to mental cUrangement caused by the great heat.
LATEST NE WS.
There are now no unfavourable symptoms in the con- dition of Mr. Winterbuttom, M.P.
CRICKET.
Players 61 for one wicket. DISASTER IN AMERICA. 26 PERSONS DROWNED.
A Central News telegram from New York says :—The passenger steamer Western Reserve has been wrecked on Lake Superior. Twenty-six of those on board were drowned.
SUSPENSION OF A LONDON BANK.

The London and General Bank, Limited, 20, Bridge- Row. E.C., has suspended payment. There is no excite- ment outside the bank at present, and two policemen keep the pavement clear. The directors are Messrs. .1. S. Balfour, M.P. (chairman), W. Blewitt, Mr. G. E. Brook, G. Dibley, S. R. Pattison, and R. Revett. The company's authorised capital is £1,000,000, in shares five pounds each.

div.head: TERRIBLE SCAFFOLD ACCIDENT.-NINE MEN KILLED.
div.p: TERRIBLE SCAFFOLD ACCIDENT.-NINE MEN KILLED.

KOENIGSBERG, THIIRSDAT.—A scaffolding, which had been erected at the old Castle here, for the purpose of effecting repairs to the building fell in to-day. Twelve workmen engaged in the repairs were precipitated to the ground, eight of whom were killed on the spot,while of the remaining four extricaied alive on died on the way to the hospital.

div.head: FORGING A BILL OF EXCHANGE.
div.p: FORGING A BILL OF EXCHANGE.

At Cardiff, yesterday, George Colquhoun (Messrs. Maun, George, and Co.'s manager) was further charged with forging a bill of exchange foi £5,421. Mr. Ingle - dew, for the prosecutor, said that the accused opened an account with the local branch of Lloyd's bank in April last. Subsequently, he discounted with that bank the bill in question,endorsed "George Colquheun and L. Wood," and drawn by the accused. It transpired that the signature "L. Wood " was forged. THE GLADSTONE COW. ITS POST-MORTEM VALUE.

The carcase of the mad cow from which Mr. Gladstone had such a narrow escape at Hawarden, has beer the subject of considerable speculation. A local butcher boughit the hide for £2, and sold it immediately for £5. The marksman who shot the animal has taken the head, horns, and hoofs to Chester for preservation, and has al- ready refused £lO for the trophy. The teeth are said to have found a ready market at half-a-crown each. THE ALLEGED OUTRAGE IN WALES. EXTRAORDINARY CTIFESSION, The Welsh police have spent three days searching the mountains for the assailant who, it is alleged, made a brutal assualt upon Miss Jones, of Tyissa Farm, Bedwas, lancing her face and arms with a knife, and otherwise assaulting her. Miss Jones has made a full confession to the police, stating that all her wounds were self-inflicted. The explanation of her extraordinary conduct was that life had been rendered unendurable to her at Bedwas because her lover had recently left the neighbourhood. She hoped that by the sensational ruse she adopted her parents would be frightened and would allow her to procure a situation in the vicinity of her lover's new residence. 'The girl's confession has created a great pensatian in the district, and the police and inhabitants are glad the mystery is solved.
THE CHOLERA EPIDEMIC. FIRST CASE IN CHESHIRE.

In consequence of the regulation issued by the United States Government, the Inman and international Steam- ship Company announce that they will, until further notice, discontinue carrying steerage passengers. An Exchange telegram states that a woman died yes- terday from cholera at Bollington, near Macclesfield. This is said to be tlre first case in Cheshire. . . .
Yesterday another of the cholera-stricken emigrants in Liverpool died, this being the second death.

IMPROVEMENT IN PARIS. PARIS, FRIDAY.—The returns for yesterday of the cholerine epidemic in Paris show a decided improvement, fresh cases numbering only fifteen and deaths three. 2,722 DEATHS IN RUSSIA. • • • •

ST. PETERSBURG, Fn illAY.—According to official cholera returns issued this morning, 5,273 cases of cholera and 2,722 deaths occurred on the 13th ult, in the whole of Russia. In St. Petersbutg there were 144 cases and 54 deaths, while 58 patients recovered. NEW YORE. FLUDAY.—The Board of Health reports a suspected case of cholera in this city. The patient is a Russian who recently arrived hers from Europe.

div.head: MURDER AND SUICIDE.
div.p: MURDER AND SUICIDE.

A terrible tragedy occurred at Newport, Mon., on Sunday evening. Emma Conibear, wife of a railway haulier, cut the throat of her only child, Albert Wm. Conibear, and then severed her own windpipe. The husband found them both dead. The husband and wife were respectable people, and had only been married two years.

div.head: MASTER TAILORS' LOCK-OUT.
div.p: THE MASTER TAILORS' LOCK-OUT.

The secretary of the Cardiff branch of tho Amalgam- ated Society of Tailors has received a telegram from the general secretary stating that the Scotch employers ab- solutely refuse to lock-out, and that two large Man- chester and three Sheffield firms have withdrawn the lock-out. South Wales towns affected by the lock-out are Cardiff, Pontypool, and Blaine.
THE BROGEWATER LOCK CATAS- TROPHE AT RUNCORN.

Last night, Mr. Dobson, deputy coroner, held an inquest at the Burial Board Office, Runcorn, on the body of Francis King, a navvy who was found under the ruins of Bridgwater Lock, of the Ship Canal, at Runcorn, on Thursday morning. It will be remembered that on the let Feb. of this year, the walls of this lock collapsed during a violent storm and many men had very narrow escapes. The deceased was reported missing, and it was not until the removal of the debris took place that his body was found. A verdict of:" Accident al death" was recorded.

div.head: HOIST FATALITY AT WIDNES.
div.p: THE HOIST FATALITY AT WIDNES.

On Wednesday at the Widnes Accident Hospital, before Mr. S. Brighouse, an inquest was held touch- ing the death of James McAllister, who died on Saturday from injuries sustained at Messrs. Gossage and Sons' works the same day. Charles McAllister, father of deceased, living at 107 Mersey-road, said the deceased was 13 years of age and was employed as a labourer at Messrs. Gos- sage's works.— Edward Haigh, foreman of the wrapping department, said that he knew de- ceased had been working there between 18 months, anti two years, as a cutter and wrap- per. He had no business to go to the hoist. On hearing a scream he ran in the direction of the hoist, and took deceased out of the cage.—William Hague, als& foreman packer, said he had to look after the bays. The deceased was engaged in the packing department, and had no right to touch the hoist.—After a deliberation which lasted about 20 minutes, the jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death." They at the same time expressed the opinion that a competent person ought to be put in charge of the hoist.

div.head: PENKETH.
div.p: PENKETH.

ACCIDENT TO A BOY. On Saturday an accident happened to a boy named Tucker. It seems a number of boys were in the act of fishing in a pit, called "Spring pit," when he accidentally fell in, and had it not been for a boy named Denton, who was close at hand, Tucker would probably have been drowned. FRIRNDs' SCTIOnI. TRIP. On Thursday the annual • ,ip of the teachers and scholars of the Friend,' ..,chool took place. The scholars, under the s"?erintendence of Mr. J. T. Gumersall, headmast, and the teachers, proceeded to Appleton, in Coeshire, where the day was pleasantly spent. The weather was fine, though cloudy. The party arrived home about eight p.m.

The Ottoman Government has issued adenial, couch- ed in the most emphatic terms, of the statements pub- lished in a 13e1gia0 paper that it had instigated the Arah rising near Lake Tanganvika as the commencement of a holy war. The allegation is characterized as a malici( us invention.

div.head: STIOCIIING TRAGEDY IN DUBLIN.
div.p: STIOCIIING TRAGEDY IN DUBLIN.

On Thursday, in Dublin, a well-known keeper of dl5 orderly houses, Mrs. Margaret Noble, was remanded charged with the manslaughter of PDIly Parker, an F. fortunate. It was alleged that when deceased was lying ill in bed the accused pulled her on the floor, knocked her down two flights of stairs, and then kicked her. The poor creature afterwards died in the hospital.

div.head: -4,- A WHOLESALE DISASTER NARROWLY
div.p: -4,- A WHOLESALE DISASTER NARROWLY
AVERTED.
THREE LIVES LOST.

EXTRAORDINARY FEAT BY AN ENGINE. NEW YORE, THURSDAY.—A terrible disaster was narrowly averted on the Hudson River Railroad this morning. A drawbridge on the line near Hamburg WaS being closed after a boat had passed, and a Op of several feet still remained, when a fast newspaper train froin New York approached at the rate of sixty miles an hour. The engine jumped the gap, but the rear end of the tender dropped, and became jammed, thus checking the progress of the train. The cars immediately be- hind were, however, forced one upon the other by their impetus, and completely shattered. The engineer, fire: man, and mail clerk were killed. and the conductor and one of the train attendants injured. The same draw* bridge was the scene of a frightful accident twenty year ago.

div.head: _ THE FRODSHAM OUTRAGE.
div.p: _ THE FRODSHAM OUTRAGE.

PRISONER AGAIN REMANDED. On Thursday morning, at Frodsham, Charlc.s Bundle's navvy, was again brought up on remand charged with_ attempted murder. It is alleged that after a few months' absence prisoner returned to the Ship Canal huts, on Frodsham Marsh, and savagely attacked a 'woman named Mary Dukes, his former landlady, with a poker, striking ker several times on the head and rendering her unconscious. Dr. Bryant, of Helsby, stated that the woman was still unable to appear, but she would in able to attend in a week. On the application 01 Police-sergeant Doyle, Mr. Alfred Thmnas rr manded the prisoner for another week. The accused -g a powerfully built man of 55 yea,-s, and his head still bears the mark of the blow with a mallet which a° effectively prevented his escape after his murderous attack on Mrs. Dukes. The assault is attributed to j th e.alousy, the prisoner being known as e , wort:o4l boss lodger."

THE RUNCORN WESTON AND HALTON WATER- WORKS COMPANY. NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN that an EXTRA- ORDINARY GENERAL MEETING of the shareholders of the RUNCORN WESTON and HALTON WATERWORKS COMPANY will be held at the COMPANY'S OFFICES in the PUBLIC HALL RUNCORN on MONDAY the NINETEENTH DAY of SEPTEMBER, 1892, at three o'clock in the afternoon for the purpose of considering and deciding as to the terms and conditions (if any) upon which the Company will allow the Corporation of Liverpool to supply water to the Manchester Ship Canal company within or so as to be used within the limits for the supply of water authorised by the Runcorn Weston and Halton Water Works Act 1865. At this Me-ting the Directors will lay before the Shareholders the draft of a ' deed:of Agreement which has been provisionally assented to I by them on behalf of the Euncorn Weston and Halton Water I Works Company and by the Corporation of Liverpool and the Manchester Ship Canal Company embodying the terms and conditions upon which it is proposed that the Corporation of Liverpool shall be allowed to supply water to the Manchester Ship Canal Company within or so as to be used within the limits aforesaid. Dated this Ist day September. 1892. By oraer of the Directors JOHN BRUNDRIT, Chairman of Directors. WILLIAM F. SALKELD Secretary.

The Hotel, where there is every accommodation for visitors, is easily accessible by road and rail from the above-mentioned and other important manufacturing towns in Lancashire and Cheshire, and the various attractions and amusements afforded by this pleasant resort draw together large concourses of pleasure-seekers, particularly during the summer months. For further particulars apply to the owner. B. W. SANKEY Esq.. Croft; the Auctioneer. Warrington ; or to Messrs. ROBERT DAVIES, RIRKCONNEL, DAVIES, AND BURGESS Solicitors, Warrington. August, 1692.
